articles.full_text:
THE election results in America this week portend a sea change, and they have important ramifications for Pakistan. The Democrats have taken both the House and the Senate in a rout that reached Texas and Kansas. Anger over living costs, tariffs, and the war on Iran all played their part. For the remaining two years of his term, President Donald Trump will face a Congress armed with subpoena power and eager to use it.
This is no distant affair for us. Much of the world has spent two years trying to cope with Trump. Meanwhile, the leadership in Pakistan flamboyantly embraced him, though let’s not underestimate how well that worked. It got us lower tariffs, a White House lunch, and, above all, a central role when the Iran war needed an exit ramp. The question now is what that embrace will cost us as the man on the receiving end of it begins to lose his grip on Washington.
Pakistan has veered too close to Trump, and this might not go down well in the near future. The April ceasefire that we helped broker was a genuine achievement, and I said so at the time. The memorandum that followed in June has since collapsed, but the credit earned in those weeks still stands. Yet all of it could well come to be overshadowed by the single act of having nominated Trump for a Nobel Peace Prize in so conspicuous and overly generous a manner.
Showering the man with extravagant praise in highly public settings might have worked to win him over in the short term. But the praise kept coming long after the point had been made. In September, he was telling the UN General Assembly that our prime minister credits him with saving 30 million lives. Last month, on the day the Nobel went to someone else, the prime minister was on X lauding his “historic role” in South Asia. These things do not expire. There is a risk they get tagged onto Pakistan in the years to come, once Americans settle on their verdict of this presidency.

What looks clever in one season reads very differently at a hearing in the next.

Even more dangerous is the fact that the Trump family’s business dealings might come under congressional investigation. Reuters reported in September that probes could begin as early as February, with Trump-linked crypto firms of particular interest. Senator Richard Blumenthal, who is in line to chair an investigations panel, has promised to use his subpoena power. The same senator was asking questions about World Liberty Financial’s Pakistan deal in May last year.
If any ties lead back here, they could tie the country to the affair; the threads are already in public view. In January, our finance minister signed a memorandum with a World Liberty affiliate concerning its USD1 stablecoin. In September, the defence ministry placed a limited order with Powerus, a drone company in which two of Trump’s sons are investors. No wrongdoing has been established. The White House denies any conflict of interest, and as of July the stablecoin deal had produced no known transactions at all. But I have described that memorandum as an instrument of access, and access is exactly what investigators will want to look into. What looks clever in one season reads very differently at a hearing in the next.
These risks, however, are rooted more in optics and perceptions than in realpolitik. Pakistan’s thrust to find a place in the new regional order emerging in the Middle East must continue unabated. The Makkah Joint Defence Agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, and the Tehran huddle I wrote about last week, which Field Marshal Asim Munir himself proposed, have a logic of their own that does not depend on who chairs which committee in Washington. Whatever the fallout for Pakistan, the changing of the political tide in America will be an American affair first and foremost.
The most likely outcome is that the Trump administration comes to be consumed by its wrangling with the new Congress and loses its moorings in foreign policy. A White House fighting hearings and subpoenas at home will have little bandwidth for the world.
This could produce a hazardous moment. A beleaguered and irrational president might try an adventure abroad to distract from his troubles at home, and the adventure is ready to hand. The blockade of Iran remains in place, reports in September said he saw a fresh bombing campaign as likely after the midterms, and Iran’s Supreme Leader warned on Wednesday that the war’s scope will widen if the attacks are repeated. But that seems unlikely given the stakes. This is the war voters have just punished him for, and on the eve of the vote he himself cast doubt on resuming strikes.
What is more likely is an acceleration in the pace with which America withdraws from its commitments to underwrite global order, particularly its military posture in the Middle East. I argued in April that the price of getting out of this war would be a disorderly exit from the region altogether. A Congress that owes its majority partly to anger over this war will be in no hurry to fund the next one. The Gulf monarchies have seen their American protector fail to shield them from Iranian missiles, and they are drawing their own conclusions. All this will spur the search for a new security architecture among the powers of the region, a search that will definitely include Pakistan.
Three times in our history, in the 1960s, the 1980s and the 2000s, an American embrace brought dollars and a growth spurt, and each time the money stopped when Washington’s interest moved on. This time it has brought more photographs than dollars. Ironically enough, this turning inward of the United States might just be the push Pakistan needs to learn to stand on its own feet.
The writer is a business and economy journalist.

articles.title: How the UK-India Free Trade Agreement reshapes advanced manufacturing - ET Manufacturing
articles.summary: How the UK-India Free Trade Agreement reshapes advanced manufacturing  ET Manufacturing
articles.full_text:
The landmark UK-India Free Trade Agreement (FTA), formally known as the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) is creating opportunities in one of the world's fastest-growing industrial markets for British manufacturers. Here is what that means in practice for businesses.
The agreement came into force on 15 July this year, under its terms, 99% of Indian origin goods entering the UK and 90% of UK origin goods entering India will either be duty free or subject to reduced tariffs. It will benefit a wide range of industries on both sides including automotive, manufacturing, consumer goods, creative industries, and medical technology. The agreement marks the biggest milestone in the bilateral economic partnership to date. In the long run, the deal is expected to boost bilateral trade by £25.5 billion, Indian GDP by £5.1billion, and UK GDP by £4.8 billion every year.
When the UK and India signed the FTA in July 2025, it marked the biggest bilateral trade deal the UK has agreed since leaving the European Union and one of India’s most comprehensive trade deals ever.
For the UK, the calculation is different: it is about securing new anchors of growth for industry. Advanced manufacturing is one such anchor, a fact underpinned by the UK’s Modern Industrial Strategy, which places the sector at the top of its growth priorities. The FTA is, in effect, one of the most direct policy levers available to UK manufacturers looking to compete in Asia’s largest emerging market.
Why advanced manufacturing is central to the deal
Advanced manufacturing spans a cluster of sectors united by a reliance on automation, precision engineering, digital design tools, automotive electrification, scientific instruments and machinery, and advanced materials. These are precisely the sectors where UK firms lead, and where the FTA unlocks the greatest opportunity.
British aerospace, led by companies such as Rolls-Royce, BAE Systems, and supported by a deep network of specialist suppliers, is among the most sophisticated in the world. The UK is a significant exporter of turbojet engines, aircraft components, precision instruments, and the kind of high-specification machinery that underpins industrial production across multiple sectors.
How does the UK-Indi free trade agreement work?
A Free Trade Agreement or FTA is a formal treaty between two or more countries in which the parties primarily agree to reduce or eliminate barriers to the movement of goods and services between them. In practice, an FTA means that a product manufactured in Country A can enter Country B at a lower (or sometimes zero) import duty than it would otherwise face.
The UK and India are two major economies with deep commercial, cultural and people-to-people links. This agreement gives businesses greater confidence to trade, invest and collaborate across a fast-growing economic corridor. As a Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, it also addresses services, customs, intellectual property, government procurement, non-tariff barriers and other areas of cooperation.
Addressing non-tariff barriers
Tariffs are visible and quantifiable: a 100% duty on an imported car is a blunt and measurable obstacle. Non-tariff barriers (NTBs) are the subtler, often more stubborn impediments to trade: divergent product standards, cumbersome customs documentation requirements, opaque licensing regimes, and differing certification processes. A British machinery exporter might face zero tariff at India’s border, yet struggle to secure Indian certification for its equipment. The UK-India FTA addresses such friction points, committing both sides to simplifying documentation, accelerating customs clearance, and enabling UK conformity assessment bodies to certify certain products against Indian regulatory standards before goods even leave British shores.
Changes in tariff architecture
The tariff provisions of the UK-India FTA are structured around tariff-rate quotas (TRQs) for vehicles and immediate/staged tariff liberalisation schedule for other tariff lines.
This granular, product-by-product approach determines exactly what duties apply to which goods and when.
Aerospace: Among the most immediately impactful provisions for the UK’s advanced manufacturing is the treatment of aerospace components.
Tariffs on aircraft parts, which were as high as 11%, fell to zero from the first day the FTA entered into force.
For a sector defined by long supply chains and razor-thin margins on complex components, this is a structural shift in competitiveness.
Similarly, most scientific and technical measuring instruments, a category that encompasses the precision tools essential to both aerospace production and industrial quality control, get lower duty under the FTA.
Auto and Future Mobility: For this sector, the deal’s architecture is more phased, reflecting the political and economic sensitivity.
India’s automobile market is one of the most protected in the world, with import duties on fully assembled cars exceeding 100% in some cases, effectively pricing most foreign vehicles very highly.
The FTA changes this, but carefully.
The UK’s internal combustion engine vehicles gain access via a TRQ, with duties falling from their triple-digit starting point to a range of 30 to 50% initially, and eventually to 10% by year five.
The TRQ begins at 20,000 units in year 1 and rises to 37,000 by year 5.
Manufacturing, Textile Machinery and Industrial Technologies: For the UK’s wider manufacturing offer, the agreement is relevant where it lowers the cost base of the equipment underpinning India’s industrial modernization across machinery, electrical systems and automation.
Industrial machinery tariffs across many categories reduce to zero within five years.
Immediate tariff cuts on Robotics and automation (e.
g.
industrial robots to get tariff free entry into India) improve investment payback economics.
Tariffs on all Textile Machinery will be eliminated within 5 years.
Tariffs on most Test and Measurement equipment  will be reduced and become zero duty within ten years.
Deep reductions across electrical machinery strengthens the UK’s positions across advanced manufacturing supply chains.

Customs, Digital Trade and SMEs
Even the most ambitious tariff reductions mean little if goods are stuck at the border. A consignment of precision aircraft components that sits in a customs queue for three weeks is a problem for an aerospace manufacturer regardless of the duty rate. This is why the FTA’s provisions on customs and trade facilitation provisions matter as much as the tariff schedule itself.
Opening the procurement door
One of the most significant elements of the FTA is its chapter on government procurement. The deal includes India’s first comprehensive government procurement chapter in an FTA. Government procurement, in simple terms, covers how public bodies, including ministries, agencies, and state-owned enterprises, purchase goods and services. It is a large and steady source of demand in any economy, and one that governments have typically kept outside the scope of trade liberalisation.
The IP foundation
Advanced manufacturing is underpinned by innovation. Turbojet engines, precision machinery, and next-generation battery chemistry are the result of years of research and development (R&D), built on proprietary processes and deep engineering expertise. This know-how, often embedded in design, production techniques, and materials science, is what gives firms their competitive advantage.
When leadership signals commitment
Political will drive the momentum of -behind any trade agreement, and the UK-India FTA has had no shortage of it.
Vision 2035
The UK and India have also endorsed ‘Vision 2035’ - an ambitious, future-focused agreement which underscores the two nations’ resolve to work together for mutual growth, prosperity and to help shape a secure, and sustainable world at a time of rapid global change. This Vision 2035 embeds the trade deal within a more ambitious agenda: structured collaboration on frontier technologies that will define the next generation of advanced manufacturing.

articles.full_text:
ISLAMABAD: Despite having Generalised Scheme of Preferences (GSP+) status, Pakistan’s exports to major western and eastern European markets fell in the first quarter of 2026-27 compared with the previous year.

Overall exports to Europe dipped modestly, with a slight increase in proceeds from southern and northern European countries during the July-September quarter, raising serious concerns for policymakers.

The ongoing Middle East conflict has accelerated the decline in exports to these markets, along with the European Union’s preferential market access offered to India, one of Pakistan’s key competitors in textiles.

Data compiled by the State Bank of Pakistan showed that exports to European countries contracted 1.84pc to $2.350 billion in 1QFY27 from $2.394bn a year ago.

Trade analysts warn that the Middle East conflict could further dampen export demand, as rising energy costs are likely to squeeze consumer spending in Europe, which is already under strain from the economic fallout of the Ukraine war.

Exports to northern Europe increased by 21.07pc to $236.321m in 1QFY27 from $195.191m a year ago.

Exports to southern Europe grew 5.26pc to $879.896m in 1QFY27 from $835.862m in the corresponding period last year. In this region, exports to Spain rose 17.78pc to $451.244m from $383.122m in the preceding year.

Exports to Italy declined 8.49pc to $298.731m in 1QFY27, compared with $326.460m in the same period last year. Exports to Greece grew 3.52pc to $34.961m during the months under review, compared with $33.774m over the previous year.

However, exports to eastern Europe fell 15.05pc to $168.761m in 1QFY27 from $198.677m.

Before Brexit, the United Kingdom was Pakistan’s major export destination. In the post-Brexit period, Pakistan’s exports to the UK increased 6.64pc to $612.305m in 1QFY27 from $574.171m a year ago.

Western Europe, which includes countries such as Germany, the Netherlands, France, Italy, and Belgium, accounts for the largest share of Pakistan’s exports to the EU. However, exports to this region shrank 8.51pc to $1.065bn in 1QFY27 from $1.164bn in 1QFY26.

Exports to Germany dipped 12.77pc to $389.116m in 1QFY27 from $446.100m. Similarly, exports to the Netherlands, the second-largest market for Pakistani goods, fell by 3.07pc to $370.005m from $381.752m a year ago.

Exports to France fell by 0.47pc to $136.030m in 1QFY27 from $136.686m, followed by a 7.57pc decline to Belgium’s $127.431m against $137.871m.

articles.title: Bangladesh garment protests shut 670 factories; India monitoring situation - The Federal
articles.summary: Bangladesh garment protests shut 670 factories; India monitoring situation  The Federal
articles.full_text:
Commenting on the situation, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said India remains committed to a positive and constructive relationship with Bangladesh
New Delhi, Nov 3 (PTI) India on Tuesday said it is following the situation arising out of the protests by garment workers in Bangladesh.
The garment workers are holding protests over their demand for higher pay, prompting authorities to deploy additional paramilitary forces after reports surfaced of vandalism and violence.
The latest wave of protests has forced 670 of around 4,000 registered garment factories to shut in Dhaka, Gazipur and central Mymensingh, according to the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA).
"We have been following the situation in Bangladesh. There have been developments there, and we continue to follow those developments," External Affairs Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said.
"As far as the India-Bangladesh relationship is concerned, we want to work towards a positive, forward-looking, and constructive relationship," he said at his regular media briefing.
To a question on the Ganga Water Treaty between India and Bangladesh, Jaiswal said both sides have a "joint rivers commission and it is the structured mechanism for discussion on all cross-boundary rivers, including Ganga".
The Ganga water treaty was inked in December 1996 that provides for a mechanism for sharing of the river water between the two riparian states. The treaty expires this year.
Jaiswal gave an indirect response to a question on whether Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman would undertake a visit to India.
"We have already extended an invitation to the Prime Minister of Bangladesh to visit India, and if there is an update, I will keep you informed," he said. PTI

However, it cautioned that the immediate economic impact on India would remain limited as key policy decisions continue to rest largely with US President Donald Trump and the White House.

However, CareEdge noted that crude prices remain sensitive to developments around the Strait of Hormuz and the risk of disruptions to energy supplies, making the outlook for India dependent on developments in West Asia.
The report said greater Democratic control could allow lawmakers to place conditions on additional funding for military operations once the new Congress convenes in January 2027, potentially increasing pressure for diplomacy. However, the risk of escalation in West Asia remains in the intervening period.

articles.summary: India, Poland discuss ways to boost trade, investment, tech cooperation  ET Manufacturing
articles.full_text:
During a recent visit to Poland, Jitin Prasada discussed enhancing bilateral trade and technology cooperation. The talks included topics such as artificial intelligence, semiconductors, and agri-tech innovations.
The matters were discussed during the two-day visit of Minister of State for Commerce and Industry Jitin Prasada to the central European nation. The visit concluded on November 3.
During the visit, Prasada met the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Digital Affairs of Poland Krzysztof Gawkowski.
The discussions focused on expanding bilateral cooperation in emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI), semiconductors, data centres and cybersecurity, the commerce ministry said.
It added that Prasada held discussions on opportunities emerging from the India-European Union Free Trade Agreement (FTA), which will come into effect next year.
During a meeting with Deputy Minister for Economic Development and Technology of Poland Michal Baranowski, the Indian minister deliberated upon ways to expand cooperation in critical minerals, semiconductors and startup partnerships.
The bilateral trade between the two countries grew 4.16 per cent to $4.04 billion ($2.8 billion and imports $1.25 billion) in 2025-26 from $3.88 billion in 2024-25.

articles.title: DHAKA EYES STEADIER US TRADE, FEWER NEW TARIFFS - www.daily-sun.com
articles.summary: DHAKA EYES STEADIER US TRADE, FEWER NEW TARIFFS  www.daily-sun.com
articles.full_text:
Print: 05 Nov 2026
Bangladeshi exporters and economists expect Democratic control of both chambers of the US Congress to make new American tariffs harder to impose and to support export growth in Bangladesh’s largest single-country market.
They caution, however, that the existing 10% duty and a pending US investigation into excess production capacity are unlikely to change soon.
They said the result also signals support for a rules-based global trading system under the World Trade Organisation (WTO) rather than unilateral tariffs, which could benefit Bangladesh’s trade with the US and the wider world.
According to Export Promotion Bureau (EPB) data, Bangladesh’s exports to the US rose 11.51% year on year to $3.35 billion in July-October of FY27, from $3 billion a year earlier. The country’s total exports in the first four month of this fiscal year stood at $7.75 billion.
Bangladesh exported goods worth $48 billion in FY26, with ready-made garments accounting for 80.62%.
‘A positive development’
Professor Mustafizur Rahman, Distinguished Fellow of the Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD), told Daily Sun the results showed voters wanted change and were dissatisfied with some policies of the Trump administration. How far this would influence US trade policy remained to be seen, he said.
“The bilateral trade agreement between Bangladesh and the United States has been signed, but its ratification and implementation status needs to be considered. In the changed political circumstances, the need to secure congressional support for certain aspects of the agreement may become more challenging,” he said.
He noted that while the US president holds considerable executive authority, Congress plays an important role in trade policy. Certain executive trade measures are time-limited and may need congressional approval or further legislation. With Democrats controlling both chambers, securing support for new trade measures could become harder for the administration, he said.
“I believe this political development could have a positive influence on Bangladesh-US bilateral trade relations in the coming days,” Prof Mustafizur said.
He added that trade and investment do not depend on political decisions alone.
“The overall business environment and Bangladesh’s own competitiveness are equally important. Ultimately, our ability to compete in the global market will determine how much we can benefit.”
He said Bangladesh has considerable potential to expand exports to the US as China’s role in that market has declined, but has been unable to capitalise because of limited product diversification and other policy shortcomings.
Existing duties, investigations remain
Mohiuddin Rubel, founder and CEO of Bangladesh Apparel Voice (BAV) and a former director of the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA), said Democratic control of Congress changes US trade politics but would not alter garment duties soon.
The president can still veto bills, and current tariffs rest on powers Congress delegated years ago, he said.
Bangladeshi goods currently face an additional 10% duty under Section 301, on top of the normal import duty.
This began after the Supreme Court struck down the reciprocal tariffs and the temporary charge expired.
“Exporters should not expect this 10% to go away when planning 2027 orders,” he said.
Mr Rubel identified possible gains. New tariffs would be harder to introduce, since anything requiring Congress would now go to a Democratic majority that campaigned against tariffs.
“If policy becomes steadier, US buyers can plan orders more easily. That helps Bangladesh, since we sell mostly low-priced basic items,” he said.
He expected the duty-free quota for garments made with US cotton and synthetic fibre to remain. The president established it without Congress, it benefits American farmers, and Democrats also want forced labour removed from supply chains. However, it removes only the additional 10%; the normal duty still applies, quantities are limited and it runs for three years.
On shipping, he said that if Congress pushes to calm the Iran war, freight costs may fall. War-risk charges have been $2,000-$4,000 per container.
Among the challenges, Mr Rubel said Democrats would find it hard to oppose a tariff aimed at forced labour, so such a measure was likely to stay.
He expected closer scrutiny of workers’ rights, wages and the origin of Bangladesh’s cotton.
“We lost US GSP in 2013 because of labour problems, and that could matter again,” he said.
If Congress blocks new legislation, the White House may act more on its own, he added. The biggest risk, he said, is the Office of the US Trade Representative’s (USTR) investigation into excess production capacity, which names Bangladesh. Weak US demand and buyers pushing down prices matter more than which party controls Congress, he said.
‘Supply chains to improve’
Mohammad Hasan Arif, vice chairman and chief executive (additional secretary) of the EPB, called the Democrats’ victory “a positive development, reflecting the aspirations of the American people”. He said it indicated voters wanted a change from unilateral tariffs and trade wars.
“The result also signals support for a rules-based global trading system under the WTO, rather than imposing tariffs unilaterally. This could have a positive impact on Bangladesh’s trade with the United States and the rest of the world,” he said.
He cautioned that the situation would not improve overnight, as tariffs and geopolitical conflicts had disrupted supply chains and restoring normal trade flows would take time.
On the bilateral trade agreement, he said it was a government-to-government decision. “A change in congressional control will not automatically alter it. Any changes would require discussions and mutual agreement between the two governments.”
Arif said exports to the US had continued to grow despite tariffs, in the last fiscal year and in the first four months of the current one.
He saw further scope for growth, citing Bangladesh’s garment manufacturing capacity.
If geopolitical tensions ease and supply chains improve, energy supplies could also improve, allowing factories to raise output, he said.
Export diversification remained the main challenge, with the government and private sector working to reduce dependence on a single sector.
Tariff background
The US initially imposed reciprocal tariffs on Bangladesh, with rates proposed at around 37% and later adjusted to 20% following mid-2025 negotiations.
After a federal trade court struck down President Donald Trump’s worldwide reciprocal tariffs and ordered their collection stopped, Washington imposed a 10% tariff on imports from Bangladesh and 17 other countries.
On 9 February 2026, the two countries signed the Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (ART) to restructure bilateral trade and tariff frameworks. It has yet to be ratified.

articles.title: India’s Port Capacity Is Growing, but Export Cargo Still Waits Beyond Approval: FICCI–Kearney - The Policy Edge
articles.summary: India’s Port Capacity Is Growing, but Export Cargo Still Waits Beyond Approval: FICCI–Kearney  The Policy Edge
articles.full_text:
Key Details
FICCI and Kearney’s India’s Maritime Agenda for 2030 examines whether improvements inside ports are translating into better connections between Indian businesses and overseas markets.
| Measure | Finding | 
|---|---|
| Cargo handled at major and non-major ports | 1,668 million tonnes in FY2025–26, up 38% from FY2017–18 | 
| Annual handling capacity | 2.8 billion tonnes, up 22% over the same period | 
| Export time at four seaports in the 2025 National Time Release Study | About 30 hours to approval, followed by 158 hours from approval to vessel departure | 
| Containers transshipped through overseas ports | About 75% of India’s transshipment containers as of May 2025 | 
| Identified road and rail links to ports | 84 of 294 projects completed by July 2026 | 
Faster Ports Do Not Guarantee Faster Shipments
India’s ports are handling more cargo, while average vessel turnaround at major ports has fallen to about 49 hours. The study argues that the next constraint is not simply a shortage of berths or cranes. Exporters also depend on reliable inland links, available shipping services and coordination between the many organisations that move a shipment.
At four seaports, 84% of the measured time from export processing to vessel departure came after export approval. That does not mean all 158 post-approval hours are avoidable: they include logistics activity and waiting for scheduled sailings. It does show why quicker customs approval alone may have a limited effect on the time an exporter waits to ship goods.
Different Ports Need Different Trade Strategies
The study proposes distinct plans for container gateways, transshipment hubs, industrial and energy gateways, and specialised export corridors. Each would be developed around the cargo it can attract, the industries and inland markets it serves, and its connections to overseas routes.
Transshipment illustrates the challenge. Around three-quarters of India’s transshipment containers were handled abroad as of May 2025. Vizhinjam has since added domestic deepwater capacity, but attracting and retaining shipping-line services is a separate commercial task from building the port.
Policy Relevance
The study shifts attention from how much capacity India builds to how reliably a shipment reaches its market. It recommends prioritising road and rail links around actual cargo flows and using shipment-time data to identify where time is spent. A designated coordinator for each gateway could give projects a clear owner, funding route and milestone.
For exporters, the meaningful measures would be total shipment cost, predictable transit times and access to shipping routes—not port capacity alone. Those outcomes would also show whether investments across ports, transport links and logistics services are working together.
Relevant Question for Policy Stakeholders: Which port-to-market routes should receive priority investment, and who will be accountable for improving the total time and cost of moving cargo through them?
Follow the Full Press Release Here: FICCI–Kearney on India’s Maritime Agenda for 2030

An Indian tourist has died after two helicopters collided while attempting to land near the base camp of Mount Everest, two officials have confirmed to the BBC.
Verified footage of the crash showed the helicopter blades of the two aircraft clipping each other as they came into land at around 08:15 local time (02:30 GMT) in Pheriche, approximately 12km (7 miles) south of Mount Everest Base Camp.
Helicopter company Fishtail Air named the man killed in the crash as Vasanth Kumar Balaramudu.
The helicopter company said one of its vehicles was involved in the collision and that another passenger and the helicopter's captain had been injured.
The injured passengers and crew members on board were rescued and taken to Kathmandu, Fishtail Air added in a statement.
The injured passenger was a tourist from New Zealand, an official of Solukhumbu district, Bhupendra Thapa, told BBC Nepal.
The other helicopter involved was operated by Air Dynasty and had been carrying cargo, the company said.
It was operated by one crew member who sustained no injuries, it added.
A spokesman for Nepal's Civil Aviation Authority, Gyanendra Bhul, said: "It appears the accident happened when two helicopters... attempted to land at the same spot."
In the video footage of the incident, the weather conditions look clear and no strong wind effects are visible. One helicopter appears to be making a more rapid descent than the other.
Helicopters are widely used for transport in the Himalayan nation due to its challenging terrain. But its rapidly changing weather conditions and high altitude often make aviation operations hazardous.
The village of Pheriche, located on the trekking route to the summit of the world's tallest mountain, Mount Everest, is just over 4,000m (13,120ft) above sea level.
Climbing expeditions to Everest and Ama Dablam mountain are currently under way in the region, as autumn is a popular climbing season.

articles.summary: Bangladesh garment workers stage 4th day of protests, clash with police  Kuwait Times
articles.full_text:
DHAKA: Garment workers in Bangladesh staged a fourth day of wage protests on Tuesday, with police firing tear gas to disperse demonstrators as unrest disrupted factory operations and transport links in the country’s vital export sector. The unrest, which began on Saturday, has intensified despite the government’s move to form a six-member wage board to review pay in Bangladesh’s garment sector, the world’s second-largest apparel exporter after China.
It comes at a critical time for manufacturers entering the peak production season for spring and summer export orders. The industry employs about 4 million workers, supplies global brands such as H&M, Zara and Gap, and accounts for more than 80 percent of the country’s export earnings.
Clashes were reported across industrial belts around Dhaka, including Ashulia, Gazipur and the capital’s Mirpur area, as workers staged fresh demonstrations and attempted to block major highways. Dozens of people, including several police officers, were injured in the clashes.
In Ashulia, police fired tear gas and sound grenades after protesters threw bricks and stones at law enforcement personnel, said Mohammad Mominul Islam Bhuiyan, superintendent of Ashulia Industrial Police. Similar crowd-control measures were used in Dhaka’s Mirpur area, police said. Additional security forces were deployed to contain the unrest, police said. Several factories in Gazipur and Ashulia again suspended operations or declared holidays after nearly 700 factories shut a day earlier.
Workers are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka ($245), up from the current 12,500 taka, arguing that rising living costs and persistent inflation have eroded their purchasing power. Several factories were also vandalized during the unrest. Industry officials warn prolonged closures could delay shipments and damage Bangladesh’s reputation as a reliable sourcing hub as it competes with rivals such as Vietnam and India for global apparel orders. The wage dispute comes amid mounting pressure on workers from rising prices. The government formed the wage board on November 1 to review pay in the garment sector, but the move has yet to calm the protests.
Factory owners said they are contending with rising operating costs, uncertainty in energy markets linked to conflict in the Middle East, and softer demand in key export markets.
They warn that prolonged unrest could disrupt production schedules and jeopardize export orders, while workers continue to press for higher wages and better working conditions.
Police have filed cases against thousands of unidentified protesters for torching police vehicles and damaging property, with 58 officers injured since protests began, police spokesperson Kamarum Munira said. Workers said scores of protesters have also been injured, with demonstrators seen hurling bricks at police who in turn used batons and fired tear gas to disperse the crowds.
“Some factories are closed and workers have taken to the streets,” Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said on Tuesday. “Some miscreants are trying to incite violence and make the situation more complicated.” The paramilitary Border Guard Bangladesh force said it had deployed forces in Gazipur and Narayanganj, key industrial suburbs around Dhaka, and were using drones to monitor the unrest.
The garment industry generates around four-fifths of Bangladesh’s export earnings, worth up to $38 billion, and employs more than four million people. Workers say the rising cost of food, housing, transport and healthcare has eroded their purchasing power in a country with eight percent inflation.
They are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka ($245) -- a 140 percent increase from the current 12,500 taka. Industry representatives said on Monday workers from at least 670 factories had walked out. Protesters in Gazipur blocked the Dhaka-Tangail highway and set fire to roadside debris, but were later cleared by police. In Mirpur in Dhaka’s northeast, a few hundred workers wielding sticks left their workplaces to join the protest, clashing with security forces.
“The law enforcement agencies used force against unarmed workers. What options did the workers have except taking to the streets?” said Begum, a garment worker in Gazipur who gave only one name.
She said she feared that the protest would not subside unless the wage board announced a salary increase. “We pay the same prices for commodities like milk, fish and chicken as government officials do. The government readily announced a pay rise for them. Why didn’t they form the wage board beforehand? Why did they wait until we took to the streets?” she said. — Agencies

articles.title: Bangladesh Accuses Deposed PM Hasina Of Fuelling Garment Workers’ Unrest As Protests Turn Violent - ETV Bharat
articles.summary: Bangladesh Accuses Deposed PM Hasina Of Fuelling Garment Workers’ Unrest As Protests Turn Violent  ETV Bharat
articles.full_text:
The workers are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka (approx. INR 23,000), citing rising prices of food, housing, transport and healthcare
Dhaka: The Bangladesh government on Tuesday accused deposed prime minister Sheikh Hasina of fuelling labour unrest as violent garment workers' protests over higher wages entered the fourth day, forcing hundreds of factories to suspend operations and prompting authorities to deploy additional paramilitary forces.
According to the Bangladesh Garments Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA), fresh violence forced another 300 factories to shut down, taking the number of affected units to nearly 1,000 since the latest wave of protests began on October 31.
The unrest has spread across Dhaka and its industrial outskirts, including Gazipur, Ashulia, Mirpur and Narayanganj, and Mymensingh district with workers clashing with police, blocking roads and disrupting production.
The workers are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka (approx INR 23,000), more than double the existing 12,500 taka (approx INR 9,507), citing rising prices of food, housing, transport and healthcare that have eroded their purchasing power.
Prime Minister's Information Affairs Adviser Zahedur Rahman accused Hasina of being behind the unrest, saying he did not believe she would allow the government to function peacefully as long as she remained alive.
“I do not believe Sheikh Hasina will let the government remain in peace as long as she is alive. As long as Hasina would remain alive, acts of sabotage could continue,” he told a media briefing, alleging that the ousted premier is an architect of the protests.
The remarks marked a shift from Rahman's earlier assertion that Hasina and her disbanded Awami League were politically irrelevant in Bangladesh.
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed on Monday also alleged that some garment factory owners linked to the Awami League were fuelling the unrest.
The minister claimed Hasina's supporters were behind the violence, while Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's labour and employment adviser Mahdi Amin said the government has found evidence of the infiltration of “fugitive evil powers” into the workers' movement, in an apparent reference to the Awami League.
Amin said those involved would be exposed and face legal action.
The allegations came despite the home minister's assertion in July that the Awami League had been "politically destroyed" and would never be able to return to politics in Bangladesh.
The protests come at a critical time for Bangladesh's readymade garment industry, which employs about four million workers and accounts for more than 80 per cent of the country's export earnings.
Bangladesh is the world's second-largest garment exporter after China, supplying major international brands such as H&M, Zara and Gap.
Manufacturers have warned that prolonged disruption during the peak production season for spring and summer orders could delay shipments, threaten overseas buyers' confidence and lead to cancellations.
Police have arrested more than 100 people in connection with the unrest, officials said, adding that around 50 of them were linked to Awami League politics.
Hasina fled to India after her government was ousted in a student-led uprising on August 5, 2024. A special tribunal during the subsequent interim government led by Chief Adviser Muhammad Yunus later sentenced her to death in absentia.
The government on Sunday constituted a six-member minimum wage board to review garment workers' pay and recommend a revised wage structure. The board, however, was yet to hold its first meeting as protests continued.
Workers said scores of demonstrators had been injured in clashes with police, who used batons and tear gas to disperse crowds. Witnesses said protesters threw bricks and stones at law enforcement personnel.
The Ittefaq newspaper reported fresh clashes in Narayanganj, where workers blocked a key road connecting the port town with Dhaka and set fire to discarded tyres. Police responded with tear gas and batons.
In the Ashulia industrial zone on the outskirts of Dhaka, Industrial Police fired tear gas and sound grenades after protesters allegedly hurled bricks and stones at security personnel. Similar clashes were reported in Dhaka's Mirpur area.
Authorities earlier deployed Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) personnel, with the paramilitary force saying it has deployed additional forces on Tuesday, positioning 12 platoons in Gazipur and two in the suburban river port town of Narayanganj amid continued violence.
The BGB said it was closely monitoring the situation in Dhaka and had set up a monitoring centre at its headquarters, using drones and body-worn cameras. The latest unrest began on Saturday, with workers saying a recent pay hike for government employees had further highlighted the disparity in wages.
"We pay the same prices for commodities for our living," a workers' leader told a private television channel.
Bangladesh's garment sector has been under pressure from rising production costs, inflation and intense competition in global markets. Workers, meanwhile, say their wages have failed to keep pace with the cost of living, with inflation hovering around 8 per cent.

Workers are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka ($242; £180), more than double the current standard, citing rising costs of living.

There are fears in the industry that the prolonged unrest could disrupt production and affect international buyers, state news agency BSS reported.
The garment industry generates nearly $40bn every year for Bangladesh, accounting for around 10% of its GDP.
The South Asian nation is the world's second-largest garment exporter after China - but its workers are among the lowest-paid in the world, taking home around 13,000 taka ($105; £78) a month.
"We want the government to accept our demands and increase our wages. [And] they need to instruct landlords and homeowners not to raise rent and ensure that the prices of essential commodities remain affordable," one female worker told BBC Bangla.
"Food prices, cooking gas and electricity bills have all gone up," Mamun, a 28-year-old factory worker, told AFP. "The government must either bring down the prices of essential commodities or raise our wages."
The government announced on Sunday that it had established a board to review workers' wages, and Prime Minister Tarique Rahman held an emergency meeting with ministers to address the unrest.

Authorities have accused the Awami League, the banned political party of former leader Sheikh Hasina, for taking advantage of the protest movement to instigate violence - though they did not provide any evidence of this.
Home minister Salahuddin Ahmed threatened punitive action against protesters who were trying to "destabilise the country" "under the guise of labour protests".

"I tell my fellow workers, return to work. Don't give in to anyone's incitement."

New Delhi: RITES Limited, a public sector enterprise under the Ministry of Railways, has emerged as the lowest bidder (L-1) for an international railway contract floated by Sri Lanka Railways for the supply of Broad Gauge Diesel Multiple Unit (DMU) train sets.
The proposed contract is valued at approximately Rs 400 crore and is expected to strengthen RITES’ international order book while expanding its presence in the overseas railway market.
The development marks an important step in the company’s efforts to secure international railway projects and expand its business in rolling stock supply, railway infrastructure and transportation engineering.
RITES Rs 400 Crore Sri Lanka Railway Contract: Key Details
Under the proposed contract, RITES will supply Broad Gauge Diesel Multiple Unit (DMU) train sets to Sri Lanka Railways.
As per the tender conditions, the project is expected to be executed within 12 months from the opening of the Letter of Credit (LC).
However, the contract has not yet been formally awarded. The tender process is currently undergoing final scrutiny, followed by the completion of the required documentation before the formal contract award.
Therefore, RITES’ emergence as the L-1 bidder represents a significant development, but the final award of the contract is still awaited.

L-1 Bidder Status to Strengthen RITES’ International Order Book
Emerging as the lowest bidder for the approximately Rs 400 crore contract is a potential boost to RITES’ international business operations.

RITES has been actively pursuing international projects across railway infrastructure, transportation engineering, consultancy and rolling stock supply. The Sri Lanka opportunity reflects the company’s continued focus on expanding its global presence.

articles.full_text:
New Delhi: Bangladesh's garment industry has been hit by another wave of protests, with thousands of workers demanding higher wages clashing with police, blocking major highways and forcing hundreds of factories to suspend production, even as the government accused industrialists linked to ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina's Awami League of fuelling the unrest.
The demonstrations entered their fourth consecutive day on Tuesday, November 3, with fresh clashes reported in Dhaka's Mirpur area, where several garment factories had partially resumed operations in the morning.
Workers who initially returned to their workplaces subsequently came out onto the streets, blocking roads and confronting security personnel.
Police used tear gas, water cannons and sound grenades to disperse demonstrators, some of whom reportedly hurled stones at officers.
Traffic was disrupted across parts of Mirpur, while services at the Mirpur-11 metro station were temporarily suspended amid the disturbances.
The fresh violence followed Monday's widespread demonstrations in Gazipur, Savar, Ashulia, Narayanganj and other industrial areas surrounding the capital.
In Gazipur, hundreds of workers blocked stretches of the Dhaka-Tangail highway for several hours, bringing traffic to a standstill. Vehicles, including a police vehicle, were set ablaze during the unrest, while police used tear gas to disperse protesters.
The disruption has affected one of Bangladesh's most important industries.
The country is the world's second-largest garment exporter after China, with the sector employing more than four million workers and accounting for the bulk of its export earnings.
According to Bangladesh's Industrial Police, at least 414 factories remained closed on Monday amid the disturbances.
Industry estimates suggested an even wider disruption, raising concerns about delayed shipments and possible losses of export orders.
Police have also registered cases over incidents of violence and vandalism, with at least 82 people reported arrested in Gazipur and Mirpur.
Why are garment workers protesting again?
At the centre of the unrest is a demand to increase the minimum monthly wage to 30,000 Bangladeshi taka (approximately USD 241), compared with the existing minimum of Tk 12,500.
The last wage revision took effect on December 1, 2023, when the minimum salary was increased from Tk 8,000 to Tk 12,500 following widespread protests.
Workers argue that the revised wages have failed to keep pace with rising living costs, particularly house rent, food, transport and healthcare expenses.
For many workers, household expenditure already exceeds their monthly earnings, leaving little room for savings or unexpected expenses.
The latest mobilisation comes as Bangladesh approaches its next scheduled wage revision. The existing three-year review period ends in December, and the revised wage structure is required to take effect from December 1 under the amended labour law.
The government announced a six-member minimum wage board on Sunday to examine the workers' demands and recommend a revised salary structure.
However, the announcement has failed to calm the situation, with workers continuing their demonstrations over wages and other longstanding grievances, including allegations of blacklisting and demands for the reinstatement of dismissed employees.
Kamrul Hasan, general secretary of the Ekota Garments Sramik Federation, told AFP that even labour leaders had not anticipated the scale of the unrest after the wage board was constituted.
He said workers were raising several unresolved issues beyond the proposed wage revision, while some labour leaders had gone into hiding amid the disturbances.
Government alleges Awami League involvement
The wage dispute has also developed into a political controversy after Bangladesh Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed accused factory owners and industrialists associated with Hasina's former Awami League government of deliberately encouraging the disturbances.
Addressing reporters on Monday after meeting representatives of the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) and the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA), Salahuddin claimed that several individuals previously associated with the ousted administration were involved.
"Some of them were MPs, ministers or state ministers at different times. We have information that these industrialists are behind the unrest, and it has been established," he said.
The minister alleged that supporters of the former were exploiting workers' grievances to create instability through highway blockades, arson and attacks on public property.
He further claimed that some factory owners had deliberately suspended operations to aggravate the situation, while certain individuals operating under the banner of labour organisations were encouraging violence.
According to Salahuddin, the authorities have collected video footage, audio recordings and other material relating to the disturbances.
The government has asked industry associations to identify factories suspected of deliberately shutting down operations and provide information about labour organisations allegedly involved in inciting unrest.
Bangladesh's state-run agency BSS also reported that police had arrested 19 Awami League members and activists of affiliated organisations in Dhaka on allegations of instigating demonstrations.
However, the wider allegations of organised political involvement have not been independently established. Labour representatives have continued to point to inadequate pay, rising expenses and longstanding workplace grievances as reasons for the protests.
Hasina's promised December return adds to political tensions
The allegations have emerged against the backdrop of renewed political attention surrounding former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who has been living in India since being removed from power during a student-led uprising in August 2024.
Hasina, whose Awami League has been barred from political activities in Bangladesh, has repeatedly announced her intention to return to the country in December 2026, despite facing a death sentence imposed in absentia over the crackdown on the 2024 protests.
In a July interview with Reuters, Hasina said she and senior Awami League leaders planned to return voluntarily and present themselves before a court.
She reiterated her intention in October, saying she would return in December despite the possibility of arrest or other consequences.
Her proposed return comes at a politically sensitive time for the government headed by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, particularly as the ruling administration accuses supporters of the previous government of attempting to destabilise the country.
The government has not, however, established any direct connection between Hasina's proposed return and the ongoing garment wage demonstrations.
Tarique Rahman government moves to contain unrest
With the protests spreading across industrial districts, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman convened an emergency meeting with senior ministers on Sunday evening.
Following the meeting, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said the prime minister had directed authorities to protect workers' rights, improve their living standards and ensure that industrial production and exports continued without disruption.
The government has sought to bring factory owners and labour organisations to the negotiating table while warning of stringent action against those involved in violence.
Industry representatives have also expressed concern that prolonged disruption could jeopardise deliveries to international buyers, particularly as Bangladesh's garment sector faces financial pressures, fluctuating export orders and supply chain challenges.
Some factories in Gazipur and Kaliakair reopened on Monday, while employers announced plans to resume operations at other establishments on Tuesday.
However, the renewed clashes in Mirpur show that the immediate tensions remain unresolved.
The coming weeks will test whether the government's wage board can address workers' demands before the December revision deadline, even as allegations of political interference complicate efforts to restore normalcy in Bangladesh's largest export industry.

The latest developments come amid ongoing protests by garment workers demanding a substantial increase in their minimum monthly wages, with the current minimum wage of BDT 12,500 falling short of their demand for BDT 30,000.
Earlier on Monday, Bangladesh Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed had alleged that industrialists and factory owners linked to the former Awami League government were instigating unrest in the country’s garment sector.
Speaking to reporters after a meeting with leaders of the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) and the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA) at the Secretariat on Monday, Salahuddin claimed that some former lawmakers and ministers were involved in fuelling the unrest, as reported by The Daily Star.
“Some of them were MPs, ministers or state ministers at different times. We have information that these industrialists are behind the unrest, and it has been established,” he said, as quoted by The Daily Star.
The minister alleged that groups supporting the ousted regime were exploiting workers to create instability through highway blockades, arson and violence. He also claimed that some individuals operating under the banner of labour organisations were involved in these activities.
Salahuddin said the government had collected video footage, audio recordings and other evidence relating to violent incidents, adding that some individuals had already been brought to justice.
“We want to make it clear that those involved in activities against workers’ interests, violating law and order and conspiring to create instability will be dealt with sternly,” he added, as quoted by The Daily Star.
According to The Daily Star, the minister also alleged that some factory owners had deliberately shut their establishments to aggravate the situation. BGMEA and BKMEA leaders had agreed to provide the government with a list of factories allegedly closed with ulterior motives.
The authorities had also sought details of labour leaders and organisations suspected of instigating the unrest.
The Home Minister maintained that genuine garment workers and their organisations were not involved in the violence, arguing that they would not want to jeopardise their livelihoods.
He said the government had initially attempted to resolve the situation through dialogue despite receiving intelligence warnings about possible unrest. However, law enforcement agencies had now been instructed to take firm action against attempts to incite violence or disrupt public order.
Addressing workers’ demands for higher wages, Salahuddin said the government had constituted a minimum wage board on Sunday.
He said the revised minimum wage would be determined through discussions, noting that the existing three-year wage review period ends in December.
Salahuddin further said that some factories in Gazipur and Kaliakair, which had remained closed for a day amid the unrest, reopened on Monday. However, several other units continued to remain shut due to reasons unrelated to the protests, including financial difficulties and declining export orders.
The protests have been reported in several industrial areas, including Gazipur’s Konabari and Chandra, near Dhaka, which house a large number of garment factories. Several factory owners had suspended operations amid fears of attacks and continuing security concerns.
Despite the partial reopening of factories, Tuesday’s renewed demonstrations and police deployment in Mirpur indicate that the situation in Bangladesh’s garment sector remains tense. (ANI)

articles.title: Bangladesh garment workers’ protests turn violent for 2nd day - Nagaland Post
articles.summary: Bangladesh garment workers’ protests turn violent for 2nd day  Nagaland Post
articles.full_text:
DHAKA, NOV 2 (PTI): Garment workers in Bangladesh continued their violent protests on Monday for the second day in a row over their demand for higher pay, prompting authorities to deploy additional paramilitary forces after reports surfaced of vehicle vandalism and major roads being blocked.
Demonstrators clashed with law enforcement personnel in the capital’s Mirpur area, Ashulia, Gazipur and Narayanganj, and set police vans ablaze as police used tear gas, water cannons and batons to disperse them, local media reports said.
The latest wave of protests has forced 670 of around 4,000 registered garment factories to shut in Dhaka, Gazipur and central Mymensingh, according to the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA).
The workers are demanding that the minimum monthly wage be raised to 30,000 Bangladeshi Taka (around USD 242) from the current 12,500 Taka.
Bangladesh’s garment industry employs more than four million workers and is a major source of export earnings. The country is the world’s second-largest apparel exporter after China, with garment exports worth USD 38.70 billion in the 2025-26 fiscal year, according to the BGMEA.
Bangladeshi garment products are exported to more than 150 countries, with Europe and the United States among the major markets.
The protests continued despite the government’s announcement on Sunday of a wage board, headed by Senior District and Sessions Judge Sheikh Ashfaqur Rahman, to review the existing wage structure and recommend a revision.
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed on Monday alleged that some garment factory owners linked to the currently disbanded Awami League party of deposed prime minister Sheikh Hasina were also fuelling the unrest.
“Unfortunately, factory owners, who are involved with Awami League politics, too are working to create the unrest. The former lawmakers and junior ministers are also involved,” he told a press conference at his office.
A student-led mass uprising forced former prime minister Hasina to resign and flee the country on August 5, 2024, following which the succeeding government officially banned all political and cyber activities of her party under the Anti-Terrorism Act pending the completion of trials.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s labour and employment adviser Mahdi Amin, meanwhile, claimed that the government had found evidence of “fugitive evil powers infiltration” into the workers’ movement, in an apparent reference to the Awami League. He said those involved would face legal action.
Exporters have also expressed concern that the ongoing unrest could lead to cancellations of orders from Western buyers.
“The unrest shut down more than 150 factories in Gazipur (alone) on Monday,” the district’s industrial police superintendent Amzad Hossain told reporters, as the area emerged as one of the worst-affected industrial zones.
Gazipur Deputy Commissioner Mohammad Nurul Karim Bhuiyan said 10 platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) personnel had been deployed in the industrial zone to control the situation.
Newspapers, including Prothom Alo, reported that demonstrators blocked the Dhaka-Tangail highway, which passes through Gazipur’s industrial belt, and set fire to three police vans and several other vehicles.
Protesters carrying iron rods also blocked a major road linking Dhaka with the suburban river port town of Narayanganj, setting vehicle tyres on fire.
The clashes left at least two BGB personnel and several others, including journalists, injured, according to media reports.
On Sunday, protesters torched a police vehicle in the capital, set fire to a police box in Gazipur and blocked the Dhaka-Tangail highway, prompting authorities to deploy five BGB platoons to assist police in controlling the situation.
Reports described the latest wave of protests as among the most violent in recent months, with demonstrators targeting police property and clashing with law enforcement personnel, including by throwing stones and brickbats.
The clashes on Sunday left at least 50 people, including around 15 police officers, injured, according to newspaper reports. Police used tear gas, water cannons, sound grenades and batons to disperse demonstrators at several locations.
The escalating unrest prompted Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to call an emergency meeting with the home minister, labour minister and other senior ministers on Sunday evening to discuss the situation.
Earlier on Sunday, Labour and Employment Minister Ariful Haque Choudhury announced the formation of the wage board and urged workers to return to their jobs.
“We hope the board will convene at the earliest and carry this forward to a stage,” he said.
A government statement said the board includes representatives of workers and factory owners, along with independent experts.
Dhaka Metropolitan Police, meanwhile, arrested at least 14 factory workers and leaders and activists of the disbanded Awami League over alleged involvement in sabotage and vandalism in the past two days.
The arrests were made in connection with acts of sabotage allegedly carried out “under the guise of the ongoing movement demanding a salary hike for garment workers”, according to police.

Bangladesh garment factories close as workers clash with police in protests
Hundreds of factories remained shut after days of protests disrupted the country's garment industry, which earns about $40 billion a year from exports
WebinarsNew
Deep DiveNew

Police in Bangladesh fired tear gas and used stun grenades Wednesday to disperse garment workers protesting for higher wages, police and witnesses said.
Hundreds of factories remained shut after days of protests disrupted the country's garment industry, which earns about $40 billion a year from exports. Bangladesh has some 2,500 garment factories.
Workers are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 takas ($245), up from 12,500 takas. They say rising living costs and inflation have eroded their purchasing power.
The industry employs about 4 million workers, mostly women from rural Bangladesh.
After days of demonstrations in the capital, Dhaka, violence was reported in several industrial areas on its outskirts.
In Fatullah, in Narayanganj district outside Dhaka, dozens of people were injured in clashes between protesters and police, according to media reports. Police fired tear gas and used stun grenades.
Prothom Alo, Bangladesh's largest Bengali-language daily, reported that police arrested several protesters in Fatullah.
About 100 factories remain shut in Ashulia, in Savar near Dhaka, said Mominul Islam Bhuiyan, superintendent of Ashulia Industrial Police.
Workers also blocked a major highway in Gazipur district, another major industrial hub.
More than 10,000 police officers had been deployed in Dhaka's Mirpur area, an epicenter of recent protests, to maintain order, said Mahidul Islam, a joint police commissioner.
The government has responded to the wage demands by forming a new wage board.
The board's chairman, Syed Azad Subhani, said workers would receive their first salaries under the new pay scale in January.

articles.title: US Democratic win unlikely to ease firms' cost, tariff woes in near term, executives say - The Economic Times
articles.summary: US Democratic win unlikely to ease firms' cost, tariff woes in near term, executives say  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
Some though welcomed the prospect of political stability.
Democrats seized control of both the Senate and House of Representatives, scoring sweeping victories in Republican strongholds for the first time in generations as tens of millions of voters delivered a scathing rebuke to President Donald Trump.
But it is too early to know what the results mean for the issues roiling companies worldwide, from tariffs and energy prices to inflation and consumer confidence.
Soaring costs related to the Iran war are the latest headache for companies making everything from food and drink to consumer electronics and cars, after contending last year with Trump's tariffs on imported goods.
Global stocks and the dollar rose after the results, although chip stocks in Asia came under pressure, as investors expect the Democratic-controlled Congress to apply more scrutiny to AI.
The election outcome could also have broad implications for the US fiscal outlook as well as sectors such as defence, healthcare and banking.
WHITE HOUSE COULD FACE GREATER PRESSURE TO AVOID TRADE WARS
While analysts said the White House may face greater pressure to avoid a return to the trade wars that have raised costs for American consumers, some European manufacturers expect little immediate material relief from Trump's hefty import tariffs.
The administration largely pursued its tariff agenda through executive authorities that do not require congressional approval, and those powers remain in place, said Andrew Adair, trade policy adviser for North America at German machinery association VDMA.
Congress could seek to roll back existing tariffs, but such legislation would face major political hurdles and could ultimately be vetoed by the president, he said.
"We therefore do not anticipate national politics to directly impact business conditions over the short term," he told Reuters.
Kenichi Hori, president and chief executive of Japanese trading house Mitsui, which generates significant revenue in the United States, told media that he will be closely watching US policy on tariffs, critical minerals trade and AI data centre build-outs, but he expects the business environment to remain "highly uncertain".
RESULT COULD BOOST VISITOR NUMBERS
The result could improve the United States' image abroad, which has been hurt by Trump's tougher stance on immigration and trade policies, with visitor numbers dropping sharply since he took office.
"There might be less tariff-related irritation and a greater willingness to travel, which should have a rather positive impact on the aviation sector," Fraport CEO Stefan Schulte said. "But I wouldn't overestimate the significance of this."
Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management, was among those to warn of gridlock in Washington, saying that federal funding runs out on December 11 and that Trump has promised to become "Mr Veto" against a Democratic Congress.
"Divided government means gridlock, and gridlock means noise: investigations, vetoes, funding deadlines, and very likely another government shutdown or two, or more," he said.

articles.title: Fitch raises India’s FY’27 GDP growth projections to 6.9 pc - DD News
articles.summary: Fitch raises India’s FY’27 GDP growth projections to 6.9 pc  DD News
articles.full_text:
Fitch Ratings on Wednesday raised India’s GDP growth forecast for the current fiscal year to 6.9 per cent, from 6.4 per cent, citing strong economic growth in the June quarter and overall economic resilience.
According to Fitch, India’s economic momentum is likely to moderate over the remaining fiscal year, prompting the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to increase interest rates by 0.25 per cent in its October monetary policy meeting.
A growth rate of 7.8 per cent in the June quarter indicates that the “Indian economy has shown resilience in the face of the shock from the US-Iran war, despite the strong terms-of-trade deterioration seen in the first half of 2026,” Fitch said.
It said that PMI survey data point to a slower pace of expansion in both manufacturing and services; below-normal monsoon rains will weigh on growth in agriculture and rural demand; and rising inflation will constrain real incomes and consumer dynamics.
“Private investment prospects look more buoyant, and we expect investment to rise by more than 10 per cent; non-food credit growth reached 19 per cent yoy in July,” Fitch added.
Overall GDP growth will be 6.9 per cent (revised up from 6.4 per cent in June), Fitch added.
“Given the combination of strong demand, price rises, and adverse supply developments, we expect the RBI to raise rates by 25 bp in October this year to 5.5 per cent. We then expect a further rise to 5.75 per cent in early 2027 and then for rates to ease back to 5.5 per cent in 2028,” Fitch said.
Earlier on Wednesday, S&P Global Ratings projected India’s FY’27 GDP growth at 7 per cent — the same rate Moody’s Ratings projected last week.
The Indian economy grew at 7.7 per cent in the previous fiscal year (2025-26).
-PTI

articles.title: Afcons to build connecting expressway for Jewar Airport and underground Lucknow Metro - Indian Infrastructure Magazine
articles.summary: Afcons to build connecting expressway for Jewar Airport and underground Lucknow Metro  Indian Infrastructure Magazine
articles.full_text:
Afcons Infrastructure Limited has secured two significant engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contracts in Uttar Pradesh with a combined value of nearly Rs 34.69 billion, reinforcing its strong position in the transportation and urban infrastructure segment. The projects comprise the development of the Jewar Link Expressway and a key underground section of the Lucknow Metro Phase-1B.
Mr Krishnamurthy Subramanian, Executive Chairman, Afcons, said, "The award of these prestigious projects reflects the confidence that leading infrastructure agencies place in Afcons' engineering capabilities and execution excellence. The Jewar Link Expressway and the Lucknow Metro underground corridor are transformative projects that will enhance mobility, support economic growth, and improve quality of life for billions of people across Uttar Pradesh and NCR."
Mr S Paramasivan, Managing Director, Afcons, said, "These wins further strengthen our order book and reinforce our commitment to delivering complex, nation-building infrastructure projects. With these two projects, the fresh orders secured in FY 2027 stands at Rs 194.38 billion. We look forward to partnering with our clients to deliver these projects efficiently and create long-term value for all stakeholders.”
The Uttar Pradesh Expressways Industrial Development Authority (UPEIDA) has awarded the contract, valued at approximately Rs 20.86 billion (excluding GST), for the construction of the 24.5-km access-controlled Greenfield Jewar Link Expressway. The six-lane corridor, expandable to eight lanes, will connect the Noida International Airport at Jewar, creating an integrated high-speed transportation network across the state. The expressway is expected to significantly enhance airport accessibility, reduce travel times, and improve logistics efficiency by linking two of Uttar Pradesh’s most important expressway corridors - Yamuna Expressway and Ganga Expressway. The project will support regional economic development while strengthening connectivity for passengers and freight traffic across western and central Uttar Pradesh.
In addition, Afcons has received notice of award for a major contract from Uttar Pradesh Metro Rail Corporation (UPMRC) for the design and construction of a 6.52-km underground stretch under the Lucknow Metro Phase-1B project. The scope includes seven underground metro stations, associated civil and architectural works, utility systems, fire safety infrastructure, and connectivity between underground and elevated sections. The project value is approximately Rs 13.83 billion.

articles.title: Pakistan, China’s Xinjiang explore joint investment opportunities - Business Recorder
articles.summary: Pakistan, China’s Xinjiang explore joint investment opportunities  Business Recorder
articles.full_text:
LAHORE: Pakistan and China’s Xinjiang Province have identified extensive opportunities for joint ventures and investment in agriculture, textiles, food processing, livestock and manufacturing, with a Chinese delegation inviting Pakistani businesses to translate longstanding bilateral ties into commercially viable partnerships.
The proposals were discussed at a meeting between a visiting Chinese delegation and the Lahore Chamber of Commerce and Industry (LCCI) where both sides stressed the need to strengthen direct business-to-business engagement and explore cooperation in technology transfer, cross-border e-commerce, tourism and regional connectivity.
Leader of the Chinese delegation, Ha Zengyou, said the government-level agreements could achieve their full potential only when entrepreneurs come forward to convert them into practical economic projects. He said Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps (XPCC) and Lahore had complementary industrial strengths and supply chains, creating significant scope for cooperation.
Presenting a four-pronged framework, he identified agriculture and food processing, textiles, new trade channels, and connectivity and infrastructure as priority areas. He said Pakistan had strong potential in fruits, vegetables, seafood, berries and nuts, while the XPCC could contribute expertise in modern cultivation, livestock, processing and cold-chain facilities.
He also highlighted Pakistan’s cotton spinning and weaving capabilities and Xinjiang’s integrated textile industry, proposing closer industrial linkages. The XPCC would also facilitate Pakistani businesses in understanding Chinese policies, customs and taxation procedures.
LCCI President Ali Hussam Asghar said the longstanding Pakistan-China friendship needed to be translated into stronger investment and business partnerships. He identified water-efficient farming, cotton productivity, food processing, packaging, cold-chain facilities and halal meat production as promising areas for joint ventures.
He also invited Chinese investors to explore Punjab’s province’s industrial estates and CPEC Special Economic Zones, highlighting the province’s skilled workforce and strategic market access.
LCCI Senior Vice President Sardar Usman Ghani proposed establishing a Chinatown in Lahore, equipped with security arrangements and necessary facilities, to provide a dedicated community environment for Chinese professionals, investors and businesses.
Former LCCI President Shahzad Ali Malik stressed the need to benefit from Xinjiang’s expertise in cotton cultivation, seed development and irrigation. He said Pakistan’s cotton production had fallen from a historical level of around 15 million bales to 5-6 million bales, forcing the country to import cotton from the United States and Brazil.
Meanwhile, Ethiopian Ambassador to Pakistan Dr Oumer Hussien Oba has invited Pakistani business community to explore investment and trade opportunities in Ethiopia which is a strategic gateway to African markets and highlighting its competitive energy costs, industrial infrastructure, investment incentives and growing economy.
Speaking at the LCCI, the ambassador said that Ethiopia, with a population of over 130 million, offered considerable opportunities for Pakistani investors, particularly in manufacturing, pharmaceuticals, textiles and other industrial sectors.
He said Ethiopia was opening more sectors to international investment and assured that efforts were being made to address regulatory challenges faced by Pakistani pharmaceutical companies.
