articles.title: Iran says US reply to Hormuz plan ‘unconvincing’; Trump confirms strikes - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Iran says US reply to Hormuz plan ‘unconvincing’; Trump confirms strikes  Al JazeeraIran-US deal still out of reach, Iran’s Ghalibaf says ‘ball in America's court to prevent war’  Telegraph IndiaIran says considering two-day plan to reopen Hormuz  The HinduThe importance of a unified Gulf approach to US-Iran mediation  Arab NewsUS Iran War Live Updates: Iran says it downed US drone over Qeshm Island  The Times of India
articles.full_text:
Iran has called the US response to its seven conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz “unconvincing” as US President Donald Trump confirmed launching strikes on an Iranian island near the strategic waterway.
The developments on Tuesday came as Qatar stepped up diplomatic efforts to avert a renewed war between the US and Iran and as another oil tanker was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz.
The indirect talks centre on an Iranian proposal to reopen the waterway over two days, if the US meets Tehran’s seven demands, including the lifting of sanctions and ending a US naval blockade.
Despite reports of progress in recent days, Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said on Tuesday that Washington’s response had fallen short.
“America’s response to Iran’s rights and demands was not convincing, and they must fully and explicitly address Iran’s seven conditions and act upon them,” he wrote on X.
“Only in this case will the Strait of Hormuz be reopened.”
His post came after Majed al-Ansari, a spokesperson for Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said that talks were continuing and that both sides “remain committed to the negotiation process“.
He said Qatar was facilitating the “real-time exchange of proposals between” the US and Iran.
Attack on Qeshm Island
In Washington, DC, Trump confirmed the US had struck Iran early on Tuesday, telling Fox News that the strikes had targeted an anti-aircraft facility.
He described the operation as a “minor attack” and said it “wasn’t war”.
“They built an anti-aircraft facility. It took them about two months. We watched it get built. As soon as it was completed, we hit it last night,” he said.
Iranian media said the strikes hit Qeshm Island in the Gulf near the Strait of Hormuz. Earlier in the day, US officials told US media that the strikes had been “defensive” and followed Iranian fire at an American aircraft.
The strikes came as US media, citing US officials, reported that Central Command had prepared plans for strikes that could begin as early as Wednesday, after the midterm elections, when three American aircraft carriers would be in the region.
The crucial elections could cost Trump’s Republicans control of both the House and the Senate, and fears have grown that Trump could carry out a threatened attack on Iran once the vote is over.
US media have previously reported that the planned campaign would be short and intense.
Trump meanwhile repeated warnings of further military action on Tuesday, saying, “I’m not looking to … kill lots of people” and “If we have to, we’ll have to.”
In an earlier interview with the Financial Times, he suggested he was content with the state of the stand-off with Iran. “We seem to be getting everything we want,” the paper quoted him as saying in a six-minute telephone interview.
Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, meanwhile ordered the military at the weekend to respond to any threat immediately and without geographical limits, and to update its list of targets.
Iranian officials have suggested that European countries and undersea cables in the Gulf could be targeted.
Tanker struck in Hormuz
As officials weighed the possibility of escalation, commercial shipping came under further attack.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed on Wednesday that four oil tankers were destroyed after striking naval mines while attempting to pass through a prohibited shipping lane south of the Strait of Hormuz.
The tankers remained ablaze following the explosions, the IRGC said in a statement carried by the official IRNA news agency. Two other vessels were detained for violating shipping restrictions, it added.
Earlier, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported that two unidentified projectiles struck a tanker’s engine room about 14 nautical miles (26km) northeast of Oman’s coastal village of Limah on Tuesday. No casualties were reported.
It could not be independently verified whether the incidents reported by UKMTO and the IRGC were linked.
The IRGC also claimed its air defence forces shot down a US-made MQ-9 drone over the strait at 4.30am local time (01:00GMT), describing it as the 56th such aircraft it had downed.
The statement said the operations were carried out by the IRGC’s naval and aerospace forces, which had inflicted “heavy blows on the enemy”.
John Mearsheimer, a US political scientist, questioned whether another short bombing campaign could achieve Washington’s objectives, warning that Iranian retaliation could draw the US into a longer confrontation.
“If the 40-day bombing campaign didn’t work, how is the three-day bombing campaign going to work?” he asked in a video commentary, referring to the initial US-Israeli air campaign and proposals for a shorter renewed offensive.
He argued that an Iranian response could prompt further US escalation, increasing the damage to the global economy.

articles.title: UN panel hails Pakistan’s marriage-age law, flags bonded labour
articles.summary:
• Experts seek details on child brides, rehabilitation of flood victims and reconstruction efforts• Pakistani delegation says 600,000 destroyed homes rebuilt
ISLAMABAD: The United Nations Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights on Wednesday concluded its review of Pakistan’s second periodic report under the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, welcoming the country’s 2025 legal amendment raising the minimum age of marriage to 18.
However, committee members ra...
articles.full_text:
• Experts seek details on child brides, rehabilitation of flood victims and reconstruction efforts• Pakistani delegation says 600,000 destroyed homes rebuilt
ISLAMABAD: The United Nations Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights on Wednesday concluded its review of Pakistan’s second periodic report under the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, welcoming the country’s 2025 legal amendment raising the minimum age of marriage to 18.
However, committee members raised questions about bonded labour and reconstruction efforts following the 2022 and 2025 floods, among other topics.
Committee expert and member of the task force for Pakistan, Michael Windfuhr, welcomed the 2025 amendment to the Child Marriage Restraint Act 1929, which raised the minimum age of marriage to 18 for both males and females.
However, he noted that the committee remained concerned about the high number of child brides and asked about the impact of measures taken to prevent child marriage.
Lazhari Bouzid, another committee expert and member of the task force for Pakistan, said bonded labour continued to be prevalent in agriculture and was also found in the informal sector, particularly brick making.
Construction companies and government agencies were reportedly complicit in the practice by purchasing bricks produced through debt bondage. He asked how Pakistan had responded to these reports.
Mr Windfuhr also asked how the country had coped with the impact of the devastating floods in 2022 and 2025. He inquired whether Pakistan could rebuild housing for affected people and restore their access to land or resources, and how many people remained displaced.
‘Range of measures’
Minister of State for Law and Justice and head of the delegation, Barrister Aqeel Malik, said in his opening remarks that Pakistan had taken a range of legislative, policy and institutional measures since 2017 for the progressive realisation of covenant rights.
He said child marriage restraint laws had set the minimum age of marriage at 18 for both boys and girls in Islamabad, Balochistan, Punjab and Sindh, and criminalised child, early and forced marriages.
During the ensuing dialogue, the delegation said Pakistan’s Constitution prohibited slavery and all forms of forced labour, while the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1992 had abolished the practice.
Punjab had documented more than 210,000 kiln workers, and district vigilance committees had been established in many districts. Labour inspectors had identified more than 2,900 victims of forced labour last year.
On flood recovery, the delegation said the government had established a national emergency operations centre focusing on high-risk areas and launched a national flood protection programme. The programme aimed to protect at-risk people, eight million acres of agricultural land and 2.2 million housing units.
Each province was also implementing flood protection measures. Of the 2.1 million homes destroyed in the 2022 floods, 600,000 had been rebuilt, while reconstruction of the remaining houses was under way.
In her concluding remarks, committee expert and task force leader for Pakistan, Julieta Rossi, said the delegation had outlined processes for implementing economic, social and cultural rights, as well as the significant challenges facing the country and gaps between legislative progress and implementation.
“This information would be reflected in the committee’s concluding observations, which the panel hoped that Pakistan would implement in good faith,” she added.
Mr Malik said in his concluding remarks that the delegation had outlined its efforts to bridge the gaps between constitutional guarantees and their realisation.
“The country’s trajectory was toward the progressive realisation of covenant rights,” he said, adding that despite constraints and challenges, Pakistan had made considerable progress since its first review.
“[Pakistan] hopes that the committee’s candour and rigour will help pave the way for the full realisation of economic, social and cultural rights for all,” he added.
Committee vice chair and acting chair of the dialogue, Asraf Ally Caunhye, thanked the delegation for its participation in the constructive dialogue and its expression of unwavering commitment to protecting the rights enshrined in the covenant.
The Pakistani delegation comprised representatives from the Ministry of Law and Justice, the Ministry of Human Rights and the Permanent Mission of Pakistan to the United Nations Office at Geneva.
Published in Dawn, November 5th, 2026

articles.summary:

The Democratic landslide will give the opposition power to block legislation, launch broad investigations into Trump’s administration and thwart his judicial and senior government appointments.
The vote reflected deep anger over living costs, tariffs and Trump’s war against I...
articles.full_text:
Democrats seized control of the US Congress on Wednesday, capturing the Senate and House of Representatives in a stunning, nationwide rejection of Donald Trump set to put the brakes on the final two years of his presidency.
The Democratic landslide will give the opposition power to block legislation, launch broad investigations into Trump’s administration and thwart his judicial and senior government appointments.
The vote reflected deep anger over living costs, tariffs and Trump’s war against Iran, which has sent fuel prices soaring and compounded dissatisfaction with an already deeply unpopular president.
    
            
        
    
Trump struck a conciliatory note despite his history of questioning election results, telling The New York Times: “I am absolutely willing to accept those results” and promising to “work with the Democrats”.
“I think the Democrats did a good job, I really do,” the 80-year-old told Fox News, in rare praise for his political opponents. “They fought hard.”
But he sought to distance himself from his own party’s poor showing, adding: “I don’t view it as a hit on me.”
He acknowledged that the Iran conflict had contributed to the defeat but defended the military campaign, and he suggested the rival parties could find common ground on immigration, long one of the most divisive issues of his presidency.
But minutes later on social media the 80-year-old signalled how he intends to deal with Democratic attempts to pass laws, posting a picture of a red baseball cap emblazoned: “VETO.”
    
        
    
        
    

        
    
The Democrats’ decisive Senate breakthroughs came in Kansas and Iowa, the fifth and sixth Republican-held seats to fall in the extraordinary “blue wave” election night.
In Kansas, Methodist minister Adam Hamilton defeated Republican incumbent Roger Marshall, becoming the first Democrat elected to the Senate from the reliably conservative state since 1932.
Iowa had not elected a Democratic senator since 2008, again illustrating the scale of party’s inroads into Republican strongholds.
    
        
        Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton speaks following her victory in the US midterm elections at a Democratic Election Night rally, in Columbus, Ohio, US, November 3, 2026. — Reuters
    
The upsets followed victories in Texas, South Carolina, North Carolina and Ohio, where voters rejected Republican candidates despite Trump’s intensive efforts to rally his supporters.
Democrat James Talarico ousted a Trump-backed Senate candidate, while Gina Hinojosa unseated Republican governor Greg Abbott, ending decades of Republican control of the state’s top office.
Talarico said that “we defeated Goliath” after winning a US Senate seat over Texas attorney General Ken Paxton, a close ally of President Donald Trump who was heavily backed by tech billionaire Elon Musk.
“In this race, we went up against our own Goliaths. The richest man in the world, the most powerful man in the world, and the entire Washington, DC establishment,” Talarico told a victory rally in the Texas capital, Austin.
Democrats also protected key Senate seats of their own, including Jon Ossoff’s in Georgia and an open seat in New Hampshire.
In California, Democrat Xavier Becerra handily defeated Donald Trump-backed Republican Steve Hilton in the race to become the governor, US networks said.
Partial results showed Becerra, a career politician who served in the cabinet of former president Joe Biden, had a nearly two-to-one advantage over Hilton, with about half of the ballots counted.
Becerra had run a low-key campaign in a state where Democrats heavily outnumber Republicans and where the Trump brand is almost toxic.
The son of Mexican immigrants, he will be the first elected Latino governor of California, a state that would be the world’s fourth-largest economy if it were a country.
“Ladies and gentlemen, you have now entered the Becerra era,” the former US Health and Human Services secretary told his supporters at a victory party in Sacramento.
“I didn’t run to make history,” he said. “I ran to make a difference for anyone and everyone who calls California home, whether you voted for me or not.”
Becerra will replace term-limited Governor Gavin Newsom, a Democratic Party big-hitter who is believed to have his eyes on a tilt at the White House in 2028.
    
        
        California Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra speaks at an election night event on November 3, 2026 in Sacramento, California. —AFP
    
Hilton, a British-born conservative former pundit who was once an adviser to former UK prime minister David Cameron, had always been a long shot.
He conceded he had lost a difficult race.
“Maybe this isn’t the best year to be running for office as a Republican when we see what’s going on around the country,” he said.
Republicans had held a 53-47 Senate majority.
The six-seat Democratic gain proved sufficient for networks to project a takeover despite some races remaining unresolved.
Republican heartland
Democrats also captured the House after flipping Republican-held districts in states stretching from Pennsylvania and New Jersey to Kentucky, Arizona and North Carolina.
Some victories came in territory Trump had carried comfortably in 2024, despite Republican attempts to shore up House seats by redrawing electoral boundaries.
One bellwether was Indiana, where Democrat J.D. Ford defeated Republican congresswoman Victoria Spartz in a district Trump won by 17 points. Analysts had identified an upset there as a warning of a much wider Democratic advance.
    
        
        Supporters react to early election results in favor of US Senator Jon Ossoff at an election night watch party hosted by the Democratic Party of Georgia after the midterms election in Atlanta, Georgia on November 3, 2026. — AFP
    
In Georgia, former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor in US history, while other Democratic gains extended to statehouses across the country.
Republicans had some bright spots in Florida, where Trump-backed Byron Donalds won the governorship, becoming the state’s first Black governor, and Ashley Moody kept a Senate seat.
George Washington University professor Todd Belt called the Democratic advance “a big wipeout and a strong repudiation of Donald Trump and his policies,” citing voters’ concerns about the economy, corruption and the Iran conflict.
Trump on defensive
Democrats will now be able to block Trump’s legislation, investigate his administration over corruption allegations, the Iran war and immigration enforcement, and use Senate control to thwart judicial appointments and senior nominations.
Robert Garcia, a Democrat expected to lead the powerful House Oversight Committee, warned Republicans on social media: “LAWYER UP.”
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries declared Trump’s MAGA movement “on the run from sea to shining sea.”
    
        
        House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) speaks during a press conference with the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) at the AC Hotel Washington DC Capitol Hill Navy Yard on November 03, 2026 in Washington, DC.
    
Jeffries is also positioned to become the first Black speaker of the House when the new Congress convenes in January, if elected by his colleagues.
As speaker, Jeffries, representing a New York City congressional district, would preside over a majority that will be sworn in the first week of January, taking the reins from Republicans who controlled the House for the past four years.
“Today begins the great American comeback,” Jeffries proclaimed in a victory speech late on Tuesday after media outlets projected the likelihood of Democratic majorities in the House and Senate.
For many voters, the central concern was Trump’s stewardship of the economy.
“Rent, groceries, utility bills, and property taxes keep climbing,” 24-year-old Los Angeles voter Taylor Cook told AFP.
A rebuke to Trump, winner says
“In sweeping and decisive victories, the American people have rebuked the depravity, corruption and incompetence of the man named President Donald J. Trump,” incumbent Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, the projected winner in Georgia, told supporters at a victory party.
In Florida, Republican Senator Ashley Moody fended off Democrat Angie Nixon but was ahead by only about three percentage points in a state Trump carried by 13 points in 2024, according to a vote count compiled by Reuters and USA Today, further evidence that even solidly Republican states were shifting dramatically toward Democrats.
Democrats held onto three House districts in Florida that Republican lawmakers had redrawn earlier this year, all of which backed Trump by at least nine percentage points, according to media projections.
    
        
        Cait Conley, Democratic candidate for the US House of Representatives in New York’s 17th Congressional District, reacts following her victory in the US midterm elections, in Pleasantville, New York, US, November 3, 2026. — Reuters
    
Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, a former mayor of Atlanta, on Tuesday was elected governor of the state of Georgia, becoming the first Black woman elected to that office in the US, media projections showed.
CNN and NBC News called the race in her favour.
Bottoms defeated billionaire health care executive Rick Jackson, who ran as a Republican. Current Governor Brian Kemp is term-limited and could not run again.
Midterm elections are typically viewed as a referendum on the president, and that is especially true for Trump, who dominates attention like no other politician. Trump himself told his supporters to “pretend I’m on the ballot” and held dozens of rallies in the closing weeks.

articles.title: Shafay ‘distances’ himself from Salik
articles.summary:

Shafay’s unequivocal support for Maryam has reportedly saved his position in the Punjab cabinet. “Shafay Hussain’s recent interviews have been supportive of Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz, so we have no plan t...
articles.full_text:
LAHORE: Punjab Commerce and Investment Minister Shafay Hussain has apparently distanced himself from his younger brother Salik Hussain, Federal Minister for Overseas Pakistanis who levelled corruption allegations against the provincial government of Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz a few days ago.
Shafay’s unequivocal support for Maryam has reportedly saved his position in the Punjab cabinet. “Shafay Hussain’s recent interviews have been supportive of Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz, so we have no plan to denotify him from the Punjab cabinet,” Information and Culture Minister Azma Bokhari told Dawn on Wednesday when asked whether the provincial government was considering removing him following his younger brother’s outburst against the chief minister.
“Shafay Hussain has rejected Salik’s allegations,” she added. The PML-Q has only one minister in the Punjab cabinet — Shafay Hussain. On Tuesday, Ms Nawaz served a Rs5 billion defamation notice on Salik over his corruption allegations against her government, demanding that he retract his remarks.
Salik said on Wednesday that he would respond to the notice.

Azma says no plan to denotify elder brother

The controversy also drew in former Punjab chief minister Chaudhry Parvez Elahi’s son, former federal minister Moonis Elahi, who took a swipe at Ms Nawaz over her remarks about Gujrat in a post on X. “Punjab was not handed over to you by my father. In fact, you became chief minister because of Form-47,” he said.
    
        
    
        
    

        
    
Meanwhile, Ms Bokhari asked Mr Salik to substantiate his corruption allegations or apologise, saying he could not enjoy the privileges of being part of the government while simultaneously engaging in political mudslinging.
She said it was unbecoming of a federal minister and a member of the ruling coalition to level allegations without producing evidence.
Defence Minister Khawaja Asif also weighed in on the controversy through a post on X, saying Mr Salik’s remarks about corruption in Punjab were beyond his limited political understanding. “Corruption is one of the biggest challenges facing our society, and it is the collective responsibility of the entire political leadership, both at the federal and provincial levels, to rid the country of this menace.”
    
        
    
        
    

        
    
The PML-Q is part of both the federal and provincial governments. We should join hands and wage a collective war against corruption,” he said.
Asif further said if Salik’s statement is part of a future political agenda aimed at targeting Ms Nawaz’s government to carve out political space for himself at both the provincial and federal levels and secure his political future, “it would make sense.”
The latest exchange comes against the backdrop of a political split within the Chaudhry family following the ouster of Imran Khan’s government through a no-confidence vote in 2022. While Chaudhry Parvez Elahi and his son Moonis Elahi aligned themselves with the PTI, Chaudhry Shujaat Hussain’s sons, Salik and Shafay, chose to side with the Sharifs.
Published in Dawn, November 5th, 2026

articles.title: Unilever Makes 35 Million-Euro Investment in Indian R&D Centers to Develop ‘Next Generation’ Products - Yahoo Finance Singapore
articles.summary: Unilever Makes 35 Million-Euro Investment in Indian R&D Centers to Develop ‘Next Generation’ Products  Yahoo Finance Singapore
articles.full_text:
AT SPEED: Unilever is investing 35 million euros in its Mumbai and Bangalore research and development centers with the aim of accelerating the development of "next-generation" products.
The consumer giant said the new investment will help the centers bring together a wide range of capabilities from consumer insight and scientific discovery to prototyping and scale-up "in one connected environment." It said the aim is to transform "world-class science into superior innovation at greater speed."
More from WWD
- Dick's Ramps Up Digital Performance With AI-Innovation Hub in India
- Rowing Blazers CFO Ditches Corporate World to Launch Badinage Brand
- Arvind Limited Opens State-of-the-Art Garment Manufacturing Facility
Richard Slater, Unilever's chief research and development officer, said the 35 million euros has been earmarked for projects including Liquids Lab of the Future; the Unilever Fragrance House; Advanced Manufacturing Center for soap bars; Packaging and Flexibles Design Lab, and AI and digital modeling platforms.
Unilever, he added, has already invested more than 20 million euros over the past five years to build those state-of-the-art capabilities.
As part of the new investment, Unilever will transform Mumbai into a product innovation center that will bring together "consumer insights, new measurement approaches, product and format science, packaging design, rapid prototyping and scale-up capabilities."
Bangalore will continue to evolve as a global science, technology and partnership hub, combining application and foundational science, digital capabilities and India Foods R&D, according to Unilever.
As part of the 35 million-euro investment, the company is earmarking 5 million euros over the next five years to establish a strategic Bio-Futures Partnership, to accelerate innovation across human biology, microbiome science, biotechnology and bio-manufacturing.
Across both India sites, AI, automated experimentation, predictive modeling and digital twins "will enable the Unilever scientists and product developers to explore more possibilities, learn faster and translate promising ideas into scalable innovations with greater speed and precision," according to the company.
Slater said India already plays a central role in Unilever's global innovation network, and the new investment "will further strengthen its position as one of our largest R&D hubs."
India is also one of Unilever's most important growth markets, "and it's changing fast. Consumer expectations are rising, needs are evolving and the pace of innovation keeps on accelerating. That makes it an incredibly important place for us to learn, create and scale new ideas," Slater added.

articles.title: Trump's midterm defeat gives China, Canada, India and Africa's largest economy fresh leverage in US trade talks - Business Insider Africa
articles.summary: Trump's midterm defeat gives China, Canada, India and Africa's largest economy fresh leverage in US trade talks  Business Insider Africa
articles.full_text:
- Democrats gaining control of both US Congress chambers has weakened President Trump's position, providing new leverage to major trading partners like China, Canada, India, and South Africa.
- India may delay making further concessions to Washington, as higher US tariffs on Indian goods and Democratic opposition to Trump's trade agenda improve India's negotiating stance.
- Canada's Prime Minister Carney signals readiness to wait out Trump for a fairer trade deal, expecting increased Democratic support for removing tariffs harming Canadian businesses.
- South Africa hopes the Democratic victory will prevent its removal from the AGOA program, with President Ramaphosa welcoming the chance for improved bilateral trade and investment relations.
The November 3 midterm elections saw Republicans lose their majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives, with Democrats securing victories in Republican strongholds, including Texas, Kansas and South Carolina.
Republicans suffered the setback amid rising living costs, Trump's tariffs and the eight-month Iran war, which disrupted energy supplies and pushed Brent crude to $138.21 per barrel in April, its highest level since 2008, fuelling US inflation.
From what Business Insider Africa has gathered, the results could encourage America's trade rivals and dissatisfied partners to resist Washington's demands, delay investments and seek better trade deals as Trump will now have to answer to a Democrat-controlled Congress.
China seeks tariff relief as Trump loses control of Congress
China is among the countries that could use Trump's weakened political position to push for more favourable trade terms, particularly as Beijing seeks to recover exports lost to American tariffs.
The impact of those restrictions is reflected in US trade figures, which show that America's goods trade deficit with China narrowed from $295.5 billion in 2024 to $202.1 billion in 2025.
With a temporary trade truce approaching expiration in January 2027, Beijing could seek lower tariffs and fewer technology restrictions, calculating that Trump faces greater political resistance to another trade war.
Saul Eslake, an economist at Corinna Economic Advisory in Australia, believes China could take advantage of the changing political balance in Washington.
"Xi Jinping will recognize that Trump's authority has been greatly weakened by these results, and will no doubt be thinking about ways of exploiting that," Eslake told Reuters.
Although Beijing has not publicly indicated plans to exploit Trump's political setback, China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning described the elections as an internal US matter, saying the country would continue managing differences and expanding cooperation with Washington.
Canada signals willingness to wait out Trump
Canada could also find greater support in Washington after months of difficult trade negotiations between Prime Minister Mark Carney and Trump's administration over tariffs and market access.
Talks stalled in August after Ottawa rejected American demands, while tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminium and other products continued to strain relations between the neighbouring economies.
In an October 30 interview with POLITICO, Carney indicated that Canada would rather wait for another American president than accept an unfavourable agreement.
Asked whether Canada could hold out until Trump's successor took office, he replied: "Well, if that's what it takes, yeah."
His position could receive support from Democrats, particularly Senator Ron Wyden, a senior member of the Senate Finance Committee, who has called for removing tariffs on Canadian goods because of their impact on businesses and consumers.
India could delay concessions to Washington
India could gain negotiating flexibility as New Delhi seeks better trade terms while American consumers face higher prices on imported goods.
Washington imposed tariffs of up to 50% on Indian products in 2025 amid trade disputes and disagreements over India's purchases of Russian oil. The restrictions affected textiles, jewellery and footwear, increasing costs for American importers.
The countries agreed in February 2026 to a framework reducing tariffs on most Indian goods to 18%, but negotiations remain unfinished.
Indian Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said the agreement had reached the final drafting stage, although New Delhi would proceed only if it secured an advantage over competing exporters.
Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman also acknowledged in October that further concessions would be "very, very difficult" for both sides.
The Democratic victory could encourage India to resist additional demands as Trump faces greater scrutiny of his trade policies from the Democrat-controlled Congress.
South Africa seeks relief amid AGOA crisis
South Africa faces a trade setback after Washington announced on November 2 that it would remove the country from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) on January 1, 2027, following months of diplomatic tensions over Pretoria's domestic and foreign policies.
The decision threatens preferential access for South African exports, including vehicles, citrus fruits and wine, adding to existing trade pressures after the country's agricultural exports to the US fell by 28% in the second quarter of 2026.
President Cyril Ramaphosa previously urged South Africans to prepare for possible exclusion, saying: "We should not go out and jump off tall buildings and think that this is the end of the world."
However, in a sharp reversal of his earlier cautious stance, Ramaphosa welcomed the Democratic victory on November 4, saying: "We have seen that the Democrats have taken control of the Senate and of the House, and the people of America have spoken."
He added that the results could introduce "a new era in world relations", raising hopes of improved ties with Washington.
"We're hoping that, on a bilateral basis, there will be a coming together of minds, where we will find a proper path forward on geopolitics as well as on trade matters and investment matters," Ramaphosa said.

articles.title: Trump's midterm setback may give India an edge in trade deal - Livemint
articles.summary: Trump's midterm setback may give India an edge in trade deal  Livemint
articles.full_text:
New Delhi: The US has sought to allay concerns that the Republicans’ midterm election defeat could derail trade talks with India, with an American embassy spokesperson telling Mint that President Donald Trump remains firmly in charge of Washington’s trade agenda.
Experts in India see challenges as well as opportunity from the development. While a Democrat-controlled Congress could make the ratification of a trade deal harder to accomplish, Trump’s political setback may also give New Delhi greater leverage at the negotiating table.
President Trump “remains firmly in command” of the country's foreign policy, including the trade agenda, the embassy spokesperson in New Delhi, said. “The midterm election results do not change our commitment to strengthening our partnership (with India),” the spokesperson said in response to Mint’s query on whether the Democratic control of the Congress would in any way impact the ongoing trade deal negotiations.
American voters have given the opposition Democratic Party control of the US Congress and flipped key gubernatorial posts. Trump’s Republican Party faced stunning defeats in its strongholds such as Texas, Georgia, Iowa and Ohio, where it lost the governors’ posts to the Democrats.
Indian strategic and trade experts reckoned that the setback to Trump's party could bring in fresh uncertainty over the trade deal prospects. Any agreement on the trade deal will need the Congress backing to be ratified, complicating the path to a final deal, they said.
“I think it would be very difficult for Trump to give us substantial comparative advantage in the trade deal vis-a-vis our competitors, as there is uncertainty now over Congress’ backing to any such deal,” said Jayant Dasgupta, former Indian Ambassador to the World Trade Organization.
But the result also opens a window to repair ties strained in recent years over India's purchases of Russian oil, with New Delhi asserting it will take all necessary steps to ensure its energy security amid geopolitical conflicts that have disrupted supplies and pushed up oil prices.
A White House facing fresh political constraints may now be more willing to accommodate India’s concerns, while New Delhi could enter any fresh rounds of talks with a stronger leverage, experts said.
“India now has greater leverage, and I hope we use it well,” said Biswajit Dhar, economist and a former professor at the Jawaharlal Nehru University.
Commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal had last month exuded optimism about an early closure and operationalization of the trade agreement, but only after India secures an export advantage over its competitors.
The US is India’s largest export market. India’s exports to the US were at $87 billion last fiscal.
Queries on the impact of the US midterm election result on India emailed to the spokespersons for the ministries of finance and external affairs did not receive an immediate response. A spokesperson for the commerce and industry ministry declined to comment.
Energy and markets
The poll outcome could calm the global oil markets if Trump steps back from escalating the ongoing war in West Asia, the experts said. But some flagged near-term risk of escalation in tensions in West Asia before the new Congress convenes in January.
Trump’s tariff strategy and war policies may face increased US Congress scrutiny in the coming months, which may result in unintended uncertainties in terms of trade policies towards India and investment flows, they said.
Brent futures were down 8.9% to $94.29 a barrel at 10.45 PM, the lowest level since 4 September, as Trump played down the prospect of Iran strikes following the Democratic sweep. Stocks of AI companies tumbled, as investors braced for greater regulation.
The Indian rupee stayed firm for the second straight session to settle 29 paise higher at 94.46 against the dollar, supported by easing crude oil prices. As of 10.45 pm pm India time, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 2.9%, while the Nasdaq composite was up 2.1% higher. The Gift Nifty traded up 1.75%, indicating a strong opening for the local market.
Some policy experts advised a wait-and-watch policy for India. “We have to wait to assess how Trump may react post midterm defeat, as given his personality, he may become more reactive towards India and internationally to distract domestic public attention,” said Ram Singh, an international trade expert and a professor at IIFT, New Delhi.
Energy experts expect some measure of stability in the global oil market. Manas Majumdar, leader, oil and gas at PwC noted that the results may restrict a further escalation in the war with Iran, thereby easing oil prices.
"This will put a curb on Trump. Although it may not result in an immediate policy change, it may lead to a faster closure to the war against Iran, which will ease the prices of oil," Majumdar said.
The Democrats have been largely against Trump's tariff regime, so some relief on that front is expected, said Prashant Vashisht, senior vice-president and co-group head, corporate ratings, at Icra Ratings.

articles.title: US Midterm Elections: How Trump's West Asia, Trade Moves Will Shape Indian Markets - Rediff
articles.summary: US Midterm Elections: How Trump's West Asia, Trade Moves Will Shape Indian Markets  Rediff
articles.full_text:
Following the US midterm elections, which saw Democrats take control of Congress, analysts anticipate a significant shift in investor focus towards the US administration's moves on West Asia and global trade, with direct implications for Indian markets, crude oil prices, and various sectors.
Key Points
- The US midterm election outcome, with Democrats controlling both the House and Senate, is expected to influence Indian markets via global financial conditions, trade policy, and geopolitical shifts.
- Investor focus will shift to the US administration's actions in West Asia, as diplomatic progress or escalation could significantly impact crude oil prices and global market sentiment.
- The election results may lead to legislative gridlock in Washington, potentially limiting President Trump's domestic policy agenda and increasing scrutiny of existing tariff and immigration policies.
- Indian IT companies remain sensitive to changes in US technology spending, H-1B visa regulations, and corporate outsourcing budgets.
- A potential decline in crude oil prices, possibly due to a US-Iran deal, would benefit India by reducing input costs and import burdens for sectors like oil marketing, aviation, paints, and chemicals.
The results of the US midterm elections are likely to influence Indian markets primarily through changes in global financial conditions, trade policy expectations and geopolitical developments, analysts said.
Investors' focus will shift to the US administration's next course of action on West Asia, as any further escalation or diplomatic progress could significantly influence crude oil prices and global market sentiment in the near term, according to an expert.
Democratic Gains and Policy Implications
In a stinging rebuke to President Donald Trump, American voters on Tuesday gave the opposition Democratic Party control of the US Congress and flipped key gubernatorial posts in widely watched elections that will have consequences far beyond America.
Trump's Republican Party faced stunning defeats in its strongholds such as Texas, Georgia and Iowa, where it lost the governors' posts to the Democrats.
The grand old party also faced a drubbing in Senate races in Texas, Maine, South Carolina, North Carolina, Kansas, Iowa – where Trump campaigned with a simple message urging voters to pretend that he was on the ballot.
The widespread losses were attributed to anger against Trump's policies, including the war on Iran, which have led to increased cost of living and high diesel prices.
"The US midterm election outcome, with Democrats securing control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, is likely to influence Indian markets primarily through changes in global financial conditions, trade policy expectations and geopolitical developments.
"The result has increased the possibility of legislative gridlock in Washington, potentially limiting the implementation of President Donald Trump's domestic policy agenda and increasing scrutiny of existing tariff and immigration policies.
"The immediate market reaction has been supportive for emerging markets, with the US dollar and Treasury yields declining, offering some relief to the Indian rupee and improving foreign investor sentiment," Gaurav Garg, Head - Research, Lemonn, said.
However, the impact on Indian equities will depend more on how these developments translate into actual policy changes rather than the election outcome alone, he said.
Sectoral Impact and Market Trends
"From a sectoral perspective, IT companies will remain sensitive to changes in US technology spending, H-1B visa regulations and corporate outsourcing budgets, while any improvement in US business confidence could support demand for Indian software services.
"Pharmaceuticals could benefit if trade and regulatory uncertainties ease, although US pricing and regulatory policies remain important risks," Garg added.
Stock markets rallied for the fifth straight day on Wednesday amid foreign fund inflows and easing crude oil prices.
The 30-share BSE Sensex rose 383.55 points, or 0.50 per cent, to settle at 77,301.40, its highest close in more than two months.
The 50-share NSE Nifty was up 149.75 points, or 0.63 per cent, to end at 23,960.60.
Oil marketing companies, aviation, paints and chemicals may gain if geopolitical tensions moderate and crude oil prices further decline, resulting in reduction in input costs and India's import burden, he said.
Conversely, upstream oil and gas companies could face pressure from lower crude prices, Garg said, adding that financial stocks may also respond to movements in US Treasury yields and foreign portfolio flows.
"Overall, the election outcome is a potential short-term positive for Indian market sentiment, but sectoral performance will remain differentiated, with currency movements, crude oil prices, US trade policies and domestic corporate earnings determining the sustainability of the market reaction," he said.
In the last five trading sessions, the Sensex has jumped 4,055.37 points, or 5.53 per cent, and the Nifty surged 1,261.75 points, or 5.55 per cent.
Future Focus: West Asia and Trade Deals
"Post the US midterm elections, investor focus will shift to the US administration's next course of action on West Asia, as any further escalation or diplomatic progress could significantly influence crude oil prices and global market sentiment in the near term," Siddhartha Khemka - Head of Research, Wealth Management, Motilal Oswal Financial Services Ltd, said.
"On the global front, markets remained mixed as investors assessed the implications of the US midterm election outcome, particularly for AI-related investments, global trade and geopolitical developments," Ajit Mishra, SVP – research, Religare Broking, said.
V K Vijayakumar, Chief Investment Strategist, Geojit Investments Ltd, said the Democrats' win in both the House of Representatives and the Senate will significantly reduce the powers of the President to act as he wishes.
"A likely positive fallout is that the Trump Administration might expedite the US-India trade deal to show positive results in the face of this setback.
"Also, since the excessive price of diesel is believed to have contributed significantly to the Republican loss, the President might try to reach a deal with Iran through Qatar mediation.
"The consequent possible decline in crude prices will be beneficial for India.
"Brent has already declined from last week's high of $118 to $102 now," Vijayakumar added.
IT stocks were the laggards on Wednesday's trade, with TCS, Infosys, HCL Tech and Tech Mahindra ending lower.
"The Nifty IT declined 1.5 per cent, tracking a broader sell-off in Asian technology stocks amid concerns over rising artificial intelligence spending and potential regulatory scrutiny following the US election outcome," Khemka said.

articles.title: Midterm Losses Unlikely To Soften Trump’s Trade Stance Towards India: Experts - ETV Bharat
articles.summary: Midterm Losses Unlikely To Soften Trump’s Trade Stance Towards India: Experts  ETV Bharat
articles.full_text:
With all other countries having stopped negotiating one-sided trade deals with the US, any future FTA will essentially be economic coercion, they tell Saurabh Shukla.
New Delhi: The midterm setback is unlikely to change Donald Trump's trade policy as both Democrats and Republicans favour economic nationalism and protective tariffs. According to latest report by Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI), Trump can continue using existing executive powers to impose trade pressure without Congress. With his foreign policy facing challenges with Russia, China and Iran, he may increase pressure on India for a trade deal to demonstrate American influence, adds the report.
As both Democrats and Republicans now favour economic nationalism, domestic manufacturing and strong supply chains, experts believe tariffs are likely to remain the new normal for the foreseeable future. With Democratic lawmakers also supporting protective tariffs to safeguard local union workers, overall trade stance of the US is unlikely to change.
To act without Congressional approval, the President is likely to continue relying on executive powers, such as sections 232 and 301. Experts also believe Trump's temperament and approach are unlikely to change in the short term.
As Democrats Sweep US Congress, Here's What The Victories Of 5 Indian-Americans Mean #IndianAmericansCongress #DemocratsSweep #USMidterms2026 https://t.co/IvYyyZnTaZ
— ETV Bharat (@ETVBharatEng) November 4, 2026
Trade Deal With India
According to the report, leaders on both sides have been saying for months that the trade deal is almost ready, though its completion was likely delayed because the US offer remained unclear. Trump will now use his executive powers to pressure India for a quick deal that secures market access for US agricultural and industrial goods, alongside other major concessions for US companies.
It also says that the trade deal India is negotiating with the US differs fundamentally from all other FTAs India has signed. In standard trade agreements, both countries cut or remove their regular WTO import duties, known as Most Favoured Nation (MFN) tariffs. Under the US - India framework, Washington will retain its MFN tariffs, while India must eliminate or reduce its MFN tariffs on most industrial goods and many agricultural products.
Under the February 6 US-India joint statement, India will also align its security and economic policies with Washington, commit to buying US$ 500 billion in US goods over five years, and ease domestic regulatory oversight of American imports.
In exchange, the US offers no direct reciprocal concessions. Instead, Washington may be using tariff threats to force compliance under its Graham Act and Section 301, especially over India’s Russian oil purchases. Even if India signs the deal, the US could still impose additional tariffs of 15-18 per cent on top of regular MFN rates. The deal will essentially be economic coercion, adds the report.
The report also mentioned that in April 2025, the White House had imposed reciprocal tariffs through executive action and offered to cut these additional levies — not standard MFN duties — to pressure major trade partners like Japan, the EU, the UK, South Korea, Vietnam, Malaysia etc., into signing unequal deals.
India followed a similar path, securing the February 6 joint statement, in which the US pledged to lower reciprocal duties from 25 per cent to 18 per cent. However, the US Supreme Court’s February 20 ruling, in Learning Resources, Inc. vs Trump, struck down those executive reciprocal tariffs under the IEEPA, removing Washington’s main bargaining tool overnight, it adds.
GTRI Flags Economic Coercion
According to GTRI founder Ajay Srivastava, with that ruling, the US lost its main concession, prompting all countries barring India to stop negotiating such one-sided trade deals. The resulting deal remains entirely one-sided, driven by US tariff threats over Russian crude purchases — even as Washington imports Russian-derived diesel itself, and overlooks China’s massive Russian oil imports.
He also stressed that India should not mistake relief from threatened tariffs for a balanced trade agreement. Opening its markets, committing to large purchases, and limiting its policy choices, would carry lasting costs, while any US tariff relief could prove temporary.
New Delhi should insist on clear, enforceable reciprocal concessions, consistency with WTO rules, and full freedom to protect its energy security and development priorities. The pressure to announce a deal must not outweigh the need to secure one that serves India’s long-term interests.
US Tariffs To Stay
Talking just after midterm election results, former Chairman of the Engineering Exports Promotion Council (EEPC), Arun Kumar Garodia, said tariffs are likely to become the new normal in the coming days, as both US Democrats and Republican parties see benefits in using them. Despite the midterm setback, Trump will retain significant powers, but the Democrats increased strength will make it harder for him to take decisions as freely as before. While this may not put a complete check on his authority, it will certainly limit his room to act.
The political developments could also have a short-term impact on stock markets. The Democrats are likely to push for the removal of tariffs or repeal of the provisions that allow the President to impose them. Some tariffs may be reduced under pressure, but a complete rollback is unlikely. Tariffs have now become a political weapon in the US, and both parties are likely to use them to serve their own interests.
Trump Unlikely To Change Course
Talking to ETV Bharat, former diplomat Rajiv Dogra said former US President Bill Clinton once recalled knowing Donald Trump for nearly 25 years. Speaking about tariffs, Clinton said Trump had told him even then that he would impose tariffs if he became President. Clinton however had cautioned him that tariffs ultimately amount to a tax paid by American taxpayers, and expressed concern that Trump tends to listen only to what he wants to hear.
Dogra stressed that this gives the impression that Trump is unlikely to be influenced by the changed political circumstances and will continue to pursue what he has already decided. His old ways and approach do not seem to have changed, as reflected in his recent statements.
Therefore there is unlikely to be any immediate shift in his policies towards India. Whether it is the deportation of Indian nationals, visa-related issues, remarks concerning Sikh truck drivers, or concerns surrounding computer professionals, these issues are unlikely to see any immediate change.
For India, he said the increased influence of the opposition in the US Congress is a positive development. However its ability to influence Trump's decisions will remain limited. The one issue the world will be watching very closely is how Trump deals with Iran, added Dogra.

Banks and specialised infrastructure financiers remain central, particularly for construction and greenfield projects.Non-banking financial companies, infrastructure finance companies, multilateral institutions and development finance institutions are also expanding their role. Meanwhile, bonds, external commercial borrowings, blended finance, credit enhancement and other structured financing mechanisms are creating additional sources of long-term capital.

The National Monetisation Plan 2.0 has a target to unlock Rs 10 trillion through monetization of brownfield assets during financial year 2026 through financial year 2030.
- However, availability of capital alone cannot determine the pace of infrastructure investment. Project bankability, execution readiness, land acquisition, regulatory approvals, counterparty strength, demand and offtake visibility, contractual certainty, and effective risk allocation remain critical to financing decisions.
- Going forward, there is an urgent need to scale up private sector investments. Strengthening public-private partnerships, enhancing municipal bond markets and promoting pooled financing mechanisms will be critical for private capital to scale further. Even long-term institutional investors such aspension funds and insurers remain underexposed to the infrastructure sector, and their participation must be encouraged as vital sources of patient capital.

Summary
- Northeast India is undergoing one of the most significant infrastructure transformations in the country, driven by strategic connectivity, economic integration and the government’s Act East policy.
- Over the past decade, thousands of kilometres of national highways have been constructed or upgraded, substantially improving access to remote and border regions. Landmark road projects such as the Sela Tunnel in Arunachal Pradesh and the Dhola–Sadiya Bridge have reduced travel times, improved all-weather connectivity, and strengthened logistics and defence mobility in the region. Highway expansion under Bharatmala and border-road programmes continues to enhance links between the Northeast and the rest of India.
- Railway infrastructure has witnessed equally transformative growth. The iconic Bogibeel Bridge across the Brahmaputra river has become a critical multimodal asset, connecting Assam and Arunachal Pradesh through both rail and road networks. Major rail projects such as the Bairabi–Sairang line in Mizoram have overcome difficult mountainous terrain through several tunnels and bridges. Meanwhile, extensive railway electrification and line-doubling projects across the Northeast Frontier Railway are improving operational efficiency, reducing carbon emissions and increasing freight capacity.
- Waterways and multimodal logistics are emerging as another important pillar of infrastructure development. The Brahmaputra and Barak river systems are increasingly being leveraged as inland water transport corridors under national waterway programmes, providing cost-effective alternatives for bulk cargo movement. Future projects, including the proposed underwater highway tunnel beneath the Brahmaputra, are expected to further strengthen the connectivity and resilience of transport networks.
- Despite impressive progress, the Northeast continues to face significant construction challenges owing to challenging topography, high rainfall, seismic risks and environmental sensitivities. However, these challenges also create substantial opportunities for innovation in resilient infrastructure, green construction materials, climate-adaptive design and digital project delivery.
- In recent years, construction practices in the Northeast region have evolved rapidly. Modern tunnelling technologies, advanced bridge engineering, geosynthetics, slope stabilisation systems, prefabricated components and high-performance concrete are increasingly being adopted to improve project delivery and durability. Digitalisation is also gaining momentum through the use of building information modelling (BIM), drone-based surveying, GIS-enabled planning, remote monitoring systems and digital project management platforms.
The mission of this conference is to discuss the emerging trends in infrastructure construction in the Northeast region; highlight the upcoming opportunities across key infrastructure sectors; identify new requirements in terms of design, material, equipment and technology; and discuss the unresolved challenges and next steps. It will also offer a platform for technology and equipment providers to showcase their solutions.

articles.title: US midterm election results 2026: India sees some trade relief, new risks after US midterm vote - The Economic Times
articles.summary: US midterm election results 2026: India sees some trade relief, new risks after US midterm vote  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
The Democrats won a landslide victory in both chambers of the US Congress on Tuesday in a sharp rebuke of President Donald Trump’s policies. His trade tariffs and war with Iran have been particularly damaging for countries like India, which counts the US as its biggest export market and is a major importer of oil from the Middle East.
The election result means more oversight of Trump’s policies and restrictions on the ability of the president to unilaterally impose reciprocal tariffs. That’s an important development and a positive for countries like India, officials in New Delhi said, asking not to be identified because they were not authorized to speak publicly on the matter.
Also read: US Midterm Elections 2026: Trump's handpicked candidate bets backfire as Democrats capture key Senate seats
A bruised Trump also gives India some breathing room in negotiations over a trade deal, reducing pressure on New Delhi to agree to terms it sees as unfavorable, the officials said.
Analysts and former officials said it’s too early to say how the election result this week would play out for countries like India.
“We must watch how the dynamics of Trump and the Congress evolves,” said Arun Kumar Singh, who served as India’s ambassador to the US in 2015-16. Time will tell “how President Trump absorbs the message of the electoral verdict and how he looks at his legacy for 2028 and beyond for the Republican Party,” he said.
Also read: 'Space lasers didn't work': Elon Musk mocks own election spending after Democrats' midterm sweep
Much will depend on the ability of the Democratic-controlled Congress to curtail Trump, said Ashok Malik, a former Indian foreign policy official and currently a partner at the strategic advisory firm Asia Group.
“Trump’s actions in the near term and the rest of his presidency will be an important metric,” he said. “This is true of the Iran conflict, but more generally for the unilateralism Trump has injected into trade, tariffs and foreign policy. This has destabilized the global system.”
The election result also has likely implications for US immigration policy, a major issue of concern for India. The Trump administration has sought to curb its H-1B visa program, used predominantly to hire Indian IT workers to work in the US. Firms like Microsoft Corp. as well as some of India’s biggest IT businesses, like Tata Consultancy Services Ltd. and Infosys Ltd., rely heavily on the program for skilled labor.
Nitin Pai, founder of Takshashila Institution, a think tank based in Bengaluru, said it was difficult to predict what comes next for US-India relations, although he remained relatively pessimistic.
“My assessment is India should prepare for the rough ride we have had for the last two years,” he said. “We have to pursue what’s in our national interest regardless of the election results.” The US system gives significant power to the president and executive, “so even if Democrats have some power it doesn’t mean he can’t do what he wants.”

articles.title: Trump's midterm setback may put India under pressure for quick trade deal on US terms: GTRI - The Economic Times
articles.summary: Trump's midterm setback may put India under pressure for quick trade deal on US terms: GTRI  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
The electoral setback is unlikely to change the broader direction of US trade policy, which is increasingly driven by economic nationalism, domestic manufacturing and efforts to strengthen supply chains, Srivastava said. Support for protective tariffs cuts across party lines, with Democrats also backing measures to protect domestic industries and union workers.
Also Read: US midterm election results: What Trump & Republicans' loss means for India
"With foreign policy leverage failing against Russia, China, and Iran, Trump needs a quick win. Expect heightened pressure on India for a trade deal to prove American clout," Srivastava said.
Trump is likely to continue relying on executive powers to pursue his trade agenda, including provisions under Section 232 and Section 301, executive orders, Treasury sanctions and US Trade Representative rules, to exert unilateral pressure on trading partners.
An unequal trade framework
The proposed India-US trade agreement differs significantly from the free trade agreements India has signed with other countries, particularly in its treatment of import duties.
The February 6 US-India Joint Statement also envisages India aligning its security and economic policies with Washington, committing to purchases worth $500 billion in American goods over five years and easing domestic regulatory oversight of US imports.
Also Read: Vivek Ramaswamy beaten at US midterms: Decoding a Republican firebrand's high-decibel fall
The US, however, has offered no direct reciprocal concessions under the proposed arrangement. Instead, tariff threats, particularly those linked to India's purchases of Russian crude oil under the Graham Act and Section 301 provisions, could be used to push New Delhi towards accepting the terms.
Even after signing the agreement, India could remain exposed to additional US tariffs of 15-18 percentage points over its regular MFN duties.
"The deal will essentially be economic coercion," Srivastava said, arguing that the proposed framework offers Washington significant concessions without comparable commitments in return.
US loses key negotiating leverage
Washington's approach follows its earlier strategy of using additional tariffs to extract concessions from major trading partners.
In April 2025, the White House imposed reciprocal tariffs through executive action and offered to reduce these additional duties, rather than standard MFN tariffs, to encourage countries such as Japan, the European Union, the United Kingdom, South Korea, Vietnam and Malaysia to negotiate trade agreements.
India followed a similar route, with the February 6 Joint Statement providing for a reduction in US reciprocal tariffs from 25% to 18%.
However, the US Supreme Court's February 20 ruling in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump struck down the administration's reciprocal tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), removing a key instrument Washington had used to secure trade concessions.
The ruling weakened the US negotiating position and prompted other countries to step back from pursuing agreements on similar terms. India remains the only country continuing negotiations under the proposed framework, Srivastava said.
He also questioned the rationale behind Washington's pressure on India over Russian oil purchases, pointing to US imports of Russian-derived diesel and China's substantial purchases of Russian crude.
WTO compliance concerns
The proposed agreement could also expose India to legal and diplomatic challenges at the WTO.
International trade policy and WTO expert Abhijit Das has warned that signing the proposed agreement would violate India's commitments under the WTO's MFN principle, which requires members to extend identical tariff treatment to all other members.
Under the current terms, India would grant preferential or duty-free access to most American exports without extending similar concessions to other trading partners.
Das has also questioned whether the arrangement would qualify as a legitimate free trade agreement under WTO rules, given that the US would not be reducing its own MFN tariffs in return.
By accepting such an asymmetric arrangement, India risks undermining its legal standing, credibility and negotiating power within the multilateral trading system.
New Delhi should not mistake relief from threatened tariffs for a balanced trade agreement, Srivastava argued. Opening its markets, committing to large purchases and restricting its policy choices could carry lasting costs, while any tariff relief offered by Washington could prove temporary.
India should instead insist on "clear, enforceable reciprocal concessions", consistency with WTO rules and the freedom to protect its energy security and development priorities, he said.

articles.title: 'Cannot remain in office': Spain transport minister quits six days after train disaster kills 69 - The Times of India
articles.summary: 'Cannot remain in office': Spain transport minister quits six days after train disaster kills 69  The Times of IndiaSpanish transport minister resigns days after deadly train crash  BBCSpain’s Transport Minister offers resignation after deadly train crash  The HinduSpanish transport minister resigns after two deadly train crashes in one year  CNNAll 69 victims of Spain's Urda train collision identified  CGTN
articles.full_text:
Spain’s transport minister Óscar Puente resigned six days after a high-speed train collision south of Madrid killed 69 people. Puente took responsibility for the second major rail disaster in the country this year. He announced his decision on Tuesday after appearing before lawmakers for several hours to explain the circumstances surrounding the October 28 crash.
“A transport minister in a country like Spain cannot remain in office after two accidents of this seriousness in less than a year,” Puente said.
Puente said he had decided to step down immediately after the latest accident but had kept the decision private. His resignation comes amid mounting pressure from opposition politicians and railway workers' unions, who had called for him to quit following the disaster.
What caused the deadly train collision?
The October 28 collision occurred when a high-speed train crashed into another train that had stopped on the tracks. The accident killed 69 people and raised serious questions about safety standards across Spain's extensive high-speed rail network.
The chain of events leading to the collision began when a communication system essential to the safety mechanism on the Madrid-Seville line failed. Controllers in Madrid then took charge and authorised a state-operated Renfe high-speed train to proceed, despite another train operated by private company Iryo being stationary ahead.
“There was a red signal prohibiting movement, yet the train was authorised to proceed,” Puente said last week. “It is a decision made under inexplicable circumstances.”
Second major rail disaster on the same route this year
The latest disaster was the second major train accident on the Madrid-Seville route this year. In January, two high-speed trains collided near Adamuz, killing 46 people. The accident, which occurred more than two hours further south along the route, remains under investigation.
Earlier on Tuesday, Puente announced a series of measures to improve railway safety. These include upgrading conditions in control centres and accelerating the rollout of the European Rail Traffic Management System, a standardised technology designed to improve railway signalling and safety.
Public anger and political pressure 
The resignation also comes amid growing public anger over the accidents. On the night of the October 28 collision, police clashed with hundreds of protesters outside the transport ministry headquarters. Some demonstrators carried placards demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.
Puente's departure comes just three weeks before Spain's general election. He had already announced that he would not contest the polls. Sánchez had called the election early following a series of corruption scandals, concerns over housing affordability and setbacks for his Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE) in municipal elections.
Spain's high-speed rail network, the second largest in the world after China's, has long been regarded as one of the country's major infrastructure achievements.
Before the two deadly accidents this year, the network had gone more than three decades without a fatal crash since its launch.

articles.title: India can't afford to ignore money growth - Business Standard
articles.summary: India can't afford to ignore money growth  Business Standard
articles.full_text:
The numbers explain why. Broad money, or M3, consists principally of currency and bank deposits. Its growth accelerated from around 9.3 per cent in 2024-25 to 15.3 per cent in 2025-26, while nominal gross domestic product (GDP) grew by less than 9 per cent in the latter year. Annual money growth remained at 16 per cent on October 15. Our compilation places M3 at approximately 91 per cent of GDP in March and around 93 per cent by September, using projected GDP. The ratio was approximately 86 per cent 18 months earlier. This represents substantial monetary expansion relative to income. 
 There is, however, a serious intellectual argument against assigning money growth an independent role in policymaking. In the New Keynesian framework associated with the recent Nobel prize winners, spending responds to current and expected future real interest rates. The relevant real rate is the nominal rate minus expected inflation. Lower real rates encourage spending today and weaken the incentive to postpone consumption. When prices adjust slowly, stronger demand eventually pushes up inflation. 
 From this perspective, monetary policy works through interest rates, expectations, and financing conditions. The central bank need not separately target money if these channels adequately capture the stance. Money may expand because banks lend more and create deposits, making it partly an outcome of economic decisions rather than an independent cause. Financial innovation also makes money difficult to define, while the central bank cannot precisely control broad money. 
 Moreover, creating bank reserves does not guarantee additional lending. Banks may retain liquid assets because they fear losses, lack capital or cannot find creditworthy customers. Borrowers may prefer repayment to fresh borrowing. The American experience after the global financial crisis illustrates why reserve creation need not translate proportionately into money, credit or inflation. 
 Monetarists would respond that this places too much confidence in policymakers’ ability to identify the correct interest rate. A nominal rate can look restrictive while being expansionary once expected inflation is factored in. Sustained growth in money beyond the public’s willingness to hold it encourages adjustment through spending and purchases of assets. Money, therefore, provides information that an interest-rate diagnosis can miss. The relationship is neither immediate nor mechanically proportional: Desired money holdings and the speed of spending also change. 
 India has two reasons to take this monetarist warning seriously. 
 First, the possibility that additional liquidity remains disconnected from lending is less reassuring when credit is already expanding strongly. Bank credit reached ₹227.43 trillion on October 15, growing 18.2 per cent over the preceding year, compared with 11.6 per cent a year earlier. This does not establish that reserve creation caused every additional loan. It establishes that we are not observing abundant reserves alongside stagnant bank lending. Money and credit are expanding together. 
 Second, and more importantly, India lacks a sufficiently reliable measure of the inflation expectations driving spending, saving and price-setting. Household survey expectations persistently exceed subsequent national consumer price index-based inflation. Some discrepancy reflects households’ different consumption baskets. Survey movements can still be informative. But using these numerical expectations to calculate the real rate remains problematic. 
 Professional forecasts help predict reported inflation, but they cannot substitute for understanding the expectations governing wage negotiations, rents, school fees and contract renewals. Those decisions determine how anticipated inflation enters future prices. We need better surveys and evidence from contracts committing parties to future payments. 
 Until then, monetary aggregates offer a valuable cross-check. Even someone convinced that money has no independent causal role should ask whether its growth improves inflation forecasts. Prediction does not require establishing that the predictor independently causes the outcome. If money growth helps anticipate inflation, ignoring it because causality is disputed would discard useful information. 
 This is compatible with a New Keynesian framework. If expected inflation is mismeasured, our estimate of the real rate is wrong. Rapid monetary and credit growth should prompt a reassessment: Is policy providing more stimulus than the nominal repo rate suggests? 
 Nor is all monetary growth dangerous. A growing economy needs more money, and financial deepening can justify a higher money-to-GDP ratio. The warning is persistent, substantial expansion beyond income growth without evidence of a corresponding increase in desired money holdings. 
 India’s historical experience suggests that 80-84 per cent of GDP is a useful reference range for broad money, not a scientifically established optimum. Returning towards it gradually would require money growth to lag nominal income growth, rather than an abrupt monetary contraction. 
 The repo rate should remain the principal instrument and inflation the objective. But money growth deserves an explicit place in forecasts, minutes and communication. When expectations are poorly measured, an interest-rate framework needs more cross-checks, not fewer.
 The writer teaches at Indian School of Business

articles.title: White House list of 127 ‘promises kept’ by Trump claims India-US trade deal, India-Pak ceasefire - WION
