articles.full_text:
Just hours ahead of the US midterm elections just hours away, the White House on Monday (Nov 2) released a list of 127 promises it says US President Donald Trump has fulfilled since returning to office, highlighting what it describes as major gains in trade, foreign policy, immigration and the economy.
The document, titled “President Trump’s Second Term: Promises Made, Promises Kept, Results Delivered” was released on the final day of campaigning. Among its claims are improved trade agreements with India and Trump’s role in ending eight international conflicts, including the May 2025 India-Pakistan conflict.
India trade deal and Pakistan ceasefire feature in Trump’s list
The White House credited Trump with securing “new and improved trade agreements” with major partners, including India, China, Japan, the UK and the European Union. It said the countries covered account for more than half of global GDP. However, the India-US trade arrangement has not yet been finalised. The two countries announced a framework for an interim agreement in February, committing to work towards its implementation and a broader bilateral trade agreement.
In the list, the White House also claimed that Trump ended eight conflicts including the conflict between India and Pakistan last year.
New Delhi, however, has repeatedly rejected claims of Trump’s mediation in security a ceasefire between the two countries following Operation Sindoor in May 2025. India maintains that the understanding to halt military action came after Pakistan's Director General of Military Operations (DGMO) contacted his Indian counterpart, without third-party involvement.
Trending Stories
Border security, economy among other claims
On immigration, the White House highlighted military deployments along the US-Mexico border, resumed border wall construction and the reinstatement of the “Remain in Mexico” policy.
It claimed that southwest border apprehensions fell 95 per cent compared with the annual average under former president Joe Biden. The administration also said more than three million undocumented migrants had left the country.
On the economy, the list cited tax deductions under the Working Families Tax Cuts, increased domestic oil and gas production and investment commitments secured through Trump's trade policies.
The administration also highlighted its artificial intelligence action plan, the GENIUS Act on stablecoins and NASA’s Artemis II mission.
The claims come as Americans head to the polls on November 3 to elect all 435 members of the House of Representatives and 35 senators. The results will determine control of Congress for the next two years, making the midterms a crucial test of Trump's presidency.

articles.title: Weakened Trump faces tough trade bargaining with India after US midterm setback - Deccan Herald
articles.summary: Weakened Trump faces tough trade bargaining with India after US midterm setback  Deccan Herald
articles.full_text:
New Delhi: President Donald Trump is likely to meet Prime Minister Narendra Modi and other Quad leaders in Manila this month, ahead of his meeting with President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen in southeastern China, even as the Republican Party’s drubbing in the US midterm elections has weakened his domestic political position and exposed his trade and foreign policies to greater congressional scrutiny.
The stunning rebuke US voters delivered to Trump has triggered speculation in New Delhi about the future course of India-US relations, particularly its implications for negotiations on the much-awaited trade agreement, which was said to be nearing completion. A politically weakened Trump could turn more protectionist to shore up domestic support, but his need to demonstrate economic gains could also give India greater leverage in the negotiations.
Trump’s domestic setback to reshape negotiations with New Delhi
Modi, Trump expected to meet in Manila at ASEAN & Quad summits
US midterm losses to increase pressure on Trump to secure economic wins
New Delhi seeks clarity on stalled India-US trade negotiations
He may also seek a trade understanding with Xi to ease tariff tensions and stabilise economic ties with Beijing, but any such rapprochement could have wider strategic implications for the Indo-Pacific and Washington’s commitment to the Quad – a four-nation coalition forged by India, Japan, Australia and the US to counter China’s hegemonic aspirations in the Indo-Pacific region.
Modi and Trump are likely to travel to Manila to attend the ASEAN summits and related meetings, including the East Asia Summit, which the Philippines, under President Ferdinand Romualdez Marcos Jr., is scheduled to host between November 14 and 18.
Though a bilateral meeting between the two leaders on the sidelines of the ASEAN and EAS meetings has not yet been scheduled, they are likely to be joined by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese for a Quad summit. This would be the first summit of the grouping since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025. His predecessor, Joe Biden, had hosted three of the five Quad leaders’ summits held during his presidency.
The timing of the Quad summit is significant for New Delhi as it comes just ahead of Trump’s meeting with Xi. The US President is likely to be under greater pressure to demonstrate economic gains after the midterm elections saw the Democratic Party win control of both chambers of Congress.
While Washington’s strategic competition with Beijing remains central to its Indo-Pacific policy, a possible economic accommodation between the two powers could test the strength of US commitments to its regional partners, particularly India, Japan and Australia.
The Democratic takeover of both chambers of Congress will make it considerably harder for Trump to push through his domestic legislative agenda and expose his administration to greater congressional scrutiny. Democratic lawmakers will gain control of key committees, enabling them to summon administration officials, demand documents and investigate the President’s policies.
They will also have greater leverage over government spending and, through control of Senate committees and floor scheduling, could delay or block consideration of Trump’s nominees for senior executive and judicial positions. However, the electoral setback will not take away Trump’s executive powers over foreign policy, including his authority to conduct diplomacy and negotiate with other countries.
Nor will it automatically prevent him from pursuing trade arrangements with China or India. Instead, a Democratic-controlled Congress could make it more difficult for him to translate some of his initiatives into legislation and could subject the use of his executive powers, including tariff measures, to greater scrutiny.
Modi was among the first world leaders to meet Trump at the White House after his inauguration for a second term in January 2025. During their meeting on February 13, 2025, the two leaders agreed to pursue a bilateral trade agreement, targeting the first tranche for negotiation by autumn that year.
The relationship, however, came under strain in the months that followed, with Trump repeatedly claiming credit for brokering the May 2025 ceasefire between India and Pakistan, his administration’s growing engagement with Pakistan’s civilian and military leadership, the imposition of steep tariffs on Indian exports and Washington’s pressure on New Delhi to stop buying Russian crude oil.
India’s concerns over Washington’s failure to adequately appreciate the threat of cross-border terrorism emanating from Pakistan added to the strain. Jaishankar later said progress on the trade agreement could help improve bilateral relations, even as he stressed the need for patience and a better understanding of each other’s economic realities.
Even if the two leaders get a chance to hold a brief bilateral meeting in Manila, the India-US trade agreement is likely to feature prominently in their discussions. Both sides have repeatedly indicated that negotiations are nearing completion. Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said that most discussions had concluded and the two sides were fine-tuning the agreement. External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar, however, cautioned that the final stage could still throw up challenges.
Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said that negotiations had reached a plateau beyond which further give-and-take could prove difficult. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Washington’s Ambassador to India, Sergio Gor, meanwhile, expressed confidence that the deal is within reach. Gor said that the big issues had been settled. New Delhi would be keen to use the opportunity in Manila to take stock of the negotiations and seek clarity on the way forward, particularly on the outstanding differences over the terms of the proposed agreement.
For Trump, clinching a deal with India could offer an important economic and diplomatic success at a time when his administration faces greater political scrutiny at home.

articles.full_text:

Going forward, the setback to Trump's second term in office, with the Democrats seizing control of the House and the Senate, could henceforth provide greater clarity on tariffs and market access, helping drive India's exports to the US, experts said.
Also read | Did Iran just make Trump cry? How Republicans may have taken a direct war hit
"The results have changed the equation significantly," said Biswajit Dhar, a leading trade expert. "The power of the US President will be curtailed as Congress will not give him a free hand."
Bank of Baroda, said the US trade pact is unlikely to be affected by the election outcome, expecting the existing provisions of the deal to remain unchanged.
Tariff may be reviewed
"While the trade agreement itself is unlikely to undergo any changes, a review of tariffs remains a possibility, particularly if Americans increasingly view higher tariffs as a key contributor to rising inflation in the US," Sabnavis said, adding such a move could benefit several countries, including India.
The US is the largest export market for India.
Vijay Agarwal, former chairman of the Textile Export Promotion Council, said the Democratic Party's victory could heighten Congressional scrutiny of Trump's tariff policies, creating potential opportunities for Indian textile and apparel exporters to seek more favourable trade terms.
"However, the existing 18% tariff is unlikely to change immediately, while the India-US trade agreement may face some uncertainty and delays," he said, adding India should therefore engage proactively with both the Trump administration and the Democrat's control of Congress to secure a stable and mutually beneficial trade framework.
With trade issues within the Congress's remit, experts expect the US government's overall policy regime to remain stable for the remainder of Trump's tenure sans any further irrational tariff hikes.
"What will matter to Indian exporters in the months ahead is how US policy on tariffs and market access takes shape," said Ajay Sahai, director general of the Federation of Indian Export Organisations (FIEO). "MSMEs, in particular, need predictable trading conditions to price orders confidently and plan shipments months in advance."
Also read | What Trump & Republicans' midterms loss means for India
As part of the framework announced in February by the two countries for the first phase of the BTA, the US had committed to withdrawing the additional 25% tariff on Indian imports linked to New Delhi's procurement of Russian oil, while bringing down the reciprocal tariff to 18%.
However, the US Supreme Court, on February 20, struck down the reciprocal duties imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA).
Subsequently, US slapped fresh 10% duty on Indian goods under a Section 301 probe into alleged forced labour practices. The measure applies to 16 other countries as well and is lower than the 12.5% tariff proposed by Washington in June as part of a broader Section 301 probe.
India's exports to the US rose 11% year-on-year to $50.8 billion in the first half of FY27. Imports climbed 26% to $32.3 billion in the same period.

articles.full_text:
ISLAMABAD: The National Accountability Bureau (NAB) has summoned former federal minister for communication Asad Mahmood, who is the son of JUI-F president Maulana Fazlur Rehman, for alleged irregularities in 4,252 appointments at Pakistan Post during his 2022-23 term.
The development came after Maulana Fazl’s new tirade against the government and state institutions on issues concerning main opposition Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) and terrorism.
According to a NAB notice, the bureau is investigating alleged irregularities in appointments made at Pakistan Post during Mr Mahmood’s tenure as federal minister between 2022 and 2023. The ex-minister is accused of making as many as 4,252 appointments against fewer approved vacancies, with discrepancies in the number of sanctioned posts in Pakistan Post.
The anti-graft watchdog has directed Mr Mahmood to appear before its investigation team on Nov 10 at 11am.

Bureau to probe excessive appointments allegedly in violation of cabinet committee’s direction

Mr Mahmood had served as federal minister during the last PML-N-led Pakistan Democratic Movement (PDM) government in 2022-23. The PDM had formed the government after toppling the Imran Khan government, which had served from 2018 to 2022, through a vote of no-confidence.
The notice stated that the Establishment Division had authorised recruitment against 3,938 posts at Pakistan Post. However, 4,252 people were allegedly appointed, exceeding the approved number. The NAB said that 2,646 appointments were made against posts that had already been abolished, in violation of the directions of a cabinet committee.
The bureau said a large number of permanent appointments were made against the recommendation for recruitment on a contractual basis only. The investigation also covered allegations that the appointments placed an additional financial burden on Pakistan Post. The aspect of alleged political affiliations among some selected candidates is also being examined.
Other allegations include the use of fake and forged documents, recruitment of candidates over the prescribed age limit and violations of the domicile quota during the hiring process. The NAB has warned that failure to comply with the summons could result in legal action under Section 31 of the National Accountability Ordinance, 1999.
FIA probe
The notice by NAB has been issued at a time when the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) is also investigating alleged corruption and irregularities in Pakistan Post recruitments.
The FIA’s Anti-Corruption Circle in Islamabad had separately issued a notice summoning Mr Mahmood to record his statement in connection with the case.
Published in Dawn, November 5th, 2026

articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON: A US federal court blocked on Tuesday the Trump administration’s plans to deport scores of Afghan immigrants back to Afghanistan, a move advocacy groups said could endanger their lives.

Judge Valerie Caproni of the US District Court for the Southern District of New York ruled that the United States could not send any Afghan nationals to Afghanistan or Pakistan this week. US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Deputy Assistant Director Christopher George told the court there were “no planned or confirmed chartered or commercial flights” to deport Afghan nationals in the US to Afghanistan or Pakistan this week, according to court documents.

US media reported last week that more than 150 Afghans in the US would be deported via Pakistan to Afghanistan as part of President Donald Trump’s latest immigration crackdown. Among the group were relatives of Afghans who assisted the US military in the country prior to the fall of Kabul, according to AfghanEvac, a group seeking to help former Afghan allies.

“A week ago, there was a plane. Today, the government told a federal judge there isn’t one,” AfghanEvac President Shawn VanDiver said in a statement after Tuesday’s ruling. “That didn’t happen by accident. Veterans, advocates, 66 members of Congress, and thousands of Americans got this flight stopped,” he added. Afghanistan’s Taliban authorities voiced “serious concern” on Monday over the reported deportation plans. Advocacy groups have warned that the removal of former allies and their families could endanger their lives.

After regaining power in 2021, Taliban authorities announced a general amnesty for Afghans who worked with Western-backed forces and governments and have repeated promises this year that their former foes could safely return home. But the United Nations has recorded reports of extrajudicial killings, detentions and abuses.

articles.full_text:
India imports almost 90% of its crude oil needs and about 30% of these imports currently pass through the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran has exempted merchant vessels from India, China, Iraq and Qatar from restrictions on using the Strait of Hormuz, and the measure is aimed at facilitating the procurement of medicines from India, an influential Iranian lawmaker has said.
Amir Hayat-Moghaddam, deputy chairman of the Iranian parliament’s national security and foreign policy committee, said ships from these four countries can “pass freely” through the strategic waterway and the US too is not stopping them either.
“We have currently exempted India, China, Iraq and Qatar from transit restrictions in the Strait of Hormuz. Ships from these countries pass freely, and the Americans do not intercept them either,” Hayat-Moghaddam said in an interview with the Iranian Students' News Agency on Tuesday.
Also read | Besieged by war, Saudi Aramco continues to gush profits
The exemptions are aimed at shoring up Iran’s interests related to these countries, he indicated. Iran is facilitating the passage of Indian ships to enable the import of medicines from India, while the exemption for Chinese shipping is aimed at securing China's political support, he said, speaking in Farsi.
Hayat-Moghaddam said Iran collects transit fees from Indian and Chinese vessels, and allows Qatari vessels to pass without charges. He didn't specify whether Iraqi vessels have to pay transit fees.
India imports almost 90% of its crude oil needs and about 30% of these imports currently pass through the Strait of Hormuz. In the past, the strait accounted for 70% of India's crude imports, but the dependence has declined because New Delhi has begun diversifying imports with purchases from Russia, the US, West Africa, and Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) since the start of the West Asia conflict.
Also read | Iran president says return to war benefits 'no one', after reported US strikes on Qeshm island
However, 90% of India's LPG imports transit the Strait of Hormuz, and more than 50% of its LNG imports from Qatar and the UAE is transported through the waterway. The strait is also crucial for the country's fertiliser imports.
Following Iran’s decision to close the Strait of Hormuz and impose restrictions on the passage of merchant shipping, India has repeatedly called for the unimpeded movement of energy supplies and freedom of navigation in international waterways.
The Strait of Hormuz, located between Iran and Oman, currently accounts for almost 25% of global sea-borne oil supplies originating in West Asian countries.
Also read | Indian injured in attack on Saudi airport dies, total West Asia toll now 24
Hayat-Moghaddam’s remarks came against the backdrop of continuing restrictions on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. The European Union (EU) has said Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy has put in place a system requiring ships to provide identification and information on their cargo and destination in order to secure passage.
According to the International Maritime Organization (IMO), there were at least 70 attacks on merchant ships between the start of the conflict in February and August. These attacks resulted in the death of 19 seafarers. Fifteen seafarers are among the 24 Indians killed so far in the West Asia conflict.
- Rezaul Hasan Laskar is Foreign Editor with the Hindustan Times, which he joined in 2015. He began as a journalist in his hometown of Shillong in northeast India and has worked in newspapers and wire services over the years. He moved to New Delhi in 1997 and initially focused on defence, national security, Jammu and Kashmir and the northeast, while also working of foreign policy and international relations. He has been part of the media delegation accompanying PMs on foreign visits and has reported from destinations ranging from Tibet to Ukraine. Between 2007 and 2013, he was the Press Trust of India correspondent in Pakistan, one of only two Indian journalists allowed to report from the country. He extensively covered Pakistan’s domestic politics and the life of the common people, as well as the fallout of the 2008 Mumbai attacks on India-Pakistan relations and the subsequent trial in Pakistan of the suspects involved in the attack. As part of his reportage in Pakistan, he travelled the breadth of the country, from the Swat Valley to Balochistan. articles.title: Evolving climate architecture
articles.summary:
PAKISTAN stands at a crossroads as it prepares to attend COP31 in Turkiye next week. articles.full_text:
PAKISTAN stands at a crossroads as it prepares to attend COP31 in Turkiye next week. Every October, the Emissions Gap Report brings bad news, and every October we read it as a scorecard of how far the world is from Paris. This year, it is not a progress report. It is notice that the Paris benchmark has been breached.
The United Nations Environment Programme’s 2026 report concludes that the chance to hold warming below 1.5 degrees Celsius with no or limited overshoot “is gone”. The task now is to “minimise overshoot and return to 1.5°C”. The target survives; its meaning has flipped. No longer a ceiling, 1.5°C is a line we will cross and then try to get back under. Even the “lowest possible” overshoot peaks at 1.7 to 1.8°C.
For Pakistan, this is not abstract arithmetic. The gap between 1.5 and 1.8 is more poverty and heat in Jacobabad, wilder monsoons in Sindh, transboundary floods in Punjab, and faster glacial melt in the upper Indus. The question is simple: who pays for the overshoot years?
Just as the science matters most, the body that certifies it is going broke. For the first time in its history, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) “might not have the funds to finish an assessment report”, Nature warned recently. Contributions have fallen since 2023, and Washington has walked away. The panel needs more than CHF 20 million ($24m) to survive until 2029, less than many single-donor projects in Islamabad.
Nor can it agree on a timetable. In Addis Ababa last month, governments failed for the sixth meeting running to decide when its next reports come out. A small bloc wants the reports on emission cuts and adaptation delayed until after the 2028 global stocktake, the five-yearly review of progress under Paris. The reasons are procedural; the effect is political. For the most vulnerable countries, that delay is betrayal. Yet Pakistan, the self-declared ground zero of climate impacts, stayed away from the forum that certifies the evidence.

We need some $47bn a year to 2030 but receive under $2bn.

It is not for want of evidence. In August, the Pakistan Meteorological Department (PMD) published How the Climate of Pakistan Has Changed, a 45-year record and the most granular we have. Nights are warming faster than days, and springs across much of the country are up to 2.5°C warmer than in the 1980s and 1990s. Rain has become not scarcer but less dependable: the 2022 monsoon dumped up to 450 per cent above-average rain on the south, and three years later, the winter of 2024-25 brought a 67pc national deficit. That is the overshoot world in miniature.
The EU’s Paris Agreement Overshooting: Reversibility, Climate Impacts and Adaptation Needs (PROVIDE project), which studied exactly such risks, had an Islamabad partner, so the research clearly exists.
What is missing is the habit of carrying it into the rooms where global science, and therefore, global money, is decided. The empty chair reflects a deeper reflex. Pakistan’s climate diplomacy still treats finance as something to ask for: grants, owed as a moral debt by those who caused the problem. The argument is right on the merits and increasingly beside the point.
The COP29 goal of $300 billion a year is being hollowed out by the governments that pledged it, and what grant money remains goes to countries ready to absorb it. On that test, Pakistan fails. We need some $47bn a year to 2030 but receive under $2bn. The gap is not one of vulnerability but readiness.
Meanwhile, a new architecture is taking shape elsewhere, and in one corner of it Pakistan already leads. At the World Bank-IMF annual meetings in Bangkok last month, Islamabad took the chair of the Borrowers’ Platform, which gives debtors what creditors have in the Paris Club: a place to pool data, compare terms, and bargain as a bloc. On Nov 1, it also assumed the chair of the G-24, the developing-country caucus at the IMF and World Bank.
For a year then, Pakistan speaks for the debtors just as debt has become the main channel of climate finance. Disasters are paid for with borrowing, and each recovery loan makes the next shock harder to absorb.
Pakistan, where debt servicing eats 43pc of the federal budget, is itself a textbook case. Of the $10bn pledged at Geneva after the 2022 floods, about $8.7bn came from lenders. We were asked to borrow our way out of a disaster we did little to cause.
New instruments attack this chain link by link. Debt-pause clauses suspend repayments after a disaster; Grenada used one after Hurricane Beryl to defer about $30m. The V20, a bloc of finance ministers from the most climate-vulnerable countries, is building a Lifeline Fund that would pool members’ reserves into a $500m emergency facility. Africa’s new rating agency challenges unfair risk premiums; Mia Mottley’s Bridgetown Initiative demands cheaper, longer loans. Each treats climate as a balance sheet problem, and that is where the post-Paris order is taking shape.
Pakistan now heads the borrowers’ table and leaves an empty chair at the scientists’ table. The two are linked: a debtor bloc that wants climate risk priced into debt terms needs credible, nationally owned evidence, and the IPCC is where such evidence gains global standing.
Four steps follow before Antalya. First, rejoin the science table: pay into the IPCC trust fund, attend the resumed session in December, and back the least developed countries and small islands on a 2028 timeline. Second, put the PMD record to work in AR7, the next Nationally Determined Contributions, and the annual budgets. Third, trade appeals for readiness, with bankable adaptation projects, accredited national entities and climate tagging in the budget. Fourth, use the Borrowers’ Platform chair to make debt-pause clauses standard in sovereign lending and to tie debt and climate together at the stocktake.
The world has moved past the Paris target and is moving past COP as the only place where climate is decided. The winds of change are blowing elsewhere. Pakistan should stop treating COPs as tourist destinations and start engaging where the rules are written.
The writer is a climate expert.
Published in Dawn, November 5th, 2026

ISLAMABAD: Pakistan has secured a $3 billion rollover from Saudi Arabia, as prospects of a proposed $10bn US backstop facility appear to have waned, it emerged on Wednesday.
Speaking to journalists at Parliament House, Finance Minister Muhammad Auran­gzeb confirmed that Riy...
articles.full_text:
• Aurangzeb says proposed US facility is not essential, would provide additional support if secured• Further Eurobond, Panda bond and rupee-linked dollar-settled issuances planned• Govt targets $4bn reduction in external debt
ISLAMABAD: Pakistan has secured a $3 billion rollover from Saudi Arabia, as prospects of a proposed $10bn US backstop facility appear to have waned, it emerged on Wednesday.
Speaking to journalists at Parliament House, Finance Minister Muhammad Auran­gzeb confirmed that Riyadh had extended the $3bn financing it provided in April this year to bridge a gap arising from $3.5bn in repayments to the United Arab Emirates.
“It has been extended and for a reasonable period. You don’t need to worry as to for how long given the kind of strategic relationship we have,” he said when asked about the facility, which matured on Oct 31 under its three-month term.
He said he had a very good meeting with his Saudi counterpart, Mohammed Al-Jadaan, during the recent World Bank-IMF meetings in Bangkok. Saudi Arabia had already extended its $5bn facility until 2028.
Asked whether Pakistan had also sought additional support, the minister categorically denied it, saying this was not needed as foreign exchange reserves covered more than three months of imports and would be strengthened to provide a four-month import cover by the end of the year through capital markets.
Responding to another question about the prospects of the $10bn Exchange Stabilisation Support Facility (ESSF) requested from the US in July this year, he sought to lower expectations that he himself had raised over the past several months. “What we asked for back in July and were looking at was the market access. We have got the market access,” he said, referring to the $3bn bond Pakistan issued in September against orders worth $6bn.
“If that (ESSF) materialises, fantastic, it will be a liquidity support facility. Otherwise, we have plans for further Eurobond issuance, Panda bond issuance and rupee-linked dollar-settled bond,” the minister said.
He added that he had held meetings with 70-80 institutional investors in Bangkok, who had a very clear view of Pakistan, and that offers were available for five-year and 10-year maturities, “because clearly we are looking beyond the [IMF] programme”.
He said the government was looking at the US from a broader perspective, as the US Export-Import Bank and Development Finance Corporation (DFC) needed to support their investors and exporters in Pakistan. “That is real financing and real credit,” he said, adding that the ESSF request was for a liquidity support facility to help the sovereign. “If possible, fine; if not, we are going to move forward, with or without it.”
The finance minister also reported that the IMF Executive Board meeting to approve a disbursement of $1.2bn to Pakistan would be held in December.
External debt
Earlier, he told the Senate Standing Committee on Finance that Pakistan was targeting a reduction of $4bn in external debt during the current fiscal year and $3.5bn next year, compared with $4.5bn in the last fiscal year.
He said the government was seeking to replace expensive short-term borrowing with longer-maturity financing through bonds and private placements to reduce refinancing risks. He said external debt had been rising by $5-6bn annually, from $45bn in 2014-15 to around $100bn, but had increased by only $1bn annually over the past two years.
“Our objective is not to increase external debt. All the transactions like Eurobond, Panda bond or private placements have been replacement bonds to replace expensive with cheaper facilities,” he said, adding that fiscal discipline had helped contain the fiscal and current account deficits and, despite oil and wheat import bills, the current account deficit would be no more than 1pc this year.
“This is hard-earned stability that helped create buffers to meet our requirements despite floods and war in the region, and foreign exchange reserves crossed $21.5bn, which is the best-ever level of reserves in our history,” he said, adding that Pakistan could not afford to lose this basic hygiene.
Finance Secretary Imdadullah Bosal told the committee, which was presided over by Senator Saleem Mandviwalla, that public debt had declined to 68.6pc of GDP by the end of June 2026, from 75.1pc in fiscal year 2022-23. Year-on-year growth in public debt had slowed to 7.7pc in the last fiscal year, the lowest in 20 years, he said.
The secretary said domestic debt amounted to Rs58.8 trillion by the end of August 2026, down from Rs68.4tr at the end of June, while foreign debt remained stable at $98.2bn.
He reported net financing requirements of $11bn after rollovers and refinancing, of which $5bn had already been repaid in the first four months of the current fiscal year. The remaining $6bn was payable over the next seven months.
The committee took strong exception to the difficulties faced by parliamentarians in obtaining foreign exchange for personal travel, saying the humiliation they faced at the hands of banks and the central bank was unacceptable.
Mr Mandviwalla directed the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) to review existing procedures, including clearance requirements relating to politically exposed persons (PEPs) and the mandatory personal appearance of parliamentarians before exchange companies, despite their submission of valid passports, tickets and visas.
The committee also expressed serious displeasure over the SBP’s response, dated Oct 30, 2026, to a letter sent by the committee secretary on its behalf to the SBP governor. It observed that the matter had been addressed by a deputy director-level officer instead of an appropriately senior authority.
The chairman termed the requirement for personal appearance humiliating and called for an immediate review of the existing procedures, warning that the committee would take serious notice if the matter remained unresolved.
Published in Dawn, November 5th, 2026

articles.full_text:
Bhubaneswar-based Indian Metals & Ferro Alloys Ltd (IMFA), an integrated producer of value-added ferro chrome, on Wednesday reported revenue of ₹968.17 crore and EBITDA of ₹235.04 crore in the quarter ended September 30, 2026 (Q2 FY27), supported by higher volumes following an increase in production capacity.
The company’s Q2 FY27 revenue was up 34.7 per cent year on year from ₹718.65 crore in the corresponding quarter last year.
Exports, a key contributor to the business, increased to ₹817.54 crore in Q2 FY27 from ₹603.96 crore a year earlier.
For the first half of FY27, exports stood at ₹1,611.15 crore, up from ₹1,160.22 crore in the corresponding period last year.
Kalinganagar project increases capacity
Odisha chief minister Mohan Charan Majhi inaugurated IMFA’s greenfield project at Kalinganagar on October 14.
The first furnace is operational, and commissioning of the second furnace has commenced, with hot metal tapping expected soon.
During Q2 FY27, ferro chrome production increased to 86,652 tonnes from 65,671 tonnes in the year-ago quarter. Sales rose to 81,998 tonnes from 69,765 tonnes.
IMFA Managing Director Subhrakant Panda said the expansion of smelting capacity, following the commissioning of the Kalinganagar project, would help the company meet rising demand.
He added that the company was focusing on hybrid renewable energy, niche ferrochrome grades, and a proposed diversification into low-carbon ferrochrome to broaden its product portfolio and support margins.

articles.title: Who is Hakeem Jeffries? Democratic leader poised to become first Black US House speaker - The Times of India
articles.summary: Who is Hakeem Jeffries? Democratic leader poised to become first Black US House speaker  The Times of IndiaHakeem Jeffries, on track to make House speaker history, sees ‘mandate for dramatic change’  CNNHow Democrats' victory will reshuffle party leadership in Congress  ReutersElection 2026 live results: Hakeem Jeffries officially launches bid to be 1st Black speaker of the House  ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and VideosHakeem Jeffries poised to be...
articles.full_text:
Hakeem Jeffries is set to become the first Black Speaker of the US House of Representatives after Democrats secured majority control of the chamber in the 2026 midterm elections, setting up a historic change in congressional leadership. The 56-year-old New York lawmaker formally launched his bid for the speakership on Wednesday.
Jeffries' elevation would mark a milestone in the history of the US Congress, more than 150 years after Joseph Rainey became the first Black American elected to the House in 1870. The speakership is the only congressional leadership position established by the US Constitution and places its holder second in the presidential line of succession.
Addressing supporters at a Democratic election watch party in Washington, Jeffries was greeted with chants of "Speaker! Speaker!" as his party celebrated its return to the House majority.
"This is not a partisan moment. This is a patriotic one," Jeffries said, adding that voters had called for significant political change.
"We hear you," he said. "We're going to work hard to deliver on the dramatic change that you deserve."
Jeffries has led House Democrats for four years and is expected to succeed Republican Mike Johnson. His rise would also make him the highest-ranking Black elected official in the country.
Who is Hakeem Jeffries?
Born in Brooklyn, New York, Jeffries grew up in a family with an Air Force veteran father and a social worker mother. He has said that witnessing the effects of the crack epidemic in his neighbourhood influenced his decision to enter public service.
In an interview with The Associated Press during the campaign, Jeffries said his upbringing gave him a desire to improve conditions for working people who remained in their communities despite difficult circumstances.
He studied at the State University of New York at Binghamton, earned a master's degree in public policy from Georgetown University and graduated magna cum laude from New York University School of Law.
Before entering Congress, Jeffries worked as a corporate lawyer and served in the New York State Assembly, according to the news agency. He first ran for public office at 29 and lost two campaigns for state government before challenging a 30-year congressional incumbent in 2012. The incumbent stepped aside, allowing Jeffries to win the seat.
He represents parts of Brooklyn that were previously represented by Shirley Chisholm, the first Black woman elected to Congress. Jeffries is also a member of the Congressional Black Caucus.
Known for incorporating references to old-school hip-hop into his speeches, Jeffries has developed a public profile that combines his political messaging with his Brooklyn background. He is married and has two children.
Challenges ahead as Democrats take control of the House
Jeffries will lead a Democratic majority facing pressure to deliver on economic concerns while scrutinising President Donald Trump's administration. In a letter to fellow Democrats on Wednesday, he outlined three priorities for the next Congress: affordability, accountability and American values.
He has also promised a 100-day agenda focused on reducing living costs and launching congressional investigations into the administration. Impeachment remains among the options under consideration.
Jeffries is expected to work alongside Representative Katherine Clark of Massachusetts, who is in line to become majority leader, and Representative Pete Aguilar of California, who is expected to serve as majority whip. The three have led the party together since Jeffries took over from Nancy Pelosi after Democrats lost control of the House in 2022.
His election as speaker would also carry historical significance. The US Capitol was built partly by enslaved African Americans, while Joseph Rainey became the first Black member of the House in 1870 during the Reconstruction era. Although Rainey never held the speakership, he was the first Black lawmaker to preside over the House chamber.
More than a century and a half later, Jeffries is poised to take control of the speaker's gavel as Democrats prepare to challenge the Trump administration and establish their legislative priorities.

Even as Indian-American Democrats enjoyed several victories, the Republican side told a rather different story. 
Vivek Ramaswamy
, entrepreneur and former presidential hopeful who enjoyed Donald Trump's endorsement and considerable attention from the Republican establishment, lost the Ohio gubernatorial contest to Democrat Amy Acton after an ugly campaign which was widely criticised.
In Arizona, Democrat Amish Shah was enjoying a promising election night, leading former NFL kicker Jay Feely in the contest for the state's 1st Congressional District, which includes most of Phoenix and Scottsdale. With 54.9% against Feely's 43.2% in the early returns, Shah appeared well positioned to become another Indian-American addition to Congress. The established Indian-American Dem contingent had plenty to celebrate. Ami Bera won an eighth term in California, while Ro Khanna retained his Silicon Valley seat and Pramila Jayapal secured a sixth term in Washington state. Suhas Subramanyam also held Virginia's 10th Congressional District outside Washington DC, consolidating the desi presence in House.
Meanwhile, Los Angeles offered perhaps the most intriguing unfinished chapter of the Indian-American electoral story. Nithya Raman, the Kerala-born urban planner and Los Angeles City Council member of a socialist democrat persuasion, was locked in a dead heat with establishment Democrat Karen Bass, with leads changing frequently.
There were victories beyond Capitol Hill, too. Maryland's Aruna Miller retained her lieutenant-governorship alongside Governor Wes Moore; Wisconsin Attorney General Josh Kaul won another term; and Aparna Raj won Washington DC Council's Ward 1, which includes some of the most storied areas in capital, including Adams Morgan, Kalorama and Columbia Heights.

articles.title: ‘It would destroy Democrats’: Trump warns against impeachment after Republicans’ midterm rout - The Times of India
articles.summary: ‘It would destroy Democrats’: Trump warns against impeachment after Republicans’ midterm rout  The Times of IndiaTrump Threatens To "Destroy" Democrats If They Impeach Him  NDTVUS midterm election results: Can Donald Trump be impeached after Republican rout?  FirstpostWill Trump be impeached? What happens now Democrats have won the midterms  The TimesDemocrats win House and Senate: Trump impeachment odds surge after midterm elections - could he face a thi&...
articles.full_text:
US President Donald Trump has warned Democrats against pursuing impeachment proceedings against him when they take control of Congress next year, saying such a move would politically destroy their party.
His remarks came a day after Republicans suffered a sweeping setback in the US midterm elections, with Democrats securing control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate.
Speaking at the White House on Wednesday for the first time since the election results, Trump dismissed concerns that Democrats could initiate impeachment proceedings and said he was not worried about the possibility, AFP reported.
"No, no, no, not even a little bit," Trump said when asked whether he was concerned about Democrats seeking to impeach him.
"I think it would destroy the Democratic Party if they did that," he added, insisting there was "no reason" for impeachment. Trump questioned what grounds Democrats could cite, saying it would amount to impeachment "for having a successful country".
The US president also suggested he was open to working with Democrats in Congress, provided they did not seek to obstruct his administration.
"I'll get along probably with the Democrats unless they want to be destructive, but I have the power of the veto," he said.
Republicans suffer major setback in midterm elections
Trump's warning comes as Democrats prepare to take control of both chambers of Congress in January 2027, dealing a major blow to the Republican president and his legislative agenda.
The midterm results marked a significant reversal for Republicans, who had entered the elections controlling both the House and Senate. Democratic victories across key races have shifted the balance of power in Washington, giving the opposition party greater oversight of the Trump administration.
With control of Congress, Democrats are expected to intensify scrutiny of the administration, launch investigations and use their congressional majority to challenge Trump's policies.

articles.title: Unilever to invest euro 35 million in India R&D hubs, focus on AI-led innovation - The New Indian Express
articles.summary: Unilever to invest euro 35 million in India R&D hubs, focus on AI-led innovation  The New Indian Express
articles.full_text:
Unilever will invest euro 35 million to transform its research and development (R&D) centres in Mumbai and Bengaluru into an integrated, AI-led innovation ecosystem, strengthening India's role in the company's global research and product development network.
The investment will help develop a next-generation Product Innovation Centre in Mumbai and strengthen Bengaluru as a global science, technology and partnership hub. The facilities will bring together consumer insights, scientific research, product development, rapid prototyping and manufacturing scale-up capabilities.
The company will also invest euro 5 million over the next five years to establish a strategic Bio-Futures Partnership in Bengaluru, focusing on human biology, microbiome science, biotechnology and biomanufacturing.
Unilever's Chief Research and Development Officer Richard Slater said the additional investment would build on more than euro 20 million invested in the company's Indian R&D capabilities over the past five years.
"With India so deeply connected to our global R&D network, the capabilities and work across our India R&D hubs will help shape innovation for Unilever globally, across Beauty, Wellbeing, Personal Care, Home Care and beyond," Slater said.
The Mumbai centre will integrate consumer research, product and format science, packaging design, rapid prototyping and scale-up capabilities under one roof. It will also have collaboration spaces to facilitate partnerships with academic institutions, technology companies and innovators.
Bengaluru, meanwhile, will combine application and foundational science, digital capabilities and India Foods R&D, while expanding its role in bioscience-led innovation.

Abstract
According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Bridge Expansion Bearings market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global bridge expansion bearings market is a critical segment of the civil engineering and construction sector, providing essential components that accommodate movement, rotation, and load transfer between bridge superstructures and substructures. These bearings are indispensable for structural integrity, safety, and longevity, enabling bridges to withstand thermal expansion, seismic activity, and dynamic traffic loads. The market's trajectory is closely tied to global infrastructure investment cycles, urbanization trends, and the pressing need to rehabilitate aging transport networks, particularly in developed economies.
From 2026 to 2035, the market is projected to expand at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 4.2%, reaching a market index of 152 (2025=100) by 2035. Growth is underpinned by sustained public and private investment in new transportation projects, especially in emerging Asia-Pacific economies, coupled with mandatory refurbishment programs in North America and Europe. Technological evolution toward advanced materials and smart bearing systems with integrated monitoring capabilities is creating new value segments. However, the market faces headwinds from cyclical construction downturns, volatile raw material costs, and project-driven procurement that leads to uneven order books.
The competitive landscape features a mix of large multinational engineering conglomerates and specialized mid-sized firms, with competition hinging on technical expertise, certification, and project delivery reliability. This analysis provides a comprehensive view of market dynamics, demand drivers, restraints, segmentation, and regional outlook to 2035.
The baseline scenario for the global bridge expansion bearings market anticipates steady growth from 2026 to 2035, with a CAGR of 4.2% and a market index reaching 152 by 2035 (2025=100). This outlook is anchored in the accelerating global infrastructure investment cycle, particularly in Asia-Pacific where urbanization and transportation network expansion drive new bridge construction. In mature markets like North America and Europe, the focus shifts toward rehabilitation and replacement of aging bridge stock, creating sustained demand for retrofit bearings, especially seismic isolation devices.
The highway bridge segment remains the largest end-use sector, supported by government stimulus packages and public-private partnerships. Railway bridge demand is expected to outpace other sectors due to high-speed rail and freight corridor projects. Technological advancements, including smart bearings with embedded sensors for real-time monitoring, are gaining traction, enabling predictive maintenance and extending service life. However, the market's project-based nature introduces volatility, with order books susceptible to delays and cancellations. Raw material price fluctuations, particularly for steel and rubber, pose margin pressures.
Geographically, Asia-Pacific will dominate consumption, while Latin America and the Middle East & Africa offer emerging opportunities amid infrastructure modernization. The competitive landscape is consolidating, with key players investing in R&D and geographic diversification to capture high-value projects. Overall, the market is poised for moderate but resilient growth, driven by the non-negotiable need for bridge safety and longevity.
Demand Drivers and Constraints
Primary Demand Drivers
- Sustained global infrastructure investment, particularly in Asia-Pacific and North America, driving new bridge construction.
- Mandatory rehabilitation and replacement programs for aging bridges in developed economies, necessitating retrofit bearings.
- Increasing adoption of seismic isolation bearings in earthquake-prone regions, supported by stricter building codes.
- Growth in railway infrastructure, including high-speed rail and freight corridors, demanding high-dynamic load bearings.
- Technological advancements in smart bearings with integrated monitoring capabilities, enabling predictive maintenance.
- Urbanization and population growth in emerging economies, necessitating expansion of transportation networks.
Potential Growth Constraints
- Cyclical downturns in the construction sector and delays in project approvals can lead to uneven demand.
- Volatility in raw material prices, especially steel and rubber, exerting pressure on manufacturer margins.
- Complex and lengthy procurement processes for large infrastructure projects, resulting in extended sales cycles.
- Lack of standardized specifications across regions, increasing design and manufacturing complexity.
- Competition from low-cost regional manufacturers, particularly in price-sensitive markets.

Highway bridges represent the largest application segment for bridge expansion bearings, accounting for approximately 45% of global demand. In developed markets, aging highway bridges require frequent bearing replacement and retrofit, creating a stable aftermarket. Demand-side indicators include government transportation budgets, highway construction starts, and average bridge age. Through 2035, the segment will benefit from increased infrastructure spending, especially in Asia-Pacific and North America, where many bridges are structurally deficient.
The shift toward longer-span bridges and higher traffic loads will necessitate advanced bearings with greater load capacity and durability. Additionally, the adoption of seismic isolation bearings for highway bridges in earthquake-prone regions is expected to rise, supported by stricter safety regulations. However, the segment's growth may be tempered by budget constraints and delays in public project funding. Current trend: Steady growth driven by new road infrastructure and rehabilitation projects..

Railway bridges account for approximately 25% of the bridge expansion bearings market and are expected to be the fastest-growing end-use sector through 2035. The global expansion of high-speed rail networks, particularly in Asia and Europe, along with the development of freight corridors in North America and Africa, is driving demand for bearings capable of handling high dynamic loads and frequent cyclic movements. Railway bearings must meet stringent performance standards to ensure safety and ride comfort, often requiring specialized designs such as spherical and pot bearings with enhanced fatigue resistance. Demand-side indicators include rail infrastructure investment, track length additions, and bridge replacement cycles.

articles.title: Mercedes-Benz says India is no longer just a market, but a key part of its global innovation network - CNBC TV18
articles.summary: Mercedes-Benz says India is no longer just a market, but a key part of its global innovation network  CNBC TV18
articles.full_text:
Mercedes-Benz is increasingly looking at India as a strategic technology and innovation hub for its global operations, with the country's role extending beyond manufacturing and sales, Ola Källenius, Chairman of the Board of Management at Mercedes-Benz, has said.
In an exclusive interview with CNBC-TV18, Källenius said the company's research and development centre in Bengaluru is now fully integrated into its global engineering network, with Indian teams sharing responsibilities across mechanical engineering, electrical engineering, powertrain development and artificial intelligence (AI).
He said Mercedes-Benz is also looking to deepen its engagement with Indian technology partners and startups, particularly in emerging areas such as quantum computing and physical AI. Technologies developed in India can be tested locally and subsequently deployed across the company's global operations, he added.
Källenius said the company's approach to India goes beyond serving domestic demand, with the local technology ecosystem and supplier base increasingly contributing to its global ambitions.
However, Mercedes-Benz's current manufacturing plans remain focused on producing vehicles for the Indian market at its Pune facility. The company intends to expand production in line with domestic demand.
In the interview, Källenius also discussed India's evolving role in Mercedes-Benz's global strategy, the growing importance of its Bengaluru R&D operations, technology partnerships and the future of manufacturing in India.
This is the excerpt of the interview.
Question
Let's double down on your conviction in India. While it's been a challenging global environment for Mercedes-Benz, in India, you've delivered your best quarterly performance in your history here. So, let's talk a little about the outlook for India and what this means in terms of capital allocation and your new model offensive, if I can call it that.
Answer:
Indeed, selling more than 5,400 vehicles in Q3 and making it the best quarter ever in the history of Mercedes-Benz in India makes us optimistic about the future. So, I think this is going to be a record year, and there is no doubt that India has more potential for us. We're in the middle of the biggest product launch offensive in the history of the company, and this year alone, we will launch 12 new models in the Indian market. I will travel to Pune, where we will have the market premiere of the new all-electric GLC. The pre-orders have been fantastic, so there is a lot of momentum for Mercedes-Benz in India, and we're looking to build on that.
Question
What does that mean in terms of capital allocation, Ola? Over ₹3,000 crore has been invested by Mercedes-Benz in India in setting up your manufacturing facility here, and so on and so forth. But given the prioritisation of India for your future growth strategy, what can we now expect in terms of capital allocation?
Answer:
We have a 360-degree strategy for India. It's much more than the market. Of course, we want to develop our position in the market, and we will invest in more models at our production facility in Pune. So, in terms of capital allocation, money is going in there. But I cannot underline enough how important the research and development operation here in Bengaluru is for our global R&D network.For many years now, this has been a hub for innovation for Mercedes-Benz, and India is present in every single Mercedes-Benz car around the world. So, this team here has global responsibility for many components and systems.And even with what happened over the weekend, with Kimi Antonelli becoming the youngest Formula One world champion in the history of the sport, India is also a Formula One world champion because this team here supports our Formula One team in Brackley and Brixworth in the UK to create Kimi's car.Yet another element of our 360-degree approach is working more and more with Indian tech partners and the supply base. So, it's not just India for India; it's India for the world, as far as Mercedes-Benz is concerned.
Question
Congratulations on Kimi's podium finish. Of course, he's created a record as the youngest champion at 20, and that's a big boost for Mercedes-Benz as well. It's nice to know that there is an India connection to Kimi's victory. But let's double down on that 360-degree strategy that you spoke about for India specifically, Ola. You talked about India for the world, but from a manufacturing perspective, what can we truly expect, given the slowdown that we are now seeing for Mercedes-Benz in China and the prohibitive cost of manufacturing in Europe? Can the centre of gravity truly shift to India over the next five to 10 years from a manufacturing point of view?
Answer:
In terms of our vehicle assembly, our current plans are for India for India, but we have gone beyond that with our supply base and tech partners. So, I think the Mercedes-Benz strategy in India will contribute to the world. It will start there, with the supply base and tech partners.We will try to grow our production footprint here in line with the market. I see more growth potential over a five-to-10-year perspective. We will act in accordance with market demand, and we have that flexibility. So, I feel very comfortable with that.On the R&D side, India is now fully integrated into our R&D network, and the team is now like a full team member. It's no longer a case of us starting here, giving the team some tasks, having them solve those tasks and then passing the ball back to our R&D facilities at headquarters in Germany. Now, it's more like they're passing the ball back and forth all the time.In R&D, we cover everything: mechanical engineering, electrical engineering, powertrain engineering and, of course, AI. The AI talent we have here at MBRDI is amazing, and we can find fantastic people in this ecosystem, which is India's startup capital. This will propel our AI efforts even further and make Mercedes-Benz even more attractive to customers around the world.
Question
What is the plan now in terms of further strengthening capabilities at the tech R&D centre in Bengaluru? You've got a significant workforce there, with 10,000 people and counting. What can we now expect in terms of adding people? You talked about AI. What can we truly expect as far as AI and Mercedes-Benz, and specifically manufacturing, are concerned? What are the benefits that are already starting to accrue from the use of AI?
Answer:
I had a chance earlier today to look at some use cases that our engineering team has been working on here in India.
These are not just things that we have been doing in-house but also involve working with some very exciting startups.
We looked at one company in the quantum computing space in India.
Mercedes-Benz is also at the forefront of quantum computing.
We looked at physical AI, with robots taking over tasks in assembly, and different types of robots that are emerging.
What I see now is that the AI revolution, which is happening in every industry and in our lives, is hitting the auto industry in full force.
We will take advantage of the talent that we already have.
I'm sure we will recruit more talent in the AI space, but we will equally leverage tech partnerships and the startup scene here in Bengaluru and across the country to move faster.
We can test things here and apply some of those technologies to our operations in India, but we can also very quickly proliferate that technology across the world.
This is where the strength of the Mercedes-Benz R&D network comes into play.
Yes, our founding fathers invented the automobile 140 years ago, and we started our engineering and R&D base in Germany.
But now we have our biggest R&D centre outside Germany here in India.
We're also in the United States, China, Israel and different places around the world, where we can access talent pools and tech ecosystems.
So, it now really works like a network, and MBRDI plays a crucial role in that network.

Watch accompanying video for full conversation.
