articles.title: From Iran to India: How Trump's midterm loss could affect America's foreign policy - The Times of India
articles.summary: From Iran to India: How Trump's midterm loss could affect America's foreign policy  The Times of IndiaWhat Trump’s midterms setback could mean for Iran, Israel and Ukraine  CNNInternational politicians react to Democrats winning US midterms  ReutersBowen: Trump's loss limits powers at home, but it will likely be different abroad  BBCWhat Trump’s Midterm Defeat Means for Iran and Oil Prices  The New York Times
articles.full_text:
US President Donald Trump has faced the blues this midterm election, with Democrats sweeping both the House and Senate. As the president sees red over his party’s defeat, governments around the world are watching warily, weighing how the shift in congressional power could reshape Washington’s foreign policy and its approach to conflicts and alliances across the globe.
Iran: Khamenei says US midterm results will not change Washington’s hostility
Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said changes in the US political landscape would not alter Washington's hostility towards Tehran, after Republicans suffered setbacks in the midterm elections.
“If anyone still hopes for a change in behaviour or a shift between political parties and factions in the system of domination, they are gravely mistaken,” Khamenei said in a written message published on his official website on Wednesday to mark Iran's annual November 4 anti-US commemoration.
The message warned against making concessions to Washington, arguing that the US sought Iran's “unconditional surrender” and that any compromise would invite further demands and military attacks. It also portrayed Iran's actions in the Strait of Hormuz and against US military bases in the region as evidence that American military power was not invincible.
“Any repetition of aggression will take on far broader dimensions,” the message said.
Khamenei has not appeared in public or been heard speaking since the war began on February 28. No video or audio accompanied Wednesday's statement.
Also read:
How Trump's Iran war triggered 'regime change' at home
Israel: Democratic victory raises questions over future of US support
The Democratic takeover of Congress presents Israel with a set of challenges that extend beyond the immediate impact of the midterm elections, with uncertainty over Trump's Iran strategy, growing criticism of Israel within the Democratic Party and the political calculations surrounding the 2028 presidential race all potentially shaping ties between Washington and Jerusalem.
The first concern is how Trump responds to the electoral setback and the political costs of the war with Iran. Analysts quoted by the Jerusalem Post suggest there are two possible paths, either one of renewed diplomatic efforts and concessions to Tehran, or a short but intense military operation aimed at declaring victory and scaling back US involvement.
The new balance of power in Congress could pose another challenge. Democratic control of both chambers would give the party greater influence over committee leadership, legislative agendas and congressional scrutiny of Israeli policy, including the war in Gaza and US military assistance.
The longer-term question is how the midterm results shape the Democratic Party's approach to Israel ahead of the 2028 presidential election. Candidates who have been openly critical of Israel have seen electoral success with Israeli analysts fearing that politicians such as Zohran Mamdani and Abdul El-Sayed, alongside a new generation of Democratic lawmakers, could become reference points for candidates seeking support from the party's base. Even a nominee who does not share the most critical positions may face pressure to take a tougher line towards Israel.
India: Weakened Trump could push harder for trade deal
India could face renewed pressure to conclude a trade agreement with Washington as Donald Trump seeks to demonstrate economic and diplomatic gains following his party's defeat in the midterm elections. While Democratic control of Congress could increase scrutiny of his tariff policies, it may do little to change the administration's broader trade approach.
An analysis by the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI) suggests that Trump could turn to executive powers to maintain pressure on trading partners, including India, as both Democrats and Republicans increasingly favour economic nationalism, domestic manufacturing and stronger supply chains.
For New Delhi, the immediate concern could be the terms of the proposed bilateral trade agreement. GTRI argues that Trump, facing setbacks in his broader foreign policy efforts involving Russia, China and Iran, could seek a quick trade deal with India to demonstrate American influence.
The US could push for greater access to India's agricultural and industrial markets, alongside commitments to purchase $500 billion worth of American goods over five years and align certain security and economic policies with Washington.
The proposed arrangement has also raised concerns over the possibility of further US tariffs, including additional duties linked to India's purchases of Russian oil.
A Democratic-controlled Congress could increase legislative scrutiny of Trump's tariff policies, but businesses may not see immediate relief from existing duties.
Also read: 
Why a 'lame' duck Donald Trump may push for a quick India-US trade deal
Canada: Carney sees opening for trade deal with weakened Trump
The Republican defeat could give Canada greater leverage in its trade negotiations with Washington, with Canadian PM Mark Carney indicating that the Trump administration had already begun softening some of its demands ahead of the midterm results.
Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of a Commonwealth leaders' meeting in Antigua on Tuesday, Carney said the White House was “asking less and offering more”, adding that Washington had shifted its position on some of Canada's “red lines”. Canadian federal and provincial officials had been hoping that a Republican setback would strengthen Ottawa's negotiating position, CBC News reported.
However, Canada's former ambassador to the US, Kirsten Hillman, cautioned the Carney government against changing course abruptly, saying it should continue constructive discussions if they were moving towards an arrangement acceptable to Canada.
The election outcome also raises questions about Trump's ability to advance his domestic agenda. While Democrats will control both chambers of Congress and could pursue legislation on tariffs and other policies, Trump retains significant executive powers and can veto bills passed by lawmakers. A Democratic-led Congress could therefore constrain his agenda through investigations, legislation and scrutiny, but would not automatically be able to reverse his policies.
Europe: Democrats may offer a check on Trump, but uncertainty remains
The Democratic takeover of Congress could give European allies greater room to push back against Trump's approach to Ukraine, Russia and Nato, but it is unlikely to fundamentally alter Washington's foreign policy, with the president retaining considerable authority over diplomacy and military deployments.
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Democrats have broadly supported military assistance to Kyiv and tougher sanctions against Moscow. A Democratic-controlled Congress could make it harder for Trump to ease sanctions on Russia or pursue policies that weaken support for Ukraine.
However, the electoral setback could also push Trump to focus more heavily on foreign policy, where he retains greater executive authority. This could mean renewed efforts to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, potentially without adequately accounting for Kyiv's position.
The implications extend to European security and Nato. The Pentagon is reviewing the US military presence in Europe, with Trump favouring reductions in the number of American troops stationed on the continent. While Democrats have pledged to oppose troop withdrawals, Congress has limited ability to dictate military deployments, which remain largely within the president's authority.
With domestic policy increasingly constrained by a Democratic-led Congress, Trump could turn to foreign policy to pursue his priorities and establish his legacy ahead of the 2028 presidential election.
South Korea: Caught between the White House and Congress
Seoul could face a more complicated relationship with Washington as it navigates a Trump administration and a Democratic-led Congress with potentially different priorities. Former South Korean foreign vice-minister Choi Jong-kun, speaking to a popular Korean current-affairs show, said the country would have to deal separately with the White House and Congress, making diplomacy more challenging.
Choi pointed to President Lee Jae-myung’s efforts to secure fuel supplies for nuclear-powered submarines, warning that a Democratic-led Congress could take a stricter position on non-proliferation and create obstacles to the plan. He also questioned whether North Korean leader Kim Jong-un would have much incentive to resume high-level talks with Trump if the administration could no longer offer substantive concessions.
Economic and defence commitments could also come under greater scrutiny. South Korea has pledged $350 billion in investment in US strategic sectors, including shipbuilding and semiconductors, under an agreement signed last year. The Trump administration could also press Seoul to shoulder more of the cost of stationing US troops in the country, with potential tariff threats and troop reductions adding to the pressure, The Financial News reported.
China: Beijing seeks to insulate ties with US from midterm results
China has reacted cautiously to the Democratic Party's gains in the US midterm elections, describing the polls as an internal American matter while signalling that it would continue working with Washington to implement agreements reached by the two countries' leaders.
“The US midterm elections are a domestic affair,” Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said at a media briefing, responding to a question on Beijing's assessment of the results.
Mao said China was willing to continue working with the US to uphold and implement the important common understandings reached by president Xi Jinping and his US counterpart Donald Trump, enhance communication, properly manage differences and expand cooperation.

articles.title: Taking Stock of India-China Relations: Structural Divergences and the Limits of Diplomacy - The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
articles.summary: Taking Stock of India-China Relations: Structural Divergences and the Limits of Diplomacy  The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine

source_detail.name: The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine

articles.full_text:
Chinese President Xi Jinping’s latest visit to New Delhi to participate in the BRICS summit in September 2026, his first visit to India in seven years, came in the wake of increasing speculation of a recent thaw in India-China relations. This line of analysis emphasizes the end of a four-year standoff on their disputed border after the two sides reached an agreement on patrolling rights in the remote Ladakh region in October 2024.
Since then, there has been a regular drip-feed of news relating to India considering opening its economic doors to Chinese investments, joint ventures, and bids. The thaw has also been interpreted as being fueled in part by the return of the Trump presidency and Beijing’s and New Delhi’s respective needs for strategic and economic stability.
However, despite signs of a thaw, structural divergences both on the border issue as well as the economic relationship are growing, not receding. The recent recalibration of U.S.-China ties has also caused unease in New Delhi. Xi’s visit, therefore, has been much less momentous or even significant than anticipated. There is a discernible gap between the expectations of the would-be thaw and the structural challenges that shape the India-China relationship in the first place, with significant implications for New Delhi’s China policy going forward.
Growing Power Imbalances and the Leverage-Creep
Much of the contemporary analysis of India-China relations in the present context rests on a template established in the 2010s. This could lead to misleading inferences and conclusions, given how much has changed in the bilateral relationship since 2019-20.
The Military Balance and Zeitgeist
Despite the still significant power gap, relations between China and India in the 2010s were relatively more equal than they are now. India had arguably moved away from its focus on Pakistan as its primary security threat and invested resources in bolstering deterrence vis-à-vis China. This shift was combined with procurements, infrastructure build-up (air bases and roads), forward deployments, and a graduated shift in doctrine from deterrence by denial toward deterrence by punishment. India’s assertive intervention in the Doklam plateau in 2017, a region contested between China and Bhutan, fit perfectly into this context as India signaled that its growing military prowess could now enable it to spring surprise on its larger neighbor.
India’s strategic elite at the time appeared cautiously upbeat about the prevailing balance. They considered maritime options to put pressure on China, widely known as the Malacca option. Military officials spoke confidently of being prepared for a two-front war. India’s growing strategic partnership with the United States and like-minded partners through the Indo-Pacific and the Quad was also seen as a substantive asset, especially as Beijing’s relations with the same countries were rapidly deteriorating.
However, the 2020 border skirmish, the subsequent four-year stand-off, and parallel developments have greatly ruptured this world. The crisis compelled India to adopt a defensive posture at the border, while quasi-abandoning more forward-looking and competitive deterrence-building measures that were gradually being established in the years prior. India appears still in search of a coherent deterrence strategy that safeguards territorial integrity while not engendering a sharper security dilemma.
The military balance has become more skewed. India’s procurement and defense industrial ecosystem has also led to lags in enhancing its military power. China, on the other hand, is rapidly expanding its fleet of fifth-generation fighter jets, with production reaching 120 a year, while India’s fleet is aging fast and struggling to expand in size.
Economic Coercion
In the wake of the 2020 border clash, India chose to retaliate economically instead of pursuing a riskier strategy of military compellence. India’s growing nationalist policy was forming a consensus toward what New Delhi perceived as China’s predatory economic policies and its structural adverse impact on India and other like-minded countries. Stakeholders at the time believed that Indian manufacturing and industry could grow on its own terms and in time reduce dependency on Chinese inputs. A slew of economic measures, such as Make In India, Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes, and others were expected to attract domestic and foreign companies to bet on India — especially the ones fleeing China during U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war.
This situation has since greatly reversed. India’s manufacturing growth has declined in relative terms and advances in various sectors have been more assembly than manufacturing-based in nature. These trends have only deepened India’s reliance on Chinese capital, technology, know-how, and exports. This meant that when China instituted a complex web of export controls in April 2026, its effects were felt disproportionately in India. As Tarun Kapoor, an advisor to Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, put it in an address to a key automobile manufacturing association, “a country can hold us to ransom.” Without timely imports of key rare earth components, noted automobile companies warned that production could come to a halt within weeks or months, and that some companies may have to shift production to alternate countries.
While export controls and other restrictive measures are not India-specific by law and design, reports indicate that the strain in ties has negatively affected both the issuance of business visas for Indians as well as export shipments of critical minerals, fertilizers, and tunnel-boring machines. Hence, there is a consensus view in New Delhi that political and strategic ties determine the degree of Chinese responsiveness and supply reliability. Chinese analysts since at least 2023 have recommended that Beijing should adopt more retaliatory measures in the economic domain vis-à-vis India, including technology transfer denials and export controls. As well-known analyst Hu Shisheng suggests, China “must also improve its policy on industrial chain transfers – to India in particular – so as to avoid contributing to India’s development at the cost of China’s development.”
Beijing may officially nudge India towards win-win thinking, but concerns within the country of India emerging as a super-substitute to China through free trade, particularly considering the size of the Indian economy and the diversity in its industries, are growing stronger, as Hu Shisheng notes. According to Kapoor, this growing concern has created an “issue” that requires India to “move very fast” even as it aims to “learn” from China’s experience.
Promise and Pitfalls of the Economic Liberalization Argument
In this context, Beijing’s message to India prior to Xi’s visit for the BRICS summit had been to embrace liberalization toward Chinese businesses. This argument came through three interconnected points: India’s domestic manufacturing failures; the benefits of positive overall ties in terms of assured continuous supply of sensitive technologies, critical minerals, and exports; and the potential for India’s own growth and development through closer and more open economic cooperation with China. But due to a variety of factors related to territorial sovereignty and economic distrust, and despite pressure and persuasion from China, it appears that the Xi-Modi summit has not moved the needle on India’s position on both the economy and the border.
Due both to strong economic leverage that Beijing currently enjoys as well as the military imbalance at the border, Beijing likely expected greater moderation in India’s position vis-a-vis the border issue. This entails a more discrete handling of stand-offs and more concessions in terms of patrolling rights to the People’s Liberation Army (PLA). At the strategic level, Beijing wants India to de-link the border issue from economic development. This would have the effect of assuring Chinese businesses that “incidents” at the border do not have the potential to derail economic investments. New Delhi’s view, on the other hand, is that such a de-linking will further remove any remaining constraint on PLA aggression at the border. India needs cards with which to respond to violations, and the threat of reversion in overall relations theoretically provides some form of leverage.
India and China have still not truly fully resolved patrolling disagreements in the Western sector, contrary to reporting at the time and since. Ahead of Xi’s latest visit, Indian and Chinese patrols entered into a standoff in the Taksing region in the state of Arunachal Pradesh that could not be resolved ahead of the summit. Meanwhile, grey zone contestation and rival sovereignty claims have hardened in the Eastern sector. This has occurred even as both sides continue to securitize the border, with China also constructing dual-use border villages and logistical facilities that enable all-year troop deployment. The border remains as contested as ever.
The economic relationship has not shown no sign of a take-off, either. If anything, even as India has reluctantly come to appreciate its systemic economic dependence on China, Beijing has started to leverage India’s existing acute dependencies while also making known its concerns about India benefitting from Chinese investment, know-how, and technology. Neither has India really lifted the web of restrictions it had imposed on Chinese businesses since early 2020. India’s Press Note 3, a sweeping measure to restrict investments from China, remains in place. More recent signs of partial opening have turned out to be extremely specific, limited in scope, or simply measures that are beneficial to Indian interests. This has led the Chamber of Chinese Enterprises to describe them as “partial optimization” rather than a “comprehensive liberalization.”

articles.title: US Midterm Verdict: Why Trump's Defeat Could Give India a Diplomatic Opening - Dynamite News
articles.summary: US Midterm Verdict: Why Trump's Defeat Could Give India a Diplomatic Opening  Dynamite News

New Delhi: The sweeping victory of the Democratic Party in the 2026 US midterm elections has dealt a major political blow to President Donald Trump, with the opposition securing control of both chambers of Congress. The outcome is being closely watched in New Delhi, where concerns have mounted over Washington's increasingly unpredictable approach to trade, regional security, immigration and its strategic engagement with South Asia.
For India, the electoral setback suffered by Trump's Republican Party could offer some diplomatic relief after months of friction over tariffs, Russian oil imports, Pakistan, H-1B visas and the broader direction of bilateral relations. However, the change in the balance of power in Congress does not automatically translate into a shift in the White House's foreign policy. The next phase of India-US engagement will largely depend on how the Trump administration responds to the new political reality in Washington.
The midterm verdict has also placed the relationship between the world's two largest democracies under renewed scrutiny. New Delhi will be assessing whether the Democratic majority can act as an institutional counterweight to the President's decisions and encourage a more predictable approach towards India.
India's concerns have particularly centred on Trump's engagement with Pakistan and his public statements on the India-Pakistan relationship. The US President has developed a close working relationship with Pakistan's military leadership, particularly Field Marshal Asim Munir, and has repeatedly taken credit for facilitating the ceasefire understanding between New Delhi and Islamabad following Operation Sindoor.
Trump's claims about his role in securing the cessation of hostilities have remained a sensitive issue for India, which has consistently maintained that matters concerning Pakistan must be addressed bilaterally without third-party intervention. His public remarks on the India-Pakistan conflict have therefore added another layer of diplomatic unease.
New Delhi has also been concerned about Washington's approach towards Pakistan's economic and security requirements. While the US has extended support to Islamabad as it navigates financial difficulties, India has continued to seek a stronger and more consistent American position against cross-border terrorism.
A particularly significant development for Indian policymakers was Washington's public endorsement of Pakistan's assertion that terrorist activity against it was originating from Afghanistan. Such positions have reinforced concerns in New Delhi that the Trump administration's engagement with Pakistan could increasingly diverge from India's security priorities.
India is also likely to monitor the implications of closer US-Pakistan military engagement. Greater American support for Pakistan's defence capabilities, including the possible modernisation of its US-origin aerial platforms, could have consequences for the regional military balance and India's strategic calculations.
Trade has emerged as another major source of friction between New Delhi and Washington. The Trump administration threatened India with steep tariffs over its continued purchases of Russian oil, putting pressure on a relationship that had been projected as a central pillar of the wider Indo-Pacific partnership.
India has maintained that its energy procurement decisions are guided by national interests, energy security and the need to protect consumers from excessive price volatility. New Delhi has also defended its right to maintain diversified energy partnerships in a rapidly changing global market.
The controversy became more contentious because Washington itself moved to secure energy supplies from Russia, including a reported arrangement to purchase diesel ahead of the midterm elections. The apparent contrast between American pressure on India and its own energy-related dealings with Moscow added to questions about the consistency of the administration's approach.
Trump had also described India as a dead economy, although he subsequently praised the country's growth trajectory during a television interview earlier this year. Such contrasting remarks have contributed to uncertainty over the tone and direction of the administration's India policy.
For India, the issue is not limited to tariffs or the immediate cost of trade. It concerns the reliability of the broader economic partnership, the treatment of Indian exporters and the possibility of policy decisions being influenced by shifting political considerations in Washington.
Immigration policy has become another important area of concern for India, particularly because of the large number of Indian professionals and students who travel to the United States for employment and higher education.
The Trump administration's restrictive approach towards H-1B visas has generated anxiety among Indian technology professionals, employers and companies that depend on skilled international talent. Changes in visa rules, heightened scrutiny and uncertainty over the future of employment-based immigration have implications for India's technology workforce and the operations of Indian firms with a presence in the US.
Pressure on student visas has added to the concerns of Indian families and educational institutions. The United States remains a major destination for Indian students, and any tightening of immigration procedures can affect enrolment decisions, research collaborations and the movement of skilled talent between the two countries.
These issues have a direct domestic dimension for India. The treatment of Indian professionals and students is closely linked to public perceptions of the bilateral relationship, making immigration policy an important component of New Delhi's diplomatic engagement with Washington.
The delay in convening the Quad leaders' summit, which India was expected to host in 2025, has also attracted attention. The Quad, comprising India, the United States, Japan and Australia, is a key platform for cooperation in the Indo-Pacific region.
The grouping focuses on maritime security, critical and emerging technologies, resilient supply chains, infrastructure, regional connectivity and a rules-based regional order. For India, the Quad is an important element of its wider Indo-Pacific strategy and its efforts to maintain a stable regional balance.
The postponement of the summit has therefore raised questions about the pace of high-level coordination among the four partners. While the midterm results do not directly determine the future of the Quad, the new congressional balance could influence the political debate surrounding America's regional commitments and strategic partnerships.
New Delhi will be watching whether Washington continues to treat the Indo-Pacific as a central foreign policy priority or whether domestic political divisions and other international crises affect its engagement with the region.
India's approach to the Ukraine conflict has also been a recurring point of disagreement with Washington. New Delhi has faced criticism and pressure over its purchases of Russian crude oil, with the Trump administration linking energy trade to its wider policy towards Moscow.
India has consistently argued that its energy decisions must be assessed in the context of national requirements, affordability and the interests of its citizens. It has maintained that access to reliable and competitively priced energy supplies is essential for economic stability.
New Delhi has also advocated an end to the war in Ukraine and has emphasised the importance of dialogue and diplomacy in resolving international conflicts. Its position reflects a broader effort to maintain strategic autonomy while engaging with major global powers.
India has similarly called for an end to the conflict involving Iran, underscoring its preference for de-escalation and diplomatic solutions in regions that have a direct bearing on global energy markets and regional stability.
The Democratic victory in the US midterms may increase scrutiny of the administration's international decisions, but it does not necessarily indicate an immediate change in America's approach towards either conflict.
The Democrats' takeover of both the House and the Senate gives the party greater institutional leverage over the remaining two years of Trump's presidency. A Democratic-controlled Congress can scrutinise administration policies, conduct investigations, influence legislation and exercise greater oversight over government spending and appointments.
This could create additional avenues for Indian policymakers to engage with lawmakers across the political spectrum, particularly on trade, immigration, defence cooperation and the Indo-Pacific. It may also increase the political scrutiny of decisions that have created friction between Washington and New Delhi.
However, Congress does not independently control the entire foreign policy apparatus. The President retains substantial executive authority, including considerable influence over diplomatic engagement, trade policy and national security decisions. Any expectation that the midterm outcome will immediately reverse Trump's approach towards India would therefore be premature.
The election result should instead be viewed as a change in Washington's domestic political balance that could affect the environment in which bilateral negotiations and strategic decisions take place.
India has little reason to celebrate the electoral setback of a US President with whom it must continue to work on a range of strategic and economic issues. New Delhi's priorities remain centred on stable trade relations, predictable tariff policies, access for Indian professionals and students, counterterrorism cooperation and a balanced approach towards South Asia.

articles.title: Donald Trump loses US Congress; Netanyahu faces deadlock at home: What happens to Iran war now? - The Times of India
articles.summary: Donald Trump loses US Congress; Netanyahu faces deadlock at home: What happens to Iran war now?  The Times of IndiaIran war live: Khamenei says US hostility will persist after midterms  Al JazeeraIran unveils ‘We will kill Trump’ banner – but US president may now be tempted to resume bombing  The GuardianAfter midterm defeat, Trump faces mostly bad options in Iran  AxiosIran Says Handed Trump "Political Defeat" In Washington After Midterms Rout  ...
articles.full_text:
Two elections, two political setbacks and one unresolved war. US President 
Donald Trump
 has lost control of Congress after voters handed Democrats a sweeping victory in US midterms, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is struggling to secure a parliamentary majority following Israel's October 27 elections. Both leaders, who joined forces in the war against Iran, now face growing pressure at home even as the conflict they launched remains unresolved.
Months after the killing of Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, the war has neither delivered a decisive outcome nor brought Washington and Tehran closer to a lasting settlement. With Trump's Republicans losing both chambers of Congress and Netanyahu's bloc falling short of a majority in the Knesset, the political landscape has changed for both leaders.
The timing is significant. US strikes on Iranian targets near the Strait of Hormuz came just hours before Americans voted, amid continuing exchanges of proposals between Washington and Tehran. They also followed reports that Netanyahu had pressed Trump to consider another round of military action.
With both leaders facing pressure at home, where does the Trump-Bibi partnership go from here? Will the political setbacks push them towards a deal with Iran, or make them more inclined to take a harder line?
Trump's midterm setback: Democrats take control of Congress
The November 3 midterm elections delivered a major blow to Trump, with Democrats winning control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate. 
The Associated Press reported that Democrats flipped at least seven Senate seats, including in Kansas, Iowa, Texas, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina and South Carolina. They also gained more than two dozen House districts, including in areas that had backed Trump by double-digit margins in 2024.
Trump claims he would have won in a landslide
Trump brushed aside suggestions that the result was a personal setback, pointing out that he was not on the ballot. “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” he said.
He later congratulated Democrats but maintained that the result was not a referendum on him. “The Democrats did a good job. They fought hard,” he told Fox News. “I don’t view it as a hit on me,” he added, claiming that the country had seen “the greatest two years in the history of the presidency”.
Trump on Democrats' midterm performance
The Senate results included a series of Democratic victories in traditionally Republican states. James Talarico defeated Ken Paxton in Texas, becoming the first Democrat to win a Senate election in the state since 1988. Annie Andrews defeated Darline Graham in South Carolina, while Adam Hamilton unseated incumbent Roger Marshall in Kansas, ending a 94-year gap since the state last elected a Democrat to the Senate.
Democrat Josh Turek defeated Republican Ashley Hinson in Iowa, former Ohio senator Sherrod Brown beat incumbent Jon Husted, and former North Carolina governor Roy Cooper won the open Senate seat against Michael Whatley. Democrats also held on to seats in Georgia, where Jon Ossoff won re-election, and New Hampshire, where Chris Pappas defeated former senator John Sununu.
Talarico celebrated his Texas victory by telling supporters: “We just took back Texas.” He added: “We are tired of being told to hate each other. We didn’t win this race by alienating our neighbors or shaming our neighbors.”
The gubernatorial results also brought gains for Democrats. Keisha Lance Bottoms won in Georgia, becoming the first Black woman elected governor in the US. Amy Acton defeated Trump-backed Vivek Ramaswamy in Ohio, Rob Sand won in Iowa and Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican incumbent Greg Abbott in Texas, becoming the state’s first Latina governor. Democrats also won Nevada, where Aaron Ford defeated incumbent Joe Lombardo.
There were notable results for Indian-American candidates as well. Democrat Suhas Subramanyam retained his Virginia House seat, while Pia Dandiya won Florida’s 22nd Congressional District. Maryland lieutenant governor Aruna Miller also won another term alongside governor Wes Moore.
The new Congress will take office in January. Democrats will have greater powers to scrutinise the administration, hold hearings, investigate Trump's actions and block or delay presidential nominees. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries is also poised to become the first Black speaker of the House, subject to a vote by lawmakers.
The change could complicate Trump's domestic agenda and increase scrutiny of the Iran war. However, a Democratic-controlled Congress cannot automatically end the conflict or take military command away from the president. Trump remains commander-in-chief, while Congress can use its oversight and funding powers to exert pressure.
JNU professor Rajan Kumar told TOI that the new Congress could act as a check on Trump's approach towards Iran. “He'll be balanced by the new Congress where the Democrats would be dominant. So that will play some role,” he said, adding that the president would face challenges in securing congressional approval for funding a prolonged war.
Trump on vetoing Democratic proposals
Trump has warned that he would veto legislation he considers unacceptable. “They'll send over things that are insane, and I'll veto them,” he said. He also left open the possibility of working with Democrats, suggesting that after a few months of vetoes, lawmakers would ask how to get things done and “we'll work together”.
Did the Iran war cost Trump at the ballot box?
The election results suggest that the Iran war was one part of wider voter dissatisfaction with the administration, rather than the only reason Republicans lost control of Congress.
Reuters reported that nearly nine in 10 voters identified the cost of living as a crucial or major factor in their vote, according to exit polls. Three-quarters were angry or dissatisfied with the direction of the country, while nearly two-thirds blamed Trump for high prices.
The AP Voter Poll, which surveyed about 80,000 voters across the country, found that about six in 10 disapproved of Trump's handling of the presidency. Around seven in 10 said Congress was not doing enough to check presidential power.
The Iran conflict also featured in voters' concerns. The AP poll found that about six in 10 voters considered the US decision to take military action against Iran the wrong one, while around a third said the war was a crucial factor in their vote.
Trump says Iran partly influenced midterm results
Trump acknowledged that Iran played a part in the Republican losses, but did not indicate that he regretted the military campaign.
“I think a part of it was Iran, but at the same time people understood the importance of what I've done with Iran,” he told Fox News.
He also defended the decision to use force, saying: “I did the right thing. I would have done it again.”
Kumar told TOI that the Iran conflict had added to the wider dissatisfaction with the Trump administration, particularly because it had failed to deliver a decisive outcome.
“On the issue of Iran, first, he could not achieve any military or political breakthrough. The United States got caught in a quagmire kind of situation where it's a deadlock and he can neither win nor withdraw,” he said.
Kumar also pointed to the economic consequences of the conflict, saying the rise in diesel and fuel prices had contributed to the pressure on American households. He said domestic inflation remained a major concern, even though the US economy itself was not doing badly.
He added that Trump had promised not to intervene in international conflicts but had acted contrary to that commitment in Venezuela and Iran, among other places.
Strikes near Hormuz: Is Trump preparing for another round?
Even as election results came in, the military situation remained unsettled.
The Associated Press reported that the US carried out limited strikes on Iranian targets near the Strait of Hormuz on November 2, hours before Americans voted. Iranian state media reported explosions on Qeshm and Hengam islands and near Bandar Abbas.
A US official told the AP that the strikes targeted Iranian forces using surface-to-air missiles against US assets in the strait. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to comment publicly.
Reuters reported that US officials described the strikes as defensive and said they did not amount to a return to major combat operations. Trump later described the action as a “minor attack” and said it “wasn’t war”.
He also explained the target of the operation, saying: “They built an anti-aircraft facility. It took them about two months. We watched it get built. As soon as it was completed, we hit it last night.”
The strikes came amid uncertainty over whether Trump would order a fresh campaign after the midterms. The administration has maintained a naval blockade around Iranian ports, while thousands of US troops remain in the region. The AP has also reported that another aircraft carrier and additional troops are heading towards the Middle East.
Diplomatic contacts have continued alongside the military build-up.
Reuters reported on November 3, citing a senior Iranian official, that Washington and Tehran remained far from reaching an agreement despite intensified efforts by mediators. Qatari officials have been involved in passing proposals between the two sides.
Iran has said it is prepared to discuss its nuclear programme but wants the US to lift its naval blockade and ease sanctions on its oil sales. Tehran has also sought a ceasefire that includes Lebanon. It has maintained that the Strait of Hormuz cannot be fully reopened without its conditions being addressed.
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf said Washington had the responsibility to prevent a return to war. “The ball is now in America’s court to prevent war,” he said. He warned that Iran's armed forces remained on high d

The dramatic results of the U.S. midterms will probably have less impact on India-U.S. bilateral relations than on geopolitics and, as a result, India’s “operating environment” in the world. The elections are likely to hand Democrats a sizable majority in the House of Representatives and a comfortable edge in the Senate, which means U.S. President Donald Trump will face restraints on both domestic and foreign policy. Here are five areas where this will matter most to India.
In interviews given after the results began to come in, Mr. Trump said he stood by his decision to attack Iran in February 2026, but acknowledged that Iran was “part” of the reason for Republican losses. It isn’t clear whether this means he will give talks with Iran a greater chance and look for an early exit from the war, but New Delhi will watch closely.

articles.title: India Construction Equipment Industry: Impact of Emission Norms - IMARC Group
articles.summary: India Construction Equipment Industry: Impact of Emission Norms  IMARC Group
articles.full_text:
The India Construction Equipment Market stands at a defining crossroads where accelerating infrastructure investment collides with some of the most consequential regulatory changes the sector has ever faced. According to IMARC Group, the market was valued at USD 15.37 Billion in 2025 and is projected to reach USD 29.50 Billion by 2034, growing at a CAGR of 7.52% (2026–2034). The Government of India's Union Budget 2024–25 allocated a record capital expenditure of INR 11.11 trillion for infrastructure development equivalent to 3.4% of GDP signalling an unwavering political commitment to roads, railways, urban infrastructure, and housing that underpins the market's long-term demand floor. Simultaneously, the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, in coordination with the Bureau of Indian Standards, has been progressively enforcing Construction Equipment Vehicle (CEV) emission norms that are pushing the industry toward a fundamental technological reset.
On the demand side, an extraordinary pipeline of public infrastructure projects national highways, metro rail corridors, port modernisation, affordable housing under the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana, and the Smart Cities Mission is generating multi-year, sustained demand for heavy and light construction equipment across every major geography. On the supply side, the transition to CEV Stage IV and the roadmap toward CEV Stage V equivalent standards is forcing original equipment manufacturers to invest heavily in cleaner engine technology, electronic control systems, and advanced emissions after-treatment cost increases that are being passed through to contractors and reshaping the economics of equipment ownership, rental, and replacement.
At the segmentation level, products account for a dominant 69.0% share of the market by solution type, while heavy construction equipment leads with a 64.0% equipment-type share. Excavators command 30.0% of the equipment mix, reflecting their centrality across excavation, foundation work, mining, and civil construction. North India anchors regional demand with a 30.0% share, driven by the density of road and urban infrastructure projects across Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Haryana, and Delhi NCR. The overarching theme shaping the market is the emission-driven replacement cycle a structural force that is simultaneously creating near-term cost pressure and a long-term opportunity for manufacturers, rental operators, and technology providers.
This blog examines the India Construction Equipment Market's size and segments, recent announcements, trends shaping 2026, geographic hotspots, competitive landscape, policy environment, forecast through 2034, and the opportunities available to manufacturers, investors, rental operators, and technology providers.
Key Takeaways
According to IMARC Group, the India Construction Equipment Market reached USD 15.37 Billion in 2025 and is projected to reach USD 29.50 Billion by 2034, at a CAGR of 7.52% during 2026–2034. Growth is distributed across solution types, equipment categories, applications, and end-use industries, with the fastest expansion occurring in emission-compliant equipment segments, electric and hybrid machinery, and technology-enabled rental platforms. The leading segments are:
Recent developments in the India Construction Equipment Market include significant announcements, investments, and partnerships:
Three trends are shaping the India Construction Equipment Market in 2026:
1. The CEV Stage IV Emission Compliance Transition and Its Cost Cascade
The transition to Construction Equipment Vehicle Stage IV emission norms is the single most disruptive structural force in the India construction equipment industry in 2026. The adoption of Stage IV-compliant diesel engines which require advanced fuel injection systems, exhaust gas recirculation, diesel oxidation catalysts, and in some configurations diesel particulate filters has increased the base cost of new compliant equipment by an estimated 8–15% compared to previous-generation machines. For large infrastructure contractors and mining companies with the financial depth to absorb higher upfront costs and access equipment financing, the transition is accelerating fleet renewal and presenting manufacturers with strong upgrade-cycle demand. For small and price-sensitive contractors who collectively account for a significant share of equipment buyers in India's fragmented construction sector the cost increase is a material barrier, diverting demand toward the used equipment market, rental platforms, and delayed replacement decisions. The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways has signalled that compliance timelines will be enforced, making eventual transition non-negotiable. This regulatory certainty is prompting the rental sector to invest aggressively in compliant fleets, positioning rental-as-a-service as the most cost-accessible route for smaller operators to access modern, emission-legal machinery.
2. Telematics, AI-Enabled Diagnostics, and Smart Equipment Integration
The integration of telematics, GPS-based machine control, AI-enabled diagnostics, and predictive maintenance platforms is fundamentally changing how construction equipment is operated, maintained, and commercially managed in India. Leading original equipment manufacturers are embedding telematics units as standard equipment in their CEV Stage IV-compliant machines, providing fleet owners with real-time data on machine location, fuel consumption, utilisation rates, engine health parameters, and operator behaviour. AI-powered diagnostic platforms process this data to predict component failures before they cause unplanned downtime a capability that is particularly valuable in remote infrastructure construction sites where equipment service support is logistically challenging. The Government of India's National Infrastructure Pipeline, which targets completion of projects worth INR 111 lakh crore by 2025, includes large-scale road, bridge, and tunnel construction in geographically difficult terrain where maximising machine uptime through predictive maintenance delivers measurable project cost and schedule benefits. GPS-based machine control where the equipment's bucket, blade, or drum is guided by satellite positioning referenced against a digital terrain model is also gaining adoption in highway and grading applications, reducing material waste and rework while improving surface quality outcomes.
3. Electric and Hybrid Equipment Pilots and the Road to Electrification
While full electrification of India's construction equipment fleet remains a medium-to-long-term prospect, 2026 marks the year in which structured electric and hybrid equipment pilots by global and domestic OEMs are generating real operational data from Indian construction sites. Battery-electric compact excavators, electric wheel loaders, and hybrid energy storage systems for tower cranes are being trialled in urban infrastructure projects in major cities, where noise ordinances, air quality regulations, and access to grid power make electric equipment operationally attractive. The Bureau of Energy Efficiency and the Ministry of Heavy Industries have both indicated policy interest in incentivising the adoption of zero-emission construction machinery as part of India's broader decarbonisation agenda, aligning with the country's commitment under the Paris Agreement to reduce the emissions intensity of GDP. Global OEMs including Volvo CE, Komatsu, and Caterpillar are advancing India-specific electrification roadmaps informed by their pilot experiences, while domestic manufacturers are exploring partnerships with battery technology providers and electric drivetrain specialists. The segment remains nascent in volume terms but is attracting disproportionate strategic investment given its long-term disruption potential.
North India anchors the India Construction Equipment Market with a commanding 30.0% regional share a concentration rooted in the extraordinary density of infrastructure investment across Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Haryana, Delhi NCR, Himachal Pradesh, and Uttarakhand. The Uttar Pradesh Expressways Industrial Development Authority's ongoing expressway network expansion, including the Ganga Expressway and Bundelkhand Expressway projects, has placed the state among the single largest consumers of heavy earthmoving and road construction equipment in the country. Rajasthan's mining sector covering stone quarrying, mineral extraction, and sand mining generates sustained demand for hydraulic excavators, rock breakers, and dump trucks throughout the year. The Delhi NCR region's continuous urban infrastructure development, metro rail expansion, and commercial real estate activity creates a reliable baseload of demand for compact and medium-sized equipment. The region's road network density and proximity to major equipment manufacturing hubs in Haryana and Rajasthan also reduces logistics costs and improves after-sales service availability for equipment operators, reinforcing North India's structural demand advantage.
South India, encompassing Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Telangana, represents the second major demand concentration and is among the fastest-growing regions in percentage terms. The scale of urban infrastructure investment in Bengaluru, Chennai, Hyderabad, and Amaravati spanning metro rail, elevated corridors, IT park construction, and port expansion is driving consistent demand for excavators, cranes, and concrete equipment. Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh's active port and coastal infrastructure development programmes, including the Sagarmala scheme's port connectivity projects, are generating incremental demand for heavy marine and civil construction equipment. The South's concentration of large, financially sophisticated infrastructure contractors with access to equipment financing further supports above-average adoption of premium, emission-compliant machines.

articles.title: DEI is back: Black, Muslim, LGBTQ leaders win big in US midterms - India Today
articles.summary: DEI is back: Black, Muslim, LGBTQ leaders win big in US midterms  India TodayThe historic firsts of the 2026 election  CNNTen historic firsts: the winning US midterm candidates making waves  The GuardianThe better angels of democracy have asserted themselves in America  The Indian ExpressMidterms May Bring In Wave Of Historic Firsts For Some States, Country  NDTV
articles.full_text:
From the first Black woman governor to the first Muslim-American in the Senate, the US midterm results marked several milestones. Democratic Congressman Ro Khanna said it signalled a strong rebuke of Trump's crackdown on DEI initiatives.
The US midterm elections, which were swept by the Democrats, also delivered historic firsts, with several minority candidates breaking long-standing barriers in gubernatorial and Senate races. From the first Black woman governor, first openly gay senator, to the first Muslim-American in the Senate, the results marked several milestones. Democratic Congressman Ro Khanna said the victories signalled a strong rebuke of Donald Trump's crackdown on DEI (Diversity, Equity and Inclusion) initiatives after his 2024 win.
In a video on X, Khanna, who retained his House seat, pointed out there were now "three Black governors". Byron Donalds, David Crowley, and Keisha Lance Bottoms won their races in Florida, Wisconsin, and Georgia, respectively. Bottoms, a Democrat, made history by becoming the first Black woman governor of a US state. She also became Georgia's first woman governor.
HISTORIC FIRSTS FOR MINORITIES IN MIDTERMS
While most are Democrats, the Republican Party has also broken some new ground. Donalds made history as Florida's first Black governor. He also became the first Black Republican to be elected governor of any US state.
Khanna also highlighted how Texas elected its "first Latina governor", referring to the victory of Democrat Gina Hinojosa over Republican Greg Abbott. Hinojosa ended more than three decades of Republican control of Texas's governorship. She will also be the first woman to lead Texas since 1995.
"Tonight, DEI is back as America celebrated diversity and inclusion," Khanna said. "Three black governors, the first Latina governor in Texas, the first Muslim-American senator, the first gay senator. I love this America," the Indian-American said.
Others who made history include Democrat Chris Pappas, who has become the first openly gay man elected to the US Senate. He defeated Republican John Sununu in New Hampshire.
In Colorado, Democrat Melat Kiros won the 1st Congressional District, becoming the first Black woman from the state to be elected to the House of Representatives.
Democrat Adam Hamawy, a former US Army combat surgeon, has won New Jersey's 12th Congressional District. He becomes the state's first Muslim member of Congress. Hamawy had shot to the spotlight after he volunteered to treat patients in war-scarred Gaza.
New York's 7th Congressional District has gone to Democrat Claire Valdez, who becomes the first known Indigenous woman from the state to be elected to the US Congress. Valdez is a member of the Ysleta Del Sur Pueblo - one of three federally recognised Native American tribes.
In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed scripted history, becoming the first Muslim-American to be elected to the US Senate.
Together, these victories mark significant milestones for minorities, with political experts calling it a "huge rebuke against hate and division".
A MESSAGE TO TRUMP?
The victories carry a significant political message for Trump, whose administration has rolled back DEI programs across government departments. Trump, instead, has pushed to restore "merit-based opportunity".
Several corporates also cracked down on DEI initiatives to curry favour with Trump.
It essentially meant a reduction of policies and programs aimed at promoting diversity, equity and inclusion in workplaces.
The midterm results suggest American voters are not buying into the administration's push to dismantle DEI initiatives.
Instead, the results point to a continued demand for diversity in American politics, cutting across racial, religious and cultural lines.

articles.title: 'Trump hasn’t done anything to help': Republicans blame MAGA chief for midterm rout - The Times of India
articles.summary: 'Trump hasn’t done anything to help': Republicans blame MAGA chief for midterm rout  The Times of India'This is a disaster': Angry Republicans blame Trump for midterms defeat  BBCFrom Texas to Tehran: how papers across the world reacted to ‘Dem-olition’ job on Trump in US midterms  The GuardianRepublican Blame Game Starts As 2028 Hopefuls Angle For Position  NDTVRepublicans call for Trump to change course after midterm drubbing  Reuters
articles.full_text:
US President Donald Trump’s aggressive campaign push in the final weeks before the midterm elections failed to prevent a sweeping Republican defeat, with party insiders increasingly blaming the president for the growing public anger that fuelled the Democratic resurgence.
Just weeks before voters headed to the polls, Republicans were already struggling to contain mounting losses across dozens of races. The party’s House majority was slipping away, while control of the Senate, once considered safely Republican, had turned into a competitive battle. Trump responded by embarking on an intensive campaign tour, travelling across the country to energise voters in traditionally Republican strongholds.
But the effort came too late to reverse the political damage. According to CNN, the president repeatedly questioned how the party had reached such a difficult position, asking those around him: "How did we get here?"
Republicans, however, believed the answer lay partly in his own decisions. An unidentified Texas-based GOP operative told CNN ahead of Election Day: "People are so mad. And Trump hasn’t done anything to help any of that."
The anger stemmed from a combination of economic anxiety and dissatisfaction with the administration's policies. The unpopular war with Iran, rising fuel prices and persistent inflation had intensified concerns over the cost of living, pushing Trump's approval ratings to record lows.
The economic discontent was reflected in the AP Voter Poll, which found that around three-quarters of voters considered the economy either 'not so good' or 'poor'. Nearly eight in 10 said inflation had caused moderate or severe financial hardship for their households. Government corruption and concerns that Trump prioritised his personal interests over the country's also emerged as major issues.
Trump's campaign push fails to stop Democratic wave
The scale of the Republican defeat became increasingly apparent as Democrats made gains in states and congressional districts that had long been considered conservative territory.
Democrats secured control of both chambers of Congress, with Republicans losing several House districts that Trump had carried by more than 10 percentage points in the previous presidential election. The victories included James Talarico's breakthrough Senate win in Texas and Annie Andrews' upset victory in South Carolina.
Democrats also made significant gains in Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and North Carolina, while Republican candidates backed by Trump struggled to hold their ground. His endorsement of scandal-hit Texas candidate Ken Paxton, in particular, had raised concerns among Republicans before the election.
The results exposed cracks in the coalition that had helped Trump return to the White House, with younger voters and Latinos shifting away from Republicans, according to the AP Voter Poll.
Despite spending much of the final month campaigning almost daily, Trump could not prevent the electoral backlash. Republicans had also poured millions of dollars into competitive races and traditionally safe districts, but their financial advantage failed to stop the Democratic surge.
Trump distances himself from Republican losses
As the results began emerging, Trump sought to separate himself from the defeat, arguing that he had not been on the ballot.
"I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!" he wrote on his social media platform.
In a late-night interview with Fox News, Trump also dismissed the idea that the results represented a personal defeat, saying voters "didn't like the candidates".
However, the Democratic takeover of Congress threatens to significantly constrain the remainder of his presidency. Democratic leaders have indicated that investigations into senior administration officials, scrutiny of Trump's business interests and possible impeachment proceedings could feature prominently in their agenda.
The election results have therefore dealt Trump more than a setback at the ballot box, leaving his administration facing an increasingly hostile Congress for the final two years of his term.

articles.full_text:
Unilever today announced that it will invest a further €35 million in its research and development capabilities in India, transforming its R&D hubs in Mumbai and Bengaluru into a next-generation research and innovation ecosystem, and establishing a strategic ‘Bio-Futures’ partnership in India.
The additional investment will build on an investment of more than €20 million over the past five years in state-of-the-art capabilities including the Liquids Lab of the Future, the Unilever Fragrance House, the Advanced Manufacturing Center for Bars, the Packaging and Flexibles Design Lab, and AI & Digital modelling platforms.
Both the India R&D hubs operate as an integral part of Unilever’s global R&D network and encompass a range of new science and technology research, innovation, product development and market-facing activities. This includes consumer understanding, product adaptation, testing, validation, scale-up and deployment with different activities undertaken across the India R&D ecosystem. Both hubs leverage Unilever’s global science, technology platforms, scientific know-how and intellectual property in accordance with the respective activities undertaken across the India R&D ecosystem. India, is one of Unilever's largest global R&D hubs, bringing together 800+ scientists, researchers, digital specialists and designers.
The proposed transformation envisions the Mumbai hub as a new “Product Innovation Centre”. It will bring together AI and Digital powered foresight and insights, new measurement approaches, product & format science, product and packaging design, rapid prototyping, scale-up capabilities and market facing deployment within a single integrated environment. This New Product Innovation Center will also bring in collaborative spaces catalyzing new-age partnerships with Academia, Experts, Suppliers, Start-ups and larger design ecosystems.
The Bengaluru Center will continue to evolve as a Global Science, Technology and Partnership Hub, hosting foundational and application science platforms, digital and AI capabilities, India Foods R&D, and collaborations with Academia, Start-ups and Unilever's global innovation network.
Across both sites, AI, automated and co-bot powered experimentation, predictive modelling and digital twins will enable scientists and product developers to explore more possibilities, learn faster, and translate promising ideas into scalable innovations with greater speed and precision.
Unilever will also invest €5 million over five years in a strategic Bio-Futures partnership in India, creating a platform that connects Unilever’s global R&D capabilities with India’s rapidly growing Bioscience ecosystem. The partnership will bring together leading scientific institutions, start-ups, advanced infrastructure and talent to accelerate innovation across human biology, microbiome science, biotechnology, biomanufacturing, and digital and AI-enabled biology.
Richard Slater, Chief Research and Development Officer, Unilever, said, “India is a critical global R&D center for Unilever. This investment will enable a more connected way of innovating, bringing together science, insights, design, digital technology, AI, rapid prototyping and scale-up capabilities. By connecting Unilever with India’s world-class bioscience ecosystem, we can harness complementary science, capabilities and partnerships to accelerate the next generation of Bio-Futures innovation for India and the world.”
Priya Nair, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer, Hindustan Unilever Ltd, said, “India’s emergence as a global innovation powerhouse presents an extraordinary opportunity. As one of the world’s fastest-growing large economies, we see significant potential to bring world-class, science-led innovation to Indian consumers. This investment reinforces Unilever R&D’s long-standing commitment to India and its confidence in the country’s scientific talent, capabilities, innovation ecosystem and India’s emerging position in bio sciences and bio manufacturing.”

articles.title: Why is India choosing a different path in the global semiconductor race? - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Why is India choosing a different path in the global semiconductor race?  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
India is investing billions of dollars to become a global chip manufacturing hub, wisely choosing a different path from the major corporations racing to produce the most advanced processors to serve the AI wave.
According to Russian media on November 2nd, India has already established a significant foothold in the semiconductor design sector. Now, the country wants to build up its domestic manufacturing industry and become a reliable global supplier.
That ambition was demonstrated at the Semicon India event in New Delhi in September, when Prime Minister Narendra Modi promoted India as an alternative manufacturing destination, amid rising demand and growing concerns about global chip production bottlenecks and supply uncertainties.
Speaking at the conference, Mr. Modi said: “ The world needs new and reliable chip manufacturing locations. India is preparing for that.”
A month earlier, in his Independence Day speech, Prime Minister Modi had highlighted semiconductor development as a crucial part of the "Make in India" initiative to boost manufacturing. He stated , "Chips are indispensable. Without them, the world would come to a standstill."
This initiative is being implemented at a time when artificial intelligence, data centers, electric vehicles , and electronics manufacturing are expanding, driving demand for semiconductors. However, India's strategy is not to immediately challenge leading technology nations on their own playing field.
Jinal Shah, co-founder and chief marketing officer of chip startup Indiesemic, commented: “I think this is one of the smartest and most far-sighted choices India has ever made.”
Why is India betting on older generation chips?
While manufacturers like Taiwan's TSMC and South Korea's Samsung compete to build increasingly smaller processors, including 2-nanometer chips for high-performance computing and AI , India is currently focusing on established technologies, known as mature node processes.
These chips range in size from 28 to 180 nanometers. While not among the most cutting-edge technologies, they remain essential for automobiles, industrial machinery, telecommunications, household appliances, and power grids.
Even the AI wave requires these chips, because data centers cannot function without power management chips, networking components, and similar types of chips.
Neil Shah, co-founder and vice president of research at Counterpoint Research, said that mature node technologies account for nearly 70% of global chip production by volume. He said that starting with mature node chip manufacturing, specialized semiconductors, and conventional chip assembly and testing is the only commercially viable starting point for India.
According to the Indian government's NITI Aayog, it would cost more than $15 billion to build an advanced 3-nanometer chip manufacturing plant. Manufacturing these chips also requires specialized equipment and expertise accumulated over decades. This second factor makes it difficult for the US to quickly follow TSMC's path to success.
Recently, S. Krishnan, Secretary of India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, acknowledged that pursuing 2-nanometer chip production is too costly.
You may also like
Despite being overshadowed by AI chips, the mature node chip market remains a strong growth market. In June, industry research firm TrendForce reported that increasing demand for power-related semiconductors, including chips used in AI infrastructure, is causing production capacity shortages and could sustain price increases until 2027.
Why hasn't India started producing chips yet?
India is no newcomer to the semiconductor industry. The country has nearly one-fifth of the global chip design workforce and is home to major research and development centers for companies like Intel, Qualcomm, and Texas Instruments.
Indian engineers have contributed to the development of sophisticated chips used around the world. However, the majority of the actual manufacturing takes place overseas.
According to NITI Aayog's estimates, imports currently meet 90% to 95% of India's semiconductor needs. The organization forecasts that the country's chip market will exceed $200 billion by 2035, driven by demand from electronics, automotive, telecommunications, and digital infrastructure.
Engaging in chip manufacturing offers India two opportunities: reducing reliance on imported chips to serve its expanding domestic industries, and supplying overseas markets seeking alternative production locations.
Bridging the Gap: From Chip Design to Manufacturing
India's first semiconductor mission has led to the approval of 12 manufacturing projects, with a total projected investment of over $17 billion. These projects include a silicon chip fabrication plant, two dedicated semiconductor manufacturing facilities, and nine assembly, testing, and packaging facilities.
Five of the nine facilities have begun commercial production. These include facilities operated by the American memory chip manufacturer Micron and Indian companies Kaynes Semicon, CG Semi, CDIL Semiconductor, and Suchi Semicon. At an industry event in September, Prime Minister Modi attended the inauguration of commercial production lines at CDIL in Punjab and Suchi Semicon in Gujarat.
However, these facilities are primarily focused on assembly, packaging, and testing, rather than directly manufacturing integrated circuits on silicon wafers. Building that capability is the next big step.
The Semicon 2.0 program, backed by $13.5 billion, aims to build an ecosystem around these factories, expanding support to include manufacturers of equipment, specialty chemicals, raw materials, chip design, research and development, and workforce development.
Raghava Srinivasan Balakrishnan, Director of the Sudeet Foundation, commented: “Currently, India is almost entirely dependent on foreign countries for these basic materials and machinery.”
India's Tata Group is building an $11 billion chip manufacturing plant in Dholera, Gujarat, in partnership with Taiwan's Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation. The plant aims to begin commercial production by mid-2028, initially using 55-nanometer and 90-nanometer technologies before transitioning to 28-nanometer.
At a conference in September, the American company Applied Materials announced plans to invest $5 billion in India over the next decade, including research, domestic supply chains, and workforce development.
The government is also seeking to support Indian businesses in shifting from chip design to developing commercially viable products.
You may also like
According to technology policy researcher Pranay Kotasthane, centralizing access to professional design tools and infrastructure significantly reduces the barrier to initial investment. He welcomes the support given to chip design startups.
Can India produce advanced chips?
New Delhi's ambitions extend beyond simply producing chips using mature node processes.
In its roadmap announced in May, NITI Aayog proposed building a semiconductor value chain worth $120-$150 billion by 2035, positioning India as one of the world's top three destinations for advanced contract assembly, testing, and packaging services.
The roadmap for advanced packaging presents an opportunity. Incorporating multiple chips into increasingly sophisticated component packages can improve performance without relying solely on the transistor miniaturization race.
"Instead of falling behind in the global wafer race, India should forge its own path," the report stated.
Overall, India hasn't given up its ambition to produce the most advanced processors; it's just being more realistic by prioritizing more easily seizeable opportunities first.
Comment (0)
