articles.title: War of words - The News Pakistan
articles.summary: War of words  The News Pakistan
articles.full_text:
The war of words triggered in the past week between Maulana Fazlur Rehman and Pakistan’s ministers of defence and interior unleashed another visible drama at the centre of the country’s politics. But eventually, this episode too promises to go down in history as another hollow ring.
In time, the occasion will become a powerful reminder of a representative structure that remains detached from Pakistan’s compelling realities, with most of the country’s population facing fast-mounting challenges elsewhere. With the lives of Pakistan’s vast community of the disfranchised continuing without hope for the foreseeable future, the political elite remaining locked in this latest crossfire keeps them detached from the grassroots.
Against this backdrop, it would have been far more meaningful for members of the ruling structure and their political foes to lock horns and debate matters that have increasingly triggered the multiple crises facing the people of Pakistan. Maulana Fazlur Rehman’s initial trigger came with language mainstream parents would prefer not to teach their children at home. With much that Maulana Fazlur Rehman needs to be accounted for from his own past, taking the moral high ground in the name of protecting Pakistan’s democracy was just not his choice. His opponents from Pakistan’s ruling structure, with equally chequered histories, quickly found ammunition to respond in kind and more.
The ongoing circus at the centre of Pakistan’s highest political landscape comes at a deeply inopportune moment for the country’s present and future. It follows the recently reported hike in inflation fuelled by mounting fuel and food prices, which last week compelled the State Bank of Pakistan to raise its interest rates by half a per cent to 12 per cent.
The central bank’s choice was a powerful reminder that Pakistan’s mainstream population is bearing the brunt of worsening times. The fallout from that trend has already hit hard the average household budgets, including large parts of the middle class once considered relatively immune from previous episodes of a slumping economy.
Pakistan’s political turmoil, unleashed in recent times over controversy surrounding the conduct of the 2024 election, of course remains unending. And reversing that turmoil requires undoing all that has fuelled the rot. In this journey, the federal government’s recent decision to impose a state of emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has only added fuel to the proverbial fire that represents Pakistan’s politics today. Without resolving Pakistan’s fast-growing political discord, the country will not achieve the peace needed to recover other essential areas, notably the economy.
While Pakistan’s internal discord continues, the government and the opposition must cope with two equally essential challenges. First, the economic challenges confronting Pakistan today include alarming issues at the centre of the country’s survival. These include galloping inflation and risks tied to worsening climate change, deepening the malaise of a visibly moribund economy. For now, these challenges have kept investors – foreign and domestic – averse to becoming exposed to investing in Pakistan, notably for the long haul. This mood represents a formidable departure from eras like the 1960s when Pakistan was considered a destination of choice for investors.
The prevailing mood among investors has also been fuelled by other factors, notably the shrinking pool of well-trained labourers to meet the needs of businesses and industries. This is the tragic outcome of previous decades, spent with Pakistan’s educational system becoming increasingly neglected, barring a few notable institutions. Though successive governments have relentlessly pursued Pakistan’s labour export and the resulting inflow of foreign remittances, they have largely ignored the downside risk in this journey. That failure is not to build a pool of well-trained labourers to meet the needs of economic growth in new ventures at home.
Second, Pakistan’s domestic insecurity today continues on many fronts. These are not all just the threats from the Taliban operating from Afghanistan. Though the threat of the Taliban onslaught must never be overlooked, insecurity elsewhere cannot be ignored either. From large, thriving urban centres to every corner of Pakistan’s rural areas, insecurity is visibly growing and needs urgent attention. Even the ongoing debate over the creation of many more provinces has failed to address a fundamental question. How will such reform address the gaps in security, beyond arming the visible political elite with authority at the grassroots? That remains an unanswered question.
Besides, there is no reconciliation yet with visibly failed past reforms, notably the dismantling of the civil service at the grassroots in the name of devolution, as pursued under the rule of the late president Gen Pervez Musharraf.
Beyond the ongoing political discord, much remains to be addressed to create a new Pakistan, not just the outcome of the ongoing infighting.
The writer is an Islamabad-based journalist who writes on political and economic affairs. He can be reached at: farhanbokhari@gmail.com

articles.title: The Brahmaputra Begins in Tibet. So Does India’s Concern - Tibetan Review
articles.summary: The Brahmaputra Begins in Tibet. So Does India’s Concern  Tibetan Review
articles.full_text:
OPINION
From the journeys of Indian explorers into Tibet to China’s proposed mega-dam on the Yarlung Tsangpo, the history of the eastern Himalayas has much to tell India about its northern frontier, writes Saurabh Chauhan.*
India’s debate on China is usually dominated by the Line of Actual Control, military infrastructure and the possibility of another confrontation along the Himalayan frontier. These are important concerns, but there is a longer history behind India’s northern security questions. Much of it begins with Tibet.
For centuries, Tibet was connected to the Indian subcontinent through trade, pilgrimage and religious exchanges. Mountain passes linked communities on both sides of the Himalayas. Monks travelled between monasteries, traders carried goods across difficult routes and rivers flowing from the Tibetan Plateau sustained settlements further south. These connections existed long before the modern India-China boundary dispute.
The political transformation of Tibet in the twentieth century changed this geography. It also changed India’s relationship with its northern neighbour. Today, with China constructing a massive hydropower project on the lower reaches of the Yarlung Tsangpo, the river has become another point of concern for New Delhi.
The proposed project raises questions about water security, the availability of hydrological information and the future of communities living along the Brahmaputra. India’s response, however, cannot be limited to building infrastructure of its own. There is a history here worth revisiting and there are people whose lives will be affected by decisions taken in Beijing and New Delhi.
The explorers who mapped Tibet
India’s relationship with Tibet did not begin with the boundary dispute. Trade, religious exchanges and travel connected the two regions through Ladakh, Sikkim, Bhutan and the eastern Himalayas. These routes were familiar to local communities long before they appeared on modern maps.
The British period brought a more organised effort to map Tibet. During the nineteenth century, British India was concerned about Russian expansion in Central Asia and the security of its northern approaches. Tibet became an important part of what was later called the Great Game.
But the history of exploration is not simply a story of British officers entering an unknown land. Indian explorers made some of the most important contributions to geographical knowledge of the Tibetan Plateau. Their work is often remembered through the reports of the colonial administration rather than through their own achievements.
One of the best-known figures was Nain Singh Rawat, a Kumaoni explorer trained by the Survey of India. His journeys into Tibet were remarkable, considering the conditions under which he travelled. Disguised as a Buddhist pilgrim, he recorded distances, altitudes, routes and geographical observations using methods that allowed him to survey the landscape without attracting attention.
His journey to Lhasa in 1865–66 was particularly important. He also explored parts of the upper Brahmaputra region. T. G. Montgomerie’s report, published in the Journal of the Royal Geographical Society in 1868, records the route survey made by the explorer from Nepal to Lhasa and through the upper valley of the Brahmaputra. Its accompanying map remains an interesting historical document.
Nain Singh should not be remembered merely as an assistant to British surveyors. His ability to travel through Tibet and record its geography made a significant contribution to the understanding of the Himalayas. His story also raises a question about how India remembers those who helped document its own northern frontier.
Another important figure was Sarat Chandra Das, a Bengali scholar and explorer who travelled to Tibet in the late nineteenth century. His Narrative of a Journey to Lhasa in 1881–82, published in 1885, is an important account of Tibetan society, institutions and geography. His later work, Journey to Lhasa and Central Tibet, also remains useful to historians.
Das was not simply interested in routes and mountains. His writings offer glimpses of the society through which he travelled. They provide material on Tibetan religious institutions, customs and intellectual life, something that is often missing from accounts concerned mainly with imperial geography.
There was, of course, a colonial purpose behind much of this exploration. The British wanted information that could serve administrative and military interests. That context should not be ignored. But neither should the contribution of the Indian explorers who undertook these journeys.
Following the Tsangpo
The history of the Yarlung Tsangpo is particularly interesting because its connection with the Brahmaputra was not immediately established by European surveyors.
The river flows eastwards across Tibet before making a dramatic turn around the Namcha Barwa massif in the eastern Himalayas. It then enters Arunachal Pradesh as the Siang and flows through Assam as the Brahmaputra. Further downstream, it enters Bangladesh, where the main river is known as the Jamuna.
For a long time, the course of the river through the eastern Himalayan gorges remained uncertain. Explorers wanted to establish whether the Tsangpo continued into Assam and how it crossed the mountain system.
One of the most remarkable attempts was made by Kinthup, a Lepcha explorer who worked with the Survey of India. He was sent into Tibet to investigate the river. His mission involved releasing marked logs into the water at an agreed time so that observers downstream could identify them and establish the river’s course.
The expedition went badly wrong. Kinthup faced deception, captivity and considerable hardship. His observations were not immediately accepted and his contribution received recognition much later.
The next important stage came in 1913, when Frederick Marshman Bailey and Henry Morshead undertook an exploration of the Tsangpo gorge. Bailey was a British military officer and political officer with considerable knowledge of Tibet. Morshead was a Survey of India officer. Their journey helped clarify the geography of a region that had remained difficult for outside surveyors to access.
Bailey published his account, Exploration on the Tsang-Po or Upper Brahmaputra, in the Scottish Geographical Magazine in 1914. Morshead’s contribution to the expedition is recorded in later historical accounts, including Michael Ward’s work on the exploration of the river.
Ward’s article, The Exploration of the Tsangpo River and its Mountains, published in the Alpine Journal in 2000, is a useful starting point for understanding these journeys. More recently, historian Thomas Simpson’s 2024 study, Find the River: Discovering the Tsangpo-Brahmaputra in the Age of Empire, has examined the relationship between geographical exploration, imperial ambitions and local knowledge.
That last point deserves attention. These explorers did not travel through an empty landscape. They depended on Tibetan routes, local guides, traders and people who already knew the terrain. Pilgrimage networks and knowledge passed down through generations were essential to their journeys. The history of the river cannot be told only through the records of colonial surveyors.
There is a lesson here for India. Understanding the Himalayan frontier has never depended on maps and military surveys alone. Local knowledge has always mattered. It should matter just as much when India considers the future of its rivers.
When Tibet changed
The political history of Tibet between 1914 and 1950 is important to understanding the boundary dispute between India and China.
The Simla Convention of 1914 brought together representatives of British India, Tibet and China. The negotiations dealt with Tibet’s political position and the boundary between British India and Tibet. The McMahon Line emerged from the discussions between British India and the Tibetan representative, Lonchen Shatra.
The Chinese representative initially participated in the negotiations but did not sign the final convention. Britain and Tibet subsequently signed a separate agreement. China rejected the arrangement and its objections to the McMahon Line remain central to the eastern sector of the India-China boundary dispute.
For much of the period that followed, the Tibetan government in Lhasa exercised substantial de facto autonomy, although Tibet’s international status remained contested. British India maintained trade agencies at Gyantse, Yatung and Gartok. A British mission was established in Lhasa in 1936. These arrangements continued into the final years of British rule in India.
When India became independent in 1947, it inherited a complicated relationship with Tibet. The Indian government continued to maintain trade and diplomatic contacts with Lhasa, but the political circumstances were changing rapidly.
In 1950, the People’s Liberation Army entered eastern Tibet and defeated Tibetan forces at Chamdo. The following year, the Seventeen-Point Agreement was signed between representatives of the People’s Republic of China and the Tibetan government. It formalised Beijing’s control over Tibet, although the circumstances surrounding the negotiations and the agreement remain disputed in historical accounts.
India’s relationship with Tibet changed accordingly. The 1954 Agreement on Trade and Intercourse between the Tibet Region of China and India reflected the new political reality. It also introduced the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, commonly known as Panchsheel, into the relationship between the two countries.
The deterioration of India-China relations in the years that followed culminated in the 1962 war. The boundary dispute remained unresolved, but the political transformation of Tibet had already altered India’s strategic position along the Himalayas.

articles.title: US manufacturing strengthens in October, input prices stay high - ET Manufacturing
articles.summary: US manufacturing strengthens in October, input prices stay high  ET Manufacturing
articles.full_text:
US manufacturing activity accelerated in October, with the ISM manufacturing PMI rising to 55.5 from 54.5 in September, beating Reuters-polled economists' expectations.
US manufacturing activity picked up in October amid strong domestic demand, keeping inflation at the factory gate elevated.
They were likely referring to rising prices for a range of commodities including energy, stemming from the ongoing US-Israeli war with Iran. A recent escalation in the trade war with Canada was also cited by manufacturers as a constraint.
Economists cautioned that rising interest rates and declining inflation-adjusted household income would hamper manufacturing activity next year, especially the segments not exposed to the artificial intelligence spending frenzy.
"While AI-related investment is expected to remain strong, further shifts in AI sentiment, which has worsened in recent weeks, could weigh on investment plans," said Veronica Clark, an economist at Citigroup. "Even if current investment plans proceed, this would still suggest a slowing growth rate of future investment. Additionally, higher rates and recently tighter financial conditions could weigh on non-AI related parts of the manufacturing sector."
The ISM said its manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index increased to 55.5 last month from 54.5 in September. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the PMI would stay at 54.5. The PMI has stayed above the 50 threshold this year, indicating growth in manufacturing, a sector that accounts for about 9.4 per cent of the economy.
A measure of production at factories jumped 2.3 per cent points to 59 last month, the highest reading since November 2021.
Twelve industries reported growth, including transportation equipment, electrical equipment, appliances and components, machinery, primary metals, textile mills, and computer and electronic products. The three industries reporting a contraction were paper products, printing and related support activities, and nonmetallic mineral products.
The overall economy grew at a 3.4 per cent annualized rate last quarter after expanding at a 2.2 per cent pace in the April-June period, even as the war in the Middle East stoked inflation. The ISM survey's new orders measure edged up to 55.5 from 55.3 in September, with exports also rising.
Sentiment continues to deteriorate
Still, Susan Spence, who chairs the ISM Manufacturing Business Survey Committee, noted that "general sentiment got worse for a third month in a row." She reported that 66 per cent of commentary from respondents was negative, with pricing volatility dominating the downbeat views, followed by longer lead times, tariffs and the war.
Some makers of fabricated metal products said "customers are unwilling to make commitments to anything other than the shortest term due to the vast uncertainty." Their counterparts in the chemical products industry said "negative, inflation, in the red are the three words or phrases that best describe our strategic sourcing for 2026."

articles.title: Why Delayed Careers Are Shrinking India's Youth Aspirations - Dainik Jagran MP CG
articles.summary: Why Delayed Careers Are Shrinking India's Youth Aspirations  Dainik Jagran MP CG
articles.full_text:
Abhishek Joshi
Delayed jobs, competitive exams and financial pressure are changing young Indians' career ambitions. Why India needs better employment pathways.
When education, competitive examinations and repeated job searches consume the years meant for building independent lives, young people can begin lowering their expectations—not because they lack ambition, but because uncertainty makes long-term plans increasingly difficult.
A career delay is often described as a temporary setback. But when the delay stretches across years, it can change how a person imagines the future. A young graduate who once dreamed of starting a business, pursuing higher studies, moving to another city or building a professional career may eventually focus on a much smaller goal: finding any stable job, earning a regular income and becoming financially independent.
This shift deserves attention. India's debate about youth employment should not focus only on how many people are unemployed. It should also ask what happens to their ambitions when the transition from education to work takes too long.
Why Delayed Careers Are Creating a Generation With Shrinking Aspirations
A career delay is often described as a temporary setback. But when the delay stretches across years, it can change how a person imagines the future. A young graduate who once dreamed of starting a business, pursuing higher studies, moving to another city or building a professional career may eventually focus on a much smaller goal: finding any stable job, earning a regular income and becoming financially independent.
This shift deserves attention. India's debate about youth employment should not focus only on how many people are unemployed. It should also ask what happens to their ambitions when the transition from education to work takes too long.
When ambition meets an uncertain job market
For many young Indians, the journey from education to employment is becoming increasingly difficult. Completing a degree does not necessarily mean entering the workforce quickly, and gaining additional qualifications does not guarantee a suitable job.
Azim Premji University's State of Working India 2026 report highlights the scale of this challenge. It estimates that unemployment among graduates aged 15–25 was nearly 40% in 2023, while the rate for graduates aged 25–29 was around 20%. The report also notes that only a small proportion of graduates secure stable salaried employment within a year of completing their studies.
The figures suggest a serious mismatch between the expansion of higher education and the availability of suitable employment. For young people, this can mean spending several years moving between examinations, internships, temporary work and repeated job applications.
The longer this uncertainty continues, the harder it becomes to maintain the same expectations about the future.
From pursuing dreams to accepting whatever is available
A young person entering college may imagine a career in technology, journalism, business, healthcare, research or public administration. But after years of unsuccessful applications or competitive examination attempts, the original ambition can gradually become a question of survival.
The priority may shift from finding meaningful work to finding any source of regular income. Further education may be postponed, entrepreneurship may appear too risky, and relocation may become unaffordable.
This does not necessarily mean young people have lost their abilities or interests. It may mean that financial pressure has reduced the choices available to them.
There is an important difference between changing career goals because interests evolve and abandoning them because opportunities remain inaccessible. When the second becomes widespread, it points towards a problem that goes beyond individual motivation.
Competitive examinations can turn time into a major cost
Government employment remains an important aspiration for many Indian families because it is associated with stability, predictable income and social security.
However, intense competition means that candidates can spend years preparing for a limited number of vacancies. Delayed recruitment, examination cancellations and uncertainty over results can make the process even more difficult.
A candidate who spends three or four years preparing for competitive examinations is not simply waiting for a result. They may also be postponing professional experience, financial independence and other career options.
The opportunity cost can be substantial. Someone who eventually leaves the examination cycle may have to begin again in the private sector, sometimes competing with candidates who have already accumulated years of work experience.
The answer is not to discourage government-job preparation. It is to make recruitment predictable and transparent while ensuring that young people have credible alternative pathways into employment.
Financial pressure is narrowing career choices
Ambition requires a certain degree of security. A person who has financial support may be able to pursue higher studies, accept an unpaid internship, relocate for a promising opportunity or take the risk of starting a business.
Someone supporting a household or depending on limited family savings may not have the same freedom.
This creates an unequal environment in which career choices are shaped not only by talent and qualifications but also by financial circumstances. Young people from lower-income households may be forced to prioritise immediate earnings over long-term professional development.
The pressure can also affect families. Parents who have spent years financing education may expect their children to begin earning. Graduates, meanwhile, may feel guilty about continued dependence and gradually lower their expectations to avoid placing further pressure on the household.
In this situation, a career decision becomes an economic necessity rather than a choice based on aptitude or interest.
The problem is not only unemployment, but the quality of work
Finding employment does not always end the uncertainty. Many graduates enter jobs that offer limited pay, temporary contracts, little professional development or responsibilities unrelated to their qualifications.
The National Institution for Transforming India (NITI Aayog), in its 2026 report Reimagining Skilling for Viksit Bharat@2047, highlighted the disconnect between education and labour-market requirements. A report on its findings by The Indian Express cited an estimate that only 8.25% of graduates were employed in roles aligned with their qualifications.
This mismatch matters because a job that provides income but little scope for advancement may not fulfil the expectations associated with higher education.
When young people repeatedly encounter this situation, they may begin to question whether additional qualifications, professional training or career changes will actually improve their prospects.
Young women face additional barriers
Delayed careers can have particularly serious consequences for young women. Family responsibilities, safety concerns, limited transport, social expectations and fewer opportunities in nearby areas can interrupt their entry into employment.
A woman who takes time away from work because of family responsibilities may find it difficult to return to a career that matches her qualifications. Others may accept work with limited progression because relocation or long working hours are not practical.
NITI Aayog's 2026 skilling report also identifies barriers to women's participation in training and employment, including information gaps and constraints related to access.
Career delays should therefore be understood not simply as a question of individual timing but also as a reflection of unequal access to opportunities.
How can India prevent aspirations from shrinking?
The solution cannot be limited to asking young people to become more patient, acquire additional certificates or work harder. Individual effort matters, but it cannot compensate for a shortage of suitable opportunities.
First, recruitment systems must become more predictable. Government departments and examination agencies should follow announced schedules, communicate delays clearly and address irregularities quickly.
Second, India needs more productive entry-level employment across manufacturing, healthcare, tourism, technology, logistics, research and other sectors. Economic growth must translate into opportunities that allow young people to begin their careers without spending years waiting for a narrow set of vacancies.
Third, colleges and universities should strengthen internships, apprenticeships, industry partnerships and career guidance. Students need exposure to actual workplaces before completing their degrees.
Fourth, skill development should be affordable and accessible beyond major cities. Young people should be able to explore different career paths without depending entirely on expensive coaching or private certification programmes.
Finally, career guidance should encourage flexibility without making young people feel that changing direction is a failure. A graduate who moves from examination preparation to a private-sector job, vocational training or entrepreneurship should have access to pathways that recognise existing knowledge and experience.
India's demographic advantage depends on opportunity
India's young population is frequently discussed as an economic advantage. But a large youth population becomes a demographic dividend only when people can participate productively in the economy.
The challenge is not that every young person must achieve every ambition formed during school or college. Career paths naturally change, and not every expectation can be fulfilled. The deeper concern is whether financial pressure, limited opportunities and prolonged uncertainty are forcing people to abandon reasonable ambitions before they have had a fair chance

articles.title: What's behind new India-China border tensions in Arunachal Pradesh state? - DW.com
articles.summary: What's behind new India-China border tensions in Arunachal Pradesh state?  DW.com
articles.full_text:
Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) Director General Shatrujeet Kapur sounded alarm bells across India by confirming that Indian and Chinese troops had confronted each other at several locations along the de facto border in Arunachal Pradesh state, in India's northeast.
"In the past few days, a situation arose where a face-off happened (with Chinese troops) at various locations in Arunachal and it still continues," he told reporters last month.
"It may be difficult to counter China by conventional means because their PLA and BDR (Border Defense Regiment) have gone way ahead with investment and modernization," he said.
The disputed China-India border runs through a remote mountainous region.
Throughout the decades, clashes along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the de facto border, have repeatedly triggered security crises between the world's two most populous nations.
Ties between Beijing and New Delhi are still affected by the deadly violence in 2020, when both countries accused each other of trying to seize territory.
In June that year, a clash in the Galwan River valley in eastern Ladakh killed 20 Indian soldiers and four Chinese troops, according to Indian sources. China later confirmed four of its soldiers died.
Arunachal Pradesh leader Pema Khandu says situation normal
Kapur's remarks have brought renewed attention to the Himalayan frontier. Arunachal Pradesh Chief Minister Pema Khandu has acknowledged but also downplayed the border transgressions, saying such incidents were not new and the situation along the border was normal.
Khandu acknowledged that the border was not properly demarcated and that China did not recognize the McMahon Line, drawn by the British Empire in 1914, which separates Arunachal Pradesh from Tibet.
It was also not clear if the latest confrontations between the Chinese and Indian troops involved physical violence.
China rejects wrongdoing
The opposition Congress party criticized Khandu's remarks, and accused the ruling BJP, led by India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi, of "rationalizing" Chinese actions instead of asserting India's position.
"On this there has been a deafening silence from the PM and his establishment," Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh said in a post on X, referring to the face-offs confirmed by the border police chief.
Meanwhile, External Affairs Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal attributed the incidents to Chinese forces changing up their patrol routes.
"As we have noted in the past, the situation in the India-China border areas gets disturbed from time to time when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns," he said.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun rejected the allegations, saying Chinese troops were conducting "normal patrols" and strictly abiding by bilateral agreements.
Why do face-offs keep happening?
The LAC largely separates Indian- and Chinese-controlled territory. However, as forces from both nations patrol territory they regard as their own, they sometimes venture into disputed areas.
"There is a very simple reason — because there is no agreed line between the two," Gautam Bambawale, a former Indian ambassador to China, told DW.
The de-facto border stretches for 3,488 kilometres (2,167 miles) according to India, but China claims it is shorter. The two countries have held 25 rounds of talks between their Special Representatives since 2003, but have yet to reach a boundary settlement.
The dispute is particularly sensitive in Arunachal Pradesh, which China claims as part of southern Tibet.
China building a hydropower dam in Tibet
Aravind Yelery, a China expert at Jawaharlal Nehru University, said the region has become more strategically important to Beijing.
"Both sides patrol a contested LAC, so friction is built into the arrangement," Yelery told DW.
"What is new is China's intensified focus on the eastern sector. Since announcing the 60,000-megawatt Medog hydropower project in Tibet, Beijing has poured infrastructure, troops, engineers and machinery into the area."
He described the LAC as "not a thin line but a deep zone of overlapping claims where patrols inevitably meet." Face-offs will continue, he argued, until diplomacy produces concrete arrangements on the ground.
According to Yelery, the diplomatic pledges made by Indian and Chinese leaders will take time to implement.
"A wide gap separates the leaders' promises from the measures that would prevent a repeat of 2020, namely disengagement and mutual restraint," he added.
What is different about the latest developments?
For India, the immediate concern is whether the recent encounters reflect familiar patrol disputes or a more significant change in Chinese activity along the frontier.
Ashok Kantha, another former Indian ambassador to China, said Chinese transgressions in the eastern sector were not new, but that their location and extent mattered.
"If the Chinese have now made deeper intrusions on our side of the LAC, or established a presence in new areas, or expanded their existing presence, that would be a serious development," he added.
He also pointed to agreements signed by the two countries to maintain peace along the border.
"Any such transgression would be in complete violation of several border-related agreements India and China have signed (1993, 1996, 2005, 2012 and 2013). In these, both sides committed to respect and strictly observe the LAC, and not to alter the status quo."
The Indian government has not publicly provided details of the locations or circumstances of the latest face-offs, making it unclear whether they have changed the situation on the ground.
A fragile diplomatic thaw
The renewed encounters come as India and China try to stabilize relations and move past the 2020 clashes. Both Beijing and New Delhi made reconciliatory moves, including restoring some direct flights and easing restrictions on travel and economic exchanges.
The diplomatic reset gathered pace after Narendra Modi and Xi Jinping met at the BRICS summit in Kazan, Russia, in October 2024. They met again at the SCO summit in Tianjin in August 2025 and at the BRICS summit in New Delhi this year.
The boundary dispute, however, remains unresolved.
Alka Acharya, director of the Institute of Chinese Studies in New Delhi, cautioned against drawing conclusions about the latest encounters without more information.
The government has described the incidents as face-offs, she said, but has not indicated that Chinese troops have taken control of Indian territory.
"The question is what is the nature of the so-called 'clashes' … not why the clashes are happening again? Any opinion on this latest kerfuffle would at best be conjecture without any definitive evidence," Acharya told DW.
Border incidents have occurred regularly over the past decade and a half, despite political and diplomatic negotiations. The unresolved dispute, she added, will continue to sustain distrust and constrain the broader relationship.
Whether the latest encounters signal a more serious escalation will depend on details that New Delhi has yet to make public.
Edited by: Darko Janjevic

articles.summary: Zelio E-Mobility expands annual capacity by 72,000 units with new Hisar plant  ET Manufacturing
articles.full_text:
Zelio E-Mobility, Haryana-based electric two- and three-wheeler maker, on Tuesday said it has commenced commercial production at its new manufacturing plant in Patan, Hisar, adding 72,000 units to its annual installed capacity and taking the total to approximately 3.12 lakh units from 2.4 lakh units.
According to the official press release, the facility will have an annual capacity of 48,000 electric two-wheelers and 24,000 electric three-wheelers. 
The company said it has committed an investment of more than ₹20 crore for the facility under its approved capital expenditure plan. 
Part of the investment has been funded through proceeds from the company’s initial public offering, with the remaining requirement to be met through internal accruals.
Managing Director Kunal Arya said the new plant would help the company deepen its presence in Tier-2 and Tier-3 markets, while maintaining a focus on profitability and disciplined growth.
Targets dealer network of over 550 by FY27
Zelio currently has more than 400 dealers across over 25 states and is targeting a network of more than 550 dealerships by FY27. 
The company said the new facility would help improve product availability and replenishment timelines as it expands its market presence.

articles.title: White House touts unsigned India deal among Trump's achievements - India's News.Net
articles.summary: White House touts unsigned India deal among Trump's achievements  India's News.Net
articles.full_text:
The claim cited a February trade framework among the president's wins, although talks are still ongoing
The White House has listed an "improved" trade agreement with India among US President Donald Trump's achievements, although New Delhi and Washington are still negotiating to finalize the pact first outlined in February.
New Delhi has held off on the deal, while seeking greater tariff certainty and preferential market access for its exporters and vowing to shield its sensitive agricultural sector.
The claim appeared on a list the White House released ahead of Tuesday's midterm elections, among 127 promises that it touted Trump as having fulfilled during his second term. It also comes just two weeks after Trump himself described the deal as "pretty close" - not as finalized.
The claim, under the heading "Igniting a Blue-Collar Boom and Restoring Fair Trade," said Trump had "secured new and improved trade agreements," which cover more than half the global GDP, with major trading partners including India, the EU, Japan, and China.
The reference to India links to a February 9 fact sheet titled "The United States and India Announce Historic Trade Deal." The document only says the countries would work toward finalizing an interim agreement. A joint statement days earlier had only proposed reducing US reciprocal tariffs on Indian goods to 18%, and India lowering duties on American industrial goods and selected agricultural products.
Later that month, the US Supreme Court struck down Trump's sweeping emergency tariffs, and Washington slapped an additional 10% duty on covered Indian imports under Section 301 of the US trade law.
Around 55% of India's exports to the US are subject to the additional levy, while products including generic pharmaceuticals and smartphones remain exempt, according to India's Commerce Ministry.
Indian Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said last month that the first phase of the agreement had been finalized at the negotiating level but was still undergoing legal drafting.

articles.full_text:
India's Health Ministry is tightening drug regulatory oversight by proposing immediate suspension of manufacturing licenses for units failing critical quality benchmarks. For major pharmaceutical players like Sun Pharma, this policy shift elevates compliance requirements across domestic production lines, making strict quality control standard operating procedures central to operational stability.
Market snapshot: The Indian government has proposed draft amendments to the Drugs Rules that mandate an immediate halt on manufacturing licenses for drug companies whose samples fail essential quality tests. Operations will only be allowed to resume after full compliance and confirmed corrective measures are verified by regulators.
Data Snapshot
- Draft amendments to India's Drugs Rules propose immediate suspension of manufacturing licenses upon quality test failure, with restoration contingent on verified corrections.

articles.title: Interview | Whether India & China Remain Adversaries Is a Matter of Political Choice, Says Former Diplomat Bala Bhaskar - Outlook India
articles.summary: Interview | Whether India & China Remain Adversaries Is a Matter of Political Choice, Says Former Diplomat Bala Bhaskar  Outlook India
articles.full_text:
Why do border face-offs keep recurring?
The fundamental problem is the unresolved boundary and the absence of a mutually delineated Line of Actual Control (LAC). In certain sectors, competing territorial perceptions differ by hundreds of metres to several kilometres. Difficult terrain, extreme weather and surveillance limitations complicate patrolling, while expanding military infrastructure on both sides has increased access to previously remote areas. In a sense, India and China are still discovering the operational contours of their disputed frontier, as improved accessibility and intensified patrolling bring competing territorial perceptions into sharper confrontation.
Border confrontations must therefore be understood at four interconnected levels: ground-level patrolling encounters, military-operational calculations, differing perceptions of the LAC, and broader political-strategic objectives rooted in competing territorial claims. While geographical ambiguities can trigger confrontations, deliberate attempts to assert territorial claims, test India's responses, or strengthen negotiating positions cannot be ruled out. Local military assessments and operational decisions may influence how confrontations develop.
Do face-offs deliberately coincide with major diplomatic engagements?
There have been striking coincidences. The 2013 Depsang confrontation preceded Premier Li Keqiang's visit to India, while the Chumar standoff coincided with President Xi Jinping's September 2014 visit. Such timing raises legitimate questions about the interplay between China's political leadership and the People's Liberation Army, deliberate political signalling, operational initiatives by military commanders, or differing assessments within the decision-making establishment. However, given the opacity of China's political and military decision-making, it is difficult to establish whether these confrontations were centrally orchestrated or reflected internal differences.
India needs to judge strategic intent by the totality of evidence and patterns of behaviour, not timing alone: intelligence, troop mobilisation, logistical preparations, diplomatic signalling and subsequent Chinese demands.
How relevant is the 1993 agreement and what can India learn from former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao?
The 1993 Border Peace and Tranquility Agreement was a landmark diplomatic achievement, building on the political understanding reached during then prime minister Rajiv Gandhi's historic 1988 visit to China: the unresolved boundary dispute need not prevent the development of bilateral relations in other areas. The 1988 visit also established a joint working group to pursue a boundary settlement. Rao translated this political understanding into a formal framework for maintaining peace along the LAC while continuing boundary negotiations. Subsequent agreements in 1996, 2005 and 2013 further strengthened this framework.
How should India balance engagement, economic cooperation and national security?
India's China policy must balance credible deterrence, sustained diplomacy and selective economic cooperation, with border peace as its foundation. Complete decoupling is neither realistic nor desirable. India must distinguish beneficial economic interdependence from strategic dependence, diversify critical supply chains, and strengthen domestic industrial and technological capabilities. Strategic autonomy must remain paramount. India must pursue its national interests independently, without becoming an instrument of another power's geopolitical rivalry. Engagement must not become dependence, deterrence must not become confrontation, and strategic competition must not foreclose diplomacy.
National security extends far beyond military strength and territorial defence. It encompasses economic resilience, technological and industrial capabilities, manufacturing scale, environmental and climate security, and societal cohesion. These interconnected dimensions demand a whole-of-nation approach that integrates diplomacy, defence, economic policy, technology and industry into comprehensive national power.
What does China really want from India?
China seeks to retain India as a major economic market while constraining its emergence as a formidable strategic counterweight in Asia. Beijing is particularly wary of India's growing partnerships with the US and other Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (Quad) members, which it perceives as potentially challenging its global ambitions.
China's principal geopolitical rivalry, however, is with the US, extending across the Indo-Pacific, technology, trade, finance and the global economic order. Its expanding industrial, technological and military capabilities have strengthened its strategic influence. Beijing's approach to India must therefore be understood within this larger contest for global power, reflecting a familiar tendency among established and aspiring great powers to resist emerging strategic challengers. But the more fundamental question is what India seeks from China. India's approach has too often been reactive. Even the US, Japan and Australia continue engaging Beijing despite strategic differences, guided by their national interests. India must likewise pursue a proactive, pragmatic and independent China policy—cooperating where interests converge, resisting coercion and strengthening comprehensive national power to negotiate on more equitable terms.
Why does India remain dependent on Chinese imports?
India's dependence reflects inadequate industrial depth. China has built integrated ecosystems spanning minerals, processing, technology, logistics, and manufacturing at scale, turning economic strength into strategic leverage. India must similarly transform its resources, talent and market into competitive industrial capabilities. Trade can encourage cooperation and reduce tensions, but it cannot prevent strategic competition or guarantee peace.
How should India correct the trade imbalance and reduce strategic vulnerabilities?
India's trade imbalance with China reflects structural dependence on Chinese machinery, components and technology, compounded by weak domestic manufacturing competitiveness and limited technical skills. Import restrictions alone cannot address this imbalance. India must build integrated industrial ecosystems that link infrastructure, mineral processing, technology, and manufacturing at scale. Creating intellectual property, diversifying supply chains, increasing domestic value addition and strengthening exports must go hand in hand with continued access to essential imports. The objective is not merely to reduce Chinese imports, but to build a globally competitive industrial and technological economy.
Have three decades of diplomatic engagement with China delivered?
India's diplomacy with China cannot be dismissed as a failure. Agreements since 1993 maintained relative border peace for nearly three decades, facilitating trade and political engagement. However, the nature of border confrontations changed over time.
Depsang (2013) and Chumar (2014) exposed weaknesses in border management; Doklam (2017), eastern Ladakh (2020), Tawang in 2022 and renewed confrontations in Arunachal Pradesh in 2026 reflected persistent border tensions amid China's growing strategic assertiveness backed by rapidly expanding economic, technological, and military capabilities. Beyond Beijing's objections to India's 2019 reorganisation of Jammu and Kashmir, particularly the creation of the Union Territory of Ladakh, China's concerns over India's growing strategic partnerships with the US and Japan, and the revival of the Quad in 2017, may also have influenced its calculations.
An equally neglected dimension is the sharp divide in public perceptions between the two countries. Buddhism and ancient civilisational ties sustain spiritual and cultural affinity towards India among large sections of Chinese society. However, Indian public perceptions of China remain largely negative, shaped by the legacy of the 1962 war, recurring border disputes and Beijing's strategic partnership with Pakistan.
Recognising this deficit, Prime Minister Narendra Modi, during his first China visit in May 2015, brought chief ministers, mayors and other local political leaders to launch the India-China State/Provincial Leaders' Forum with Premier Li Keqiang. It sought to extend engagement beyond national capitals to states, cities and citizens. Unfortunately, the initiative did not develop into sustained engagement. Relations between great civilisations require more than summit diplomacy, military deterrence and trade; they demand deeper societal connections and mutual understanding.
How should India view the China-Pakistan partnership?
The China-Pakistan strategic partnership now extends beyond defence to technology, infrastructure and regional connectivity. The Iran conflict adds a new geopolitical dimension, linking South Asian security with West Asia's evolving security architecture. China's expanding engagement with Iran and the Gulf, alongside Pakistan's deepening defence ties with Saudi Arabia and Türkiye, could reshape regional strategic alignments.
Any substantial reduction in America's security role in West Asia could enhance Pakistan's strategic significance as a nuclear-armed Muslim-majority state and create opportunities for greater Chinese influence. These developments carry implications for India's energy security, maritime interests, the international north-south transport corridor and diplomatic influence.
However, China's global economic and geopolitical interests do not necessarily coincide with Pakistan's predominantly India-centric security priorities. India must recognise and leverage these divergences rather than regard the partnership as a monolithic anti-India bloc. India must also avoid being drawn into emerging rivalries within West Asia, preserving its longstanding ability to engage competing regional powers

articles.title: After seismic shift in US, a new Congress but an old consensus - The Times of India
articles.summary: After seismic shift in US, a new Congress but an old consensus  The Times of India
articles.full_text:
The shift in US Congressional control is a pivotal moment for Washington, but its impact on the India–US strategic partnership will likely be more subtle than disruptive. With President Donald Trump retaining executive control though over US foreign policy, India will need to guard against any further complication of the West Asia conflict.
The relationship rests on bipartisan support and consensus built around Indo-Pacific cooperation amid Chinese assertiveness, along with people-to-people contacts and technology and defence ties. Electoral cycles have done little to deter this momentum built over the past 25 years.
However, despite this core alignment, the strategic partnership also hit its lowest ebb in decades under the second Trump administration over issues like asymmetrical trade demands, India's reluctance to abandon its energy ties with Russia, US immigration policies and also Washington's Pakistan outreach leading effectively to the re-hyphenation of its approach to the region.
To what extent a tighter Congressional scrutiny of Trump's actions – including on issues related to Iran and Ukraine – can constrain his foreign policy is unclear, as the legislative turnaround is unlikely to dent his broad executive authority over US diplomacy and military even in the face of a domestic pushback.
Significantly, the ASEAN summit this month in Manila – where PM Narendra Modi will be present – might indicate how the midterm results could reshape Trump's approach to global affairs. 
Of immediate interest not just for India but also Japan and Australia will be the Quad leaders' summit which is scheduled for November 16 on the margins of ASEAN. Modi may have also have a bilateral meeting with Trump.
It was India's turn to host the leaders' summit for the past 2 years but Trump's apparent reluctance to travel to New Delhi amid bilateral trade discord delayed the event, leading many to conclude that the president had downgraded Quad to pursue closer ties with Beijing.
Preserving Quad for a free and open Indo-Pacific is a key foreign policy priority for India and Japan. The leaders' summit in Manila will be of particular significance as it will take place in the middle of the Philippines' continued maritime tensions with Beijing, and days before Trump's visit to China for the APEC leaders' meeting.
Strategic ties in the form of Quad, defence cooperation and initiatives like TRUST (formerly iCET) on critical and emerging technology will continue to deepen, based on the bipartisan foundation. As it negotiates its own trade agreement with the US, India will watch out though for potential legislative hurdles over labour and environmental standards.
A Democratic majority could also seek to curb the Trump administration's unilateral tariff actions, ensuring some reprieve for India. It could also offer a check against restrictive immigration legislation, providing relief potentially for high-skilled Indian professionals and H-1B visa holders. Democrats have traditionally been more vocal or even critical of India on human rights and other internal issues, but this has rarely been a deal-breaker.
After the midterm outcomes, India will look to balance its engagement with the White House by cultivating ties with key Democratic committee chairs. According to Indian officials, the relationship based on similar values and strategic goals will continue to grow.

articles.title: Costly coal-fired power agreements: Pakistan risks remaining trapped - Business Recorder
articles.summary: Costly coal-fired power agreements: Pakistan risks remaining trapped  Business Recorder
articles.full_text:
ISLAMABAD: Pakistan risks remaining trapped in costly coal-fired power agreements even as households and industries rapidly shift towards solar energy, with experts warning that declining electricity demand from the national grid, mounting capacity payments and delayed policy reforms could deepen the power sector’s financial crisis.
They were speaking at a policy dialogue titled “From Coal to Clean: Towards a Phased, Just Energy Transition,” organised on the third day of the four-day Sustainable Development Conference, held by the Sustainable Development Policy Institute (SDPI) at Allama Iqbal Open University here on Wednesday. The overarching theme of this year’s conference is “Rethinking Development in an Age of Disruption.”
The discussion exposed a fundamental policy divide over Pakistan’s energy future: whether expensive imported coal plants should be retired early through international financing arrangements or converted to indigenous Thar coal to reduce fuel imports and preserve reliable generation capacity.
Chairing the session, former federal climate change minister Malik Amin Aslam said Pakistan’s biggest obstacle was not the absence of financing but a lack of political will to dismantle costly arrangements benefiting entrenched interests.
He questioned capacity payments to underutilised power plants and alleged that earlier electricity demand projections had been deliberately inflated to encourage investments by independent power producers (IPPs).
Aslam said consumers had effectively taken the lead in Pakistan’s energy transition by installing rooftop solar systems and battery storage, while the government remained burdened by long-term power purchase agreements.
He criticised restrictions on solar incentives and urged Pakistan to explore the Asian Development Bank’s Energy Transition Mechanism and other international financing arrangements for early coal retirement.
An SDPI official said seven Chinese-financed coal plants developed under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) represented a major financial challenge, with declining utilisation, dollar-linked obligations and capacity payments placing pressure on the electricity system.
Muhammad Basit Gauri of Renewables First said imported coal plants were already becoming stranded assets as cheaper solar generation reduced their competitiveness.
Citing research on the Sahiwal coal power plant, he said negotiated early retirement could potentially avoid billions of dollars in future capacity payments. He proposed restructuring investor returns, buying out contractual obligations or repurposing existing sites for renewable energy and storage.
However, Ali Nawaz Leghari of the Private Power and Infrastructure Board defended the development of coal projects, saying they had helped overcome severe electricity shortages when alternative generation and transmission infrastructure were inadequate.
He said converting imported coal plants to Thar coal could reduce dependence on foreign fuel and generate substantial foreign exchange savings. Leghari argued that coal remained important for electricity supply during fuel disruptions and periods when renewable generation was unavailable, particularly without sufficient battery storage.
PRIED Chief Executive Officer Badr Alam challenged the government’s approach, arguing that inaccurate demand forecasting had created excess generation capacity while consumers continued facing high tariffs and unreliable supply.
He warned that converting imported coal plants to Thar coal could prolong fossil fuel dependence and create additional environmental pressures in coal-producing communities.
Badr Alam said growing rooftop solar adoption was shrinking grid electricity sales, leaving fewer consumers to bear fixed generation costs and potentially driving tariffs higher.
Yingie Chen of China’s Greenovation Hub said Pakistan-China cooperation on coal retirement would require bankable proposals, predictable regulations and credible arrangements to protect investors.
She recommended pilot projects linking renewable energy, battery storage and industrial electricity demand rather than relying solely on broad commitments to energy transition.
Dr Christoph Nedopil Wang of the University of Queensland said coal retirement negotiations should reflect the realistic future value of power plants rather than revenues guaranteed under existing contracts.
Referring to international experience, he said concessional financing, renegotiated power purchase agreements and reverse auctions could provide alternative pathways for retiring coal assets.
Michael Williamson of the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (UN ESCAP) said Pakistan faced particular difficulties because most coal plants were commissioned after 2015 and still carried substantial financial obligations.
He said a joint ESCAP-SDPI study examined repurposing coal plant infrastructure for solar and wind generation, battery storage and other productive uses.
Tom Wang, joining from China’s Shanxi province, warned that coal retirement could threaten livelihoods without adequate retraining and alternative employment. Referring to a survey of 9,000 coal-sector workers, he stressed the importance of protecting coal-dependent communities.
MNA Riaz Fatyana questioned continued IPP payments amid prolonged load shedding and urged the government to reduce electricity tariffs to stimulate consumption.
He also proposed tax relief for renewable energy equipment and small hydropower projects along Punjab’s canal network.

articles.title: Asif says Chaudhry Salik's remarks about corruption in Punjab 'beyond my understanding'
articles.summary:
Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said on Wednesday that Minister for Overseas Pakistanis Chaudhry Salik Hussain’s remarks regarding corruption in Punjab were “beyond my understanding”.

However, he had also criticised the present provincial administration, headed by Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz, alleging that he regula...
articles.full_text:
Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said on Wednesday that Minister for Overseas Pakistanis Chaudhry Salik Hussain’s remarks regarding corruption in Punjab were “beyond my understanding”.
During a talk show on a private television channel on Monday, the Pakistan Muslim League-Quaid (PML-Q) leader had lavished praise on former Punjab chief minister Chaudhry Pervez Elahi. However, he had also criticised the present provincial administration, headed by Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz, alleging that he regularly heard complaints of corruption.
    
            
        
    
On Tuesday, CM Maryam had sent a Rs5 billion defamation notice to the minister, demanding that he retract his remarks.
In a post on the social media platform X on Wednesday, Asif said, “Chaudhry Salik Sahib is very respected in my eyes; I respect his elders just as I respect my own.
“His statement regarding corruption in Punjab is beyond my limited political understanding. Corruption is the biggest issue in our society and it is the collective responsibility of the political leadership, both at the central and provincial levels, to rid the country of this curse,” he said.
He went on to say that Salik was a part of “both the federal and provincial governments and the leadership of both these governments lies with the PML-N”.
    
        
    
        
    

        
    
“If this statement is part of some future political agenda — to target Maryam Nawaz’s government and carve out space for himself in Punjab and at the Centre to secure his political future — then it starts to make sense,” Asif said.
He also praised Maryam’s performance, saying her work across Punjab’s cities and villages and the service standards being set by her government would pose a “very difficult challenge” for its opponents.
Meanwhile, Punjab Senior Minister Marriyum Aurangzeb sought an apology from Salik over his comments, saying that the PML-Q leader was “himself admitting that he has no evidence to support the allegations he made regarding corruption in the Punjab government”.
“After this, what dignity, justice, and principles demand is clear: an apology should be sought for the lack of evidence and for making baseless allegations, rather than turning the transfer of a single DC into an issue of personal ego,” she wrote.
The Punjab minister called on Salik to either fulfil his responsibilities as a minister or step down from his role “instead of engaging in empty rhetoric about eradicating corruption from society and promoting good governance”.
“We will not tolerate false and baseless allegations against the chief minister who has set an example of serving the people in Pakistan through hard work and transparency  in two and a half years,” Aurangzeb asserted.
Acknowledging that corruption existed as a “disease in every society in the world”, she contended that Punjab was the only province where the chief minister herself was “leading the campaign to eliminate corruption”.
    
        
    
        
    

        
    
What did Salik say?
During his interview, Salik had also questioned lavish government spending, particularly the use of official aircraft, arguing that public representatives should remain mindful of the country’s economic difficulties. Officials using government aircraft, he said, should be required to demonstrate the tangible outcomes and public benefits of their trips.
He further called for greater ministerial accountability, proposing that the federal as well as provincial ministers should be empowered to perform their duties, but also be held answerable for their performance.
The remarks carry particular political significance given the fractured relationship between the Chaudhry family and the PTI leadership. Salik, the younger son of PML-Q president Chaudhry Shujaat Hussain, belongs to a family whose political loyalties have diverged sharply since the ouster of Imran Khan’s government in 2022 through a no-confidence vote.
    
            
        
    
While Elahi and his son, former federal minister Moonis Elahi, aligned themselves with the PTI, the Shujaat family chose to stand with the Sharifs. Salik’s elder brother, Shafay Hussain, is also part of CM Maryam’s cabinet in Punjab.
On Tuesday, CM Maryam said the PML-Q leader’s anger stemmed from neither corruption nor progress. She said the issue was that she had changed the deputy commissioner of Gujrat a few days earlier, whereas Salik wanted a DC of his choice to be appointed.
The defamation notice — sent to Salik, ARY News host Naeem Ashraf Butt and the channel’s chairman — said the minister’s remarks were not just an expression of disagreement with policy or “ordinary political criticism”, but conveyed “serious imputations” of widespread corruption in the province.
The notice called on them to retract the remarks, publish an “unconditional and unequivocal apology and clarification” and “remove or suitably correct” the portions of the interview in question. It also demanded a sum of Rs5bn in damages.
Meanwhile, responding to Maryam’s remarks, Salik said he stood by his statement and had responded honestly to a question during the interview.
The minister’s remarks had also drawn a sharp rebuttal from Punjab Information Minister Azma Bokhari, who advised Salik not to “bite the hand that feeds him”. Bokhari also alleged that his displeasure stemmed from a request to appoint a deputy commissioner of his choice being turned down.

articles.full_text:
Mohammad Rizwan made a commanding unbeaten double century on the second day of the opening round of the Quaid-i-Azam Trophy Gold tournament, putting Peshawar Blues in a strong position against Faisalabad at the Abbottabad Cricket Stadium and delivering a timely response after a turbulent period following Pakistan’s disastrous Test series in England.
The wicketkeeper-batter, who was among seven players sent home after the second Test at Lord’s and remains under investigation by the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency over matters linked to the tour, finished the day unbeaten on 200 off 252 balls, hitting 35 fours and one six.
His innings helped Peshawar declare at 503 for four in 115.2 overs after resuming the day at 306 for three. Overnight centurion Najab Khan scored 133, while Mohammad Haris contributed an unbeaten 70 off 69 balls, including nine fours and two sixes.
    
        
    
        
    

        
    
Rizwan’s innings marked a significant personal milestone — his second double century in first-class cricket — and came shortly after the Pakistan Cricket Board cleared him to resume domestic cricket.
The former Test regular had endured a lean run with the bat in England, scoring just 61 runs in four innings before the squad overhaul and subsequent investigation into alleged dressing-room issues and related matters.
In reply, Faisalabad reached 118 for two in 35.2 overs at stumps. Both openers, Faham-ul-Haq (31) and Sameer Saqib (25), were dismissed leg-before-wicket by Mohammad Adnan.
Asim Ali Nasir (35 not out) and Atiq-ur-Rehman (24 not out) will resume their innings on Thursday.
Lean outing for Babar
Elsewhere, Babar Azam endured another modest outing, scoring just 28 as Lahore Whites were bowled out for 234 in 49.2 overs against Fata at the Diamond Cricket Ground in Islamabad, conceding a first-innings lead of 128 runs.
Fata had earlier been dismissed for 362, with debutant Fawad Arshad scoring 115. Teenage fast bowler Hammad Aziz claimed six for 97 for Lahore Whites.
Shaheen Shah Afridi and Afaq Afridi took three wickets apiece for Fata, with the latter dismissing Babar. Fata ended the day at 22 for one.
At the Shoaib Akhtar Cricket Stadium in Rawalpindi, Multan recovered from a middle-order collapse that left them struggling at 88 for five to reach 249 for seven in reply to Islamabad’s 215.
Imran Rafiq led the recovery with an unbeaten 93, while Sharoon Siraj scored 82. Musa Khan took three for 31 for the hosts.
At the National Ground in Islamabad, Karachi Blues scored 280 to secure a slender first-innings lead of 39 runs over Sialkot Blues, who closed the day at 13 without loss. Mohammad Ghazi Ghori top-scored for Karachi with 88.

Shah made the remarks at an event organised by the US-based Community Alliance for Peace and Justice on October 29, where he was asked about his dissenting opinion in the 2023 SC ruling on provincial elections in Punjab and KP and whether it was a “turni...
articles.full_text:
The Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) on Wednesday objected to remarks made by former senior puisne judge of the Supreme Court of Pakistan, Mansoor Ali Shah, regarding polls in KP and Punjab and the reserved seats case pertaining to the PTI.
Shah made the remarks at an event organised by the US-based Community Alliance for Peace and Justice on October 29, where he was asked about his dissenting opinion in the 2023 SC ruling on provincial elections in Punjab and KP and whether it was a “turning point” and the beginning of a “division” within the SC.
In its 3-2 verdict, the SC, after taking a suo motu notice, directed that elections should be held within 90 days in both provinces. Two judges, including Shah, had dissented from the ruling, saying that the suo motu proceedings initiated by then-chief justice of Pakistan Umar Ata Bandial, were “wholly unjustified”, besides being initiated with “undue haste”.
In their detailed reasoning, they explained that the SC by a majority of 4-3 and not 3-2 had dismissed the suo motu hearing on polls delay in Punjab and KP and therefore the same should be considered as the “Order of the Court”.
It had resulted in a controversy, with the government igniting a raging debate claiming that the ruling was a 4-3 majority decision in its favour and not a 3-2 verdict against.
In response to the question, Shah said that this was the time when the ex-chief justice was forming “like-minded benches”, adding that three or four judges were attending to the majority of the cases.
He said that initially the matter was taken by the high courts. He said that the SC judges had gathered in the ante-room and discussed with the chief justice at the time that suo motu notice should not be taken at this point. He said that it was “agreed” to wait but days later a SC bench took up the matter under suo motu powers as he denounced the “one-man show” going on at the time.
He said that at the time, two SC judges — Justice Yahya Afridi and Justice Athar Minallah — had dismissed the petitions in the case. He said that the SC bench was later reconstituted, adding that since two judges had decided the matter, the verdict could not be dismissed. He said that this sparked the 4-3, 2-3 debate.
Shah also defended the 2024 verdict in the reserved seats case, wherein PTI was declared eligible for seats reserved for women and minorities, in a setback to the ruling coalition.
“We said that the PTI was a political party and it was wrong to deprive [them of their symbol] … and illegal,” he said, recalling that this was a decision “that nobody liked”.
In a statement on Wednesday, the ECP referred to the remarks made by Shah, saying that they ignored “basic constitutional and legal facts related to the election matters and judicial decisions”.
“It is highly inappropriate to present the judicial record for specific purposes through selective quotations, incomplete perspectives and one-sided interpretations,” the statement said.
The electoral watchdog said that Shah had claimed that the SC’s majority decision about the elections in 2023 was a 4-3 verdict and that the suo motu notice and relevant petitions were dismissed.
    
        
    
        
    

        
    
The ECP also stated that according to Shah’s claims, the election ruling was a “minority decision” and the commission could not have held polls.
Regarding the PTI case, it said that Shah had declared the order for withdrawal of the party’s electoral symbol during the 2024 elections as “illegal”.
The commission said that the election symbol was subject to transparent intra-party elections as per Sections 208 and 209 of the Election Act 2017. It added that “till date, PTI has not been able to fulfil the requirement”.
The ECP said PTI was supposed to hold intra-party elections by June 30, 2021, and the commission had given the party three chances; however, the party failed to hold intra-party elections.
As a result, the commission said that the party’s election symbol was withdrawn, which, the ECP added, was also upheld by the SC in 2025, along with rejecting review petitions filed by the PTI.
The ECP further stated that PTI held intra-party elections after five years and its proceedings remained pending before the commission as the “PTI itself has taken a stay order from a high court”. It further stated that as per the commission’s records, the PTI was still enlisted as a political party.
The ECP added that only political parties which contested the elections had a right to the reserved seats.
“These political parties are required to submit a preferred list of candidates before the elections, while PTI has not submitted any preferred list,” it stated.
It further stated that it was mandatory for a political party to win at least one seat and that independent members were not entitled to reserved seats and therefore, the ECP gave the seats to the eligible parties.
It said that if the PTI was entitled to the reserved seats, then “Articles 51 and 106 of the Constitution and Section 104 of the Elections Act 2917 become ineffective”.
The ECP said that it was “unfortunate” that a retired judge was taking a position against the Constitution and the law.
In November 2025, Shah had resigned as an SC judge alongside Minallah, hours after the 27th Constitutional Amendment — which made significant changes to the country’s judicial system and established the Federal Constitutional Court — was signed into law by President Asif Ali Zardari.
“By fracturing the unity of the nation’s apex court, it has crippled judicial independence and integrity, pushing the country back by decades,” he wrote in the letter sent to the president.
“Staying on would not only amount to silent acquiescence in a constitutional wrong, but would also mean continuing to sit in a court whose constitutional voice has been muted,” he said.
