articles.full_text:
The federal cabinet on Wednesday ratified the defence cooperation agreement between Pakistan and Kuwait, according to a handout by the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO).
“The federal cabinet ratified a defence cooperation agreement between Pakistan and Kuwait. This agreement, which aims to foster cooperation in the defence sector between the two brotherly nations, was concluded on June 11, 2023. The Kuwaiti government had ratified the agreement on July 19,” the handout said.
    
        
    
        
    

        
    
In 2023, Pakistan and Kuwait signed a defence pact to further strengthen defe­nce cooperation and institutional linkages between the armed forces of the two countries.
The statement also said that the cabinet approved the transfer of powers delegated to the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa chief minister to the province’s governor. The Centre declared an emergency and governor’s rule in the province on Oct 11.
It said the powers included “the conduct of day-to-day affairs during the period of emergency in the province, to facilitate the smooth handling of administrative matters in KP and further improve governance”.
“The KP governor will submit a review report to the federal government every month regarding the exercise of all such powers,” the statement said.
It stated that the federal cabinet welcomed the decision and expressed the hope that the KP Advisory Council, under the leadership of the Governor Faisal Karim Kundi, would make full efforts for the welfare and prosperity of the people of the province and for establishing peace and security.
Moreover, the federal cabinet, on the recommendation of the Ministry of Finance, approved the design of new currency notes, the statement added.
“The cabinet was given a detailed briefing on the new currency notes. The briefing stated that proposals were solicited from artists and designers across the country for the design of the new currency notes and a cabinet committee established by the prime minister conducted detailed consultations on it with all stakeholders,” the handout said.
According to the statement, the meeting was informed that, along with enhancing security features to prevent counterfeit notes, modern materials would be used, which would also extend the lifespan of the notes.
The federal cabinet also approved the introduction of a Rs10 coin in place of the Rs10 banknote, the PMO statement said.
‘Pakistan continuing efforts for peace in Middle East’
Addressing the federal cabinet during televised remarks, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif noted that global oil prices had “skyrocketed” due to the instability in the region.
“Pakistan is playing its role as before in restoring peace in the region,” he said, recalling Pakistan’s recent engagements with Tehran and other regional actors in the matter, as well as engagements under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye.
    
        
    
        
    

        
    
Last month, Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir, accompanied by Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, visited Iran as part of Pakistan’s efforts to mediate between Washington and Tehran.
In another meeting in October, held under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, CDF Munir, the Saudi defence minister, and the Turkish spymaster met top Iranian officials in Tehran. Last week, the military’s spokesman said Pakistan remained “cautiously optimistic” about its mediation between the US and Iran.
On Tuesday, PM Shehbaz also recalled that the government had planned to hike fuel prices by Rs15 on Friday.
“Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik [..] talked to the refineries to bear the burden in their windfall profits. We will not let a common man bear this burden,” he added.
Speaking about the fuel subsidy scheme, launched in September, the premier said it would run till the end of December.
“Rs28 billion has been spent so far,” he said, adding that the scheme was running “successfully and transparently” and that the Intelligence Bureau (IB) continued to monitor it.
On liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), the prime minister said that the “era of mafiaa” was over and it was now being arranged transparently.
“Now when LPG is imported, competition will be promoted and it will be auctioned in lots. The government will take the profits and subsidise it for the common man,” he said.
He also stressed that the federal government was holding meetings “day and night” to meet LPG, liquefied natural gas (LNG), petrol and gas requirements ahead of winter despite challenges arising from the closure of maritime routes.
LPG supply has been disrupted in the country due to the closure of Iranian border crossings, resulting in gas cylinders being sold at twice the official rate in the open market.
PM Shehbaz also said that the federal government had finalised a proposed Rs160bn package for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
“Security is our number one, two and three priority in KP,” the premier remarked. He further noted that counterterrorism efforts continued in the region.
With the efforts of law enforcement agencies, the new government in KP and the support of the federal government, we will crush terrorism,” he said.

articles.full_text:
ISLAMABAD: The number of official, or blue, passports has been brought down to 49,000 from 74,000 in keeping with international obligations and administrative requirements, Muhammad Ali Randhawa, the director general of Immigration and Passports, disclosed on Wednesday.
He shared this information with Syedaal Khan Nasar, the deputy chairman of Senate, during a meeting.
The existing mechanism for issuance of passports, institutional performance, security features and facilities being provided to the public came under discussion during the meeting.
The meeting also discussed the proposed introduction of passport issuance facilities through the National Database and Registration Authority (Nadra) in the near future, further strengthening passport security and measures to improve the country’s ranking.

Senate deputy chairman lauds promotion of using technology to facilitate public

Mr Nasar appreciated the government’s initiatives aimed at improving the passport issuance system, promoting the use of modern technology and enhancing public facilitation.
He termed the performance of the Directorate General of Immigration and Passports and its efforts towards institutional reforms commendable, emphasising the need to further modernise the system in line with contemporary requirements.
Mr Nasar said the use of modern technology, digital systems and automation should be expanded at all stages of passport issuance to make the entire process, from submission of an application to passport delivery, faster, more transparent and accessible.
He emphasised that citizens should not face unnecessary delays, prolonged waiting periods or administrative complications, adding that an effective mechanism must be ensured for the prompt resolution of complaints.
“Effective use of modern technology and improved administrative strategies could further strengthen public confidence in the institution,” Mr Nasar added.
Meets tribal elders, lawyers
The deputy chairman also met tribal elders, lawyers, representatives of civil society, students and other prominent personalities from different walks of life. During these interactions, matters relating to problems faced by the masses and the prevailing political situation were discussed.
Mr Nasar briefed the delegations about measures taken by the government to promote economic growth, control inflation and provide relief to the nation.
He cited the reduction in fuel prices as one such step and expressed the hope that it would have a knock-on effect on the prices of other commodities.
Published in Dawn, November 5th, 2026

articles.title: 38 briefly detained in Karachi as police baton-charge protesters headed towards CM House
articles.summary:
KARACHI: Thirty-eight people were released after brief detention on Wednesday as police used tear gas and batons against protesting teachers headed towards Chief Minister House from Karachi Press Club (KPC).
Hundreds of teachers had gathered outside the press club at the call of the All Sindh Primary Teachers Association (ASPTA). They were headed towards CM House to present their demands that pertained to the service structure and called for delegating powers for transfers and postings to distri...
articles.full_text:
KARACHI: Thirty-eight people were released after brief detention on Wednesday as police used tear gas and batons against protesting teachers headed towards Chief Minister House from Karachi Press Club (KPC).
Hundreds of teachers had gathered outside the press club at the call of the All Sindh Primary Teachers Association (ASPTA). They were headed towards CM House to present their demands that pertained to the service structure and called for delegating powers for transfers and postings to district officers.
The protesters chanted slogans and attempted to move towards the CM House. However, when they arrived near Fawara Chowk, police baton-charged them and used tear gas shells to push them back toward the press club.
Adjoining roads near the KPC were closed to traffic, according to a traffic police spokesperson.
South Deputy Inspector General (DIG) Syed Asad Raza told Dawn that all detained teachers “have been released at night”, after he confirmed in earlier comments that 38 people were taken into custody.
Speaking to Dawn earlier in the day, the DIG noted that a teachers’ organisation had announced a protest at the KPC, with a march planned toward the CM House.
He said prior to the protest, the administration made concerted efforts to resolve the matter through negotiations and engaged officials from the education department to facilitate meaningful dialogue.
The official said the protest leadership was categorically told that entry into the Red Zone — a term used to denote the area surrounding Governor House and Chief Minister House — would not be permitted. Nevertheless, the administration was directed to exhaust all available resources and make every effort to ensure a peaceful resolution through dialogue, he said.
Raza alleged that around 3:15pm, the protesters turned “violent, abandoned the course of negotiations and forcibly started advancing towards the CM House.”
He claimed that the protesting teachers “breached police barricades and resorted to pelting police personnel with stones, causing injuries to one official.”
“Upon reaching and crossing Kabir Masjid on Governor House Road, the situation escalated, compelling police to resort to shelling to disperse the violent mob and restore order,” said the South police chief.
He said during the operation, 38 protesters, including ASPTA President Ghulam Rasool Mahar and General Secretary Aijaz Ali Chandio, were taken into custody.
Raza insisted that police took drastic action as the teachers tried to enter the Red Zone.
    
            
        
    
        
    
Meanwhile, Rafiq Nizamani, the vice president of the teachers’ association, told Dawn that in 2021, the Sindh government had chalked out an “education policy” under which it was decided that teachers would not be promoted and they would remain in the same pay scale.
He said they launched a protest against this “arbitrary” decision as others were being promoted, but not them. He said that at the time, the government had assured them that their demands would be addressed, but this did not happen.
He said apart from the service structure, their other demands pertained to delegating the powers of posting primary teachers to district government officials. He said that they wanted recruitment and the transfer/posting of teachers to be delegated to district officials.
According to Nizamani, as the protesters moved from KPC towards CM House, police resorted to tear gas and a baton charge.
He claimed that two teachers were also injured. Nizamani said that they had decided to set up a protest camp outside the KPC for the fulfilment of their demands.
He admitted that the education officials had approached them for talks, but said they considered it “delaying tactics” in view of their past unfulfilled promises and decided to hold a protest march.

articles.title: Govt says Islamabad's One Constitution Avenue to be turned into a five-star hotel
articles.summary:
The federal government on Wednesday said that a joint investigation team had revealed that Islamabad’s One Constitution Avenue was built on “irregularities and rigging” and announced that the residential building will soon be turned into a five-star hotel.
The building, a skyscraper in the federal capital that houses residential apartments, had its lease cancelled by the Capital Development Authority (CDA) due to the company behind the project defaulting on payments. The decision was upheld by t...
articles.full_text:
The federal government on Wednesday said that a joint investigation team had revealed that Islamabad’s One Constitution Avenue was built on “irregularities and rigging” and announced that the residential building will soon be turned into a five-star hotel.
The building, a skyscraper in the federal capital that houses residential apartments, had its lease cancelled by the Capital Development Authority (CDA) due to the company behind the project defaulting on payments. The decision was upheld by the Islamabad High Court (IHC) in April.
The building was initially supposed to be a five-star hotel project; however, instead of functioning as a five-star hotel, it was converted into residential apartments and commercial areas. The IHC’s order led to the mass evictions of residents in May, following which Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif formed a joint investigation team (JIT) to probe the matter.
Addressing a press conference on Wednesday alongside Information Minister Attaullah Tarar and State Minister for Interior Tallal Chaudhry, Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said the JIT presented its report to the federal cabinet today, noting that the project was fraudulent.
He said that the report had input from the National Accountability Bureau (NAB), the Federal Investigation Agency, the Federal Board of Revenue, the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan, the Intelligence Bureau and Inter-Services Intelligence.
“They carefully assessed this project and presented the report, and it was approved,” Iqbal said. “The JIT has clearly identified that the project was created based on irregularity and rigging and that the bidding process was manipulated.”
Iqbal added that, according to the report, rules were ignored to provide benefits and the company which was given the lease had no rightful claim.
“In this whole matter, the CDA was found complicit, and similarly, the conditions of the bank guarantee were removed to provide benefits to the developers,” he stated. “The work which was carried out was conducted in a very suspicious manner and the apartments were sold illegally.”
He noted that the project was initially approved as a five-star hotel two decades ago, but later it was turned into apartments.
“The JIT has identified Abdul Hafeez Sheikh, who has been called the mastermind and was found to be in connivance with CDA officials,” the planning minister added.
“CDA officers such as Kamran Lashari, who was chairman at the time, Dr Faisal Awan, Azhar Ali Chaudhry, Brigadier (retired) Nasrullah and Marhoom Rai Nawaz Kharal were found to be colluding in fraud,” he said.
Iqbal said that as a result of the scheme, the national exchequer suffered losses, while the aforementioned people “gained financially and defrauded the Pakistani people of their invested capital”.
“The JIT recommended that Sheikh and his company be blacklisted from future public projects and that proceedings be launched against him,” the minister added.
It was further recommended that the project be reviewed and work undertaken to achieve its original purpose as a hotel. Additionally, the report recommended that the project be started anew and auctioned in a transparent manner, he said.
“Security clearance and clearance from other institutions should also be sought so that future projects have a steady framework to prevent this type of fraud from happening again,” Iqbal said, adding that fire safety and other protocols must also be ensured.
He added that according to the JIT, the project should be renamed, as the name ‘One Constitution Avenue’ was the same address as the finance ministry.
“They used this address for marketing purposes only,” the minister asserted.
“There will be action taken against those found involved in fraud. The government has a responsibility to protect those who were robbed or swindled.”
    
            
        
    
        
    
Iqbal said it was decided that those defrauded would receive compensation, their principal investments would be refunded and payments would be adjusted against their Kibor interest “so they do not suffer losses”.
“It was also recommended that the CDA and its ordinance be overhauled and that an independent master plan commission be formed to shut the door on such fraud in the future,” he announced.
Iqbal added that all of the records must be digitised and officers should be rotated between the state planning, enforcement and building control departments every two years.
“People have held offices for 20 years and opened offices of fraud. With this constant rotation, it will close the door on these corrupt projects,” he explained.
“In the same way, pre-audit auctions and contracts from third parties will be consulted, and in light of this JIT report, NAB has been ordered to take action against anyone involved in this project, and those who facilitated it,” Iqbal said.
Meanwhile, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi also addressed a press conference on Wednesday and said that the government had now regained possession of the skyscraper, vowing to turn the building into a five-star hotel within months.
“In official documents, we always had possession of this building, and after the cabinet’s approval, it is now legally in our possession,” Naqvi maintained.
He regretted that the government’s decision to regain control of the building earlier this year had been portrayed as a “crime”, decrying how Islamabad’s land had been infringed upon.
“We will try our best to convert this building into a five-star hotel in months,” the interior minister announced, reaffirming that this had been the project’s primary objective.
“There is a severe shortage of hotels in Islamabad. We will soon try to make an agreement with a large chain of hotels and convert this building into a five-star hotel,” he stated.
He commended the CDA chairman and legal team for pursuing this case; however, Naqvi also reproached the CDA for being at fault.
“NAB will tell who is responsible,” he said.
“As per JIT recommendations, we will try to make rightful payments to the occupants,” Naqvi said. “This is binding for us after the report.”
The interior minister said he was grateful to PM Shehbaz, recalling that the prime minister had assured him that the right decision would be taken.
Naqvi further said that a residents’ committee, which was overseeing the building’s affairs, had been abolished.
“A CDA member will look after the building’s matters from now on,” he said, reiterating that the hotel would be operational soon and be a “gift to the people of Islamabad”.

articles.full_text:
— Dawn
    
LAHORE/DERA GHAZI KHAN: The closure of Chashma Right Bank Canal (CRBC), especially in its stretch falling in Punjab, has been affecting farmers badly due to inadequate repair/maintenance and water theft as there seems to be none in the provincial and federal governments to listen to the affected.
The situation worsened after a portion of the CRBC — an inter-provincial canal irrigating huge chunks of land in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Punjab – was breached, forcing the Water and Power Development Authority to stop releasing water into the canal from the Chashma Barrage over Indus.
“You cannot imagine the situation we have been in for a long time. In Kharif (April), we received 77pc water shortage, followed by May, June, July and August wherein we witnessed 78pc, 95pc, 98pc and 96pc shortage, respectively, in our command area,” reveals an officer of the Punjab Irrigation Department.
The situation, according to him, worsened further when the canal was breached in Paharpur tehsil of KP in September, leaving authorities with no option but to stop releasing water to CRBC.
“Since September, we have no water and the canal banks have not been repaired. It seems no one is taking this matter on a priority basis,” the official deplored.
The CRBC is an inter-provincial gravity irrigation system serving KP and Punjab. During Kharif 2026, Punjab suffered a severe canal water shortage despite substantial flows at the Chashma.
The CRBC command area consists of approximately 606,000 acres, of which 240,000 acres (about 97,125 hectares) are in Punjab. The main canal is about 274km long, including a 103km reach in Punjab, which receives its supply at RD-513.
The system/head design discharge is about 4,825 cusecs and the Punjab’s design capacity is 1,834 cusecs, with an operational daily indent of 1,800 cusecs, served by 30 distributaries and 32 minors totalling about 440km. Groundwater in much of the Punjab command is brackish and unsuitable for irrigation.
“The closure has disrupted planned irrigation regime in the Punjab command area. The cumulative deficit during the Kharif season, coupled with zero supplies during the latter part of September, has exposed crops to severe water stress and increased the risk of production losses,” he added.
Wapda had constructed CRBC during 1998-2002 as a perennial canal off-taking from the right bank of Chashma Barrage (design discharge 4,825 cusecs), including the canal system, outlets and chakbandi.
In May 2002, distributaries and minors D-24 to D-53 in Punjab were handed over to the Punjab Irrigation Department under a formal agreement, while the main canal and its structures, including 21 cross-drainage structures, remained with Wapda.
Following a Council of Common Interests (CCI) decision of Aug 8, 2020, and a bilateral agreement on March 14, 2022, the Punjab section of the main canal and its structures was handed over to the Punjab Irrigation Department/CRBC Division, Taunsa Sharif. The operational control of upper portion of the main canal still remains under the Wapda authorities.
The official correspondence reveals that the irrigation authorities repeatedly raised the issue of inadequate supplies with Wapda. “The situation further deteriorated when a major breach in the main canal at RD 185 Left, within the KP portion, took place on Sept 14, 2026. Head supplies remained suspended on Sept 15 and 16, and the discharge at the Punjab border (RD 513) remained zero from Sept 17 to 30,” the official said.
He said according to information, Wapda authorities awarded the emergency works for closure of the breach and concrete lining of critical reaches on Sept 30, 2026, at a total bid cost of approximately Rs385 million. The rehabilitation work is presently under execution at site, with an estimated completion period of about 45 days.
“Until completion of the works and restoration of canal operation, Punjab area remains deprived of its normal canal supplies,” he added.
According to him, the actual extent of crop damage and financial loss should be prepared through a properly documented field assessment, including crop-wise and area-wise verification, in accordance with the applicable provisions of the Cost Sharing Agreement.
He said the shortage of water supplies to Punjab during the Kharif season was due to illegal extraction and theft of water from the canal by the farmers in KP.
“We have been told by the KP irrigation authorities that as many as 1,000 cusecs of water is allegedly stolen by the people in KP,” he said.

articles.title: Swat basin faces over 5°C warming by century’s end

articles.full_text:
ISLAMABAD: A glacier risk assessment of the Swat watershed has war­ned that the basin is expected to warm by more than 5°C by the end of the century, particularly bet­ween October and June. 

Winter rainfall is expected to change little, but summer rainfall could more than double under some climate scenarios, according to the assessment carried out by the Green Climate Fund (GCF), with support from the Asian Development Bank (ADB). 

The changes are likely to increase the risk of severe floods and erosion, cause a short-term rise in water availability due to glacier melt and runoff, and lead to long-term declines as glaciers continue to recede, according to the assessment made available on Wednesday. 

The Swat basin, which has more than 10,000 glaciers, faces an increased risk of infrastructure failure and resulting floods. The assessment also warned of agricultural losses, erosion in valley areas, and a short-term water surplus followed by a long-term deficit. 

The GCF has conducted glacier risk assessments for four representative wat­e­rsheds: Kura (Arme­nia, Azerbaijan and Georgia), Naryn (Kyrgyz  Republic, with downstream links to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan), Pyanj (Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Afghanistan) and Swat (Hindu Kush-Karakoram-Himalaya). 

The four pilot basins capture diverse glacier and hydrological conditions across Central and West Asia. Together, they illustrate how elevation, glacier mass and snow duration shape regional water supplies and risks. 

These assessments serve as initial pilots under the ‘Glacier to Farms’ (G2F) programme and complement the existing ADB country-level climate risk assessments. Although only four basins were studied, they were strategically selected to represent the nine developing member countries covered by G2F and inform the programme’s future expansion to other transboundary watersheds and basins in the region. 

The climate risk and capacity assessment of the four glacier-fed watersheds in Central and West Asia highlights accelerating glacier retreat, growing water security risks and priority actions to strengthen resilience, adaptation and regional cooperation. 

The assessment analysed 40 years of weather records to identify spatial and temporal variations in temperature, rainfall and snowfall across mountain and lowland areas. Historical data were used to bias-correct global climate models to improve their local accuracy. Statistical clustering of multiple models produced basin-specific projections focused on glacier, snow and permafrost areas, providing a realistic basis for understanding future climate impacts across the G2F region. 

It analysed long-term temperature, precipitation and cryosphere trends across the four watersheds to establish a regional baseline and develop future scenarios for 2035, 2055, 2085 and 2100. Using multi-model climate datasets validated against regional observations, the analysis identified key impact pathways, sectoral risks and opportunities to strengthen resilience in agriculture, energy and human settlements. 

Across the G2F basins, temperatures are projected to rise by around 3°C to 5°C by the end of the century, accelerating the loss of glaciers, snow and permafrost. Seasonal water availability will shift, with earlier snowmelt and river flow peaks, while hotter summers will increase drought risks and water demand. Although some areas may receive more winter precipitation, overall water availability will decline as glacier-fed runoff diminishes. 

The assessment examines how projected changes in temperature, precipitation and glacier mass will affect hazards, water resources and livelihoods across the G2F region. It highlights the main risks — glacier retreat, slope instability and shifting water availability — and explains how these processes interact to shape local and downstream impacts. 

Risks associated with glacier melt and extreme events, such as glacial lake outburst floods (Glofs) and landslides, are already high across High Mountain Asia and are expected to intensify as the climate continues to warm. However, the assessment notes that appropriate resilience measures can reduce these risks to manageable levels. 

As glaciers and permafrost melt, slopes and natural dams become unstable, increasing the likelihood of rockfalls, ice avalanches and Glofs. Such events can travel long distances, threatening homes, roads and other infrastructure in mountainous and downstream areas. 

Heavier rain and snowfall, followed by rapid spring melting, are likely to trigger flash floods and debris flows. Inadequate watershed management will exacerbate these effects, accelerating soil erosion, degrading water quality and compromising the integrity of dams and irrigation systems. 

Higher temperatures will increase water demand, particularly during summer. Glacier melt has historically provided a buffer against drought in the region, but this buffer will disappear as glaciers retreat and heatwaves intensify, reducing water supplies when they are most needed.

Published in Dawn, November 5th, 2026

articles.title: Petrol price dropped by Rs7.06 per litre, high-speed diesel by Rs3.71
articles.summary: & · ●  ●
articles.full_text:
The government on Wednesday cut the price of petrol by Rs7.06 per litre and that of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs3.71.
Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs362.00 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs387.81 on Nov 5 (Thursday), according to a notification by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra).
Wednesday’s cut is the third consecutive reduction in fuel prices.
It came as international oil prices fell under $100 in volatile trade on Wednesday, with investors awaiting Washington’s next move in the US-Israeli war with Iran after President Donald Trump’s Republican Party lost control of Congress in midterm elections.
Brent futures were down $4.50, or 4.3 per cent, to $99.07 a barrel at 1619 GMT (9:19pm, PKT), while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures are down $4.13, or 4.3pc, to $92.02.
The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel.
Under an arrangement announced on Monday for 30 days, oil refineries will contribute to the petroleum levy by bearing a cumulative impact of Rs15 billion, according to the government. This allows a Rs14.71 reduction in the petrol price at the consumer end.
Addressing a press conference on Tuesday, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik said efforts were being made to introduce a similar system for liquefied petroleum gas (LPG).
Meanwhile, the Jamaat-i-Islami and the government are set to follow up on their recent discussions on possible relief in petroleum prices and hold another round of talks on Thursday, the party said.
Rise in fuel prices
The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on Feb 28.
The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March.
Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm, and fuel allocations for official vehicles have been cut by 50pc for three months.
On Sept 13, PM Shehbaz also announced a “relief scheme” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices.
Previously, on July 17, the petroleum minister announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US.
Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel.
The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give Ogra the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends.
Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes.
Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators.
Petrol and HSD are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

PARIS: World leaders voiced hopes for a reset with the United States on Wednesday after voters delivered a huge midterm election defeat to President Donald Trump and his Republican party.
Germany

articles.full_text:
PARIS: World leaders voiced hopes for a reset with the United States on Wednesday after voters delivered a huge midterm election defeat to President Donald Trump and his Republican party.
Germany
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said he hoped to see new initiatives to end the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine. “With their majority in both chambers of Congress, the De­­m­­ocratic Party will likely seek to shift the political course in the United States,” Wadephul said. Through cooperation betwe­­en the United States and Eur­ope, “there may be a new oppo­r­­­t­­unity to launch a fresh initiative” to resolve conflicts, he said.
Spain
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said Trump’s defeat showed that the global far-right was on the wane. “It happened in Brazil. It just happened in the US. And it will soon happen in Spain,” the socialist leader said, with elections looming later this month. The far-right wave is “no longer growing, it is unravelling,” he added.
Russia
Russia hopes Trump will continue his “peacemaking efforts” after the midterm elections, the Kremlin said. “President Trump continues to exercise his powers. We sincerely hope that he will also continue his peacemaking effo­r­­ts,” spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.
South Africa
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa said the result could thaw strained ties between Pretoria and Washington. “We’re hoping that on a bilateral basis, there will be a coming together of minds where we will find a proper path forward on geopolitics as well as on trade matters and investment matters,” he said. He added that he hoped the result would “introduce a new era in world relations”.
EU
The EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas voiced hope the new US Congress would support Ukraine and ramp up pressure on Russia.
“I hope that the new Congress… will continue supporting Ukraine and also putting more pressure on Russia,” she said, adding that Europe and the United States “are much stronger together” in pushing Moscow to end its war.
UK
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the result was an opportunity for the world to “unite” around resolving cost-of-living issues. “President Trump has accepted the results, and I feel the world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that’s the cost of living,” Burnham said.
Published in Dawn, November 5th, 2026

articles.full_text:
THE politics of toxicity and confrontation at home and abroad have led to a severe setback for American President Donald Trump. His Republican Party experienced a drubbing at Tuesday’s midterm polls, with the Democrats riding a decisive blue wave to power in both houses of the US Congress, and taking control of the American government’s legislative arm.
The Democrats managed wins in deeply red states, indicating the widespread dissatisfaction with Mr Trump’s style of governance. For most Americans, the unpopular war of choice with Iran and the cost-of-living crisis it has led to were reason enough to punish the Republicans at the ballot box. Mr Trump, referring to the electoral pummelling, admitted that “part of it was Iran”.
While domestically the economy and the Trump administration’s abrasive immigration policies are likely to dominate the agenda, the rest of the world would like to know if America will change course on the foreign front.
In his second term, Mr Trump has turned the old international order upside down, pushed around old allies, downplayed climate change, and talked of taking over other states’ territory.
His biggest foreign folly — in partnership with Israel — has been the war against Iran. Perhaps feeling the heat, just before the midterms, Mr Trump had announced he was ending a multibillion-dollar aid programme to Israel.
It is unlikely the decision was a moral one emanating from genuine displeasure with the Zionist state’s murderous policies. More likely, it was a last-ditch attempt to court MAGA voters, many of whom increasingly question the subservience of the American political class to Israel at the expense of their own country.
In fact, expectations of a radical shift on the foreign policy front may be premature. For one, Democratic presidents, too, have launched foreign wars, and many among the supposedly ‘liberal’ party are staunch votaries of Israel. Moreover, while the Democrats will enjoy greater legislative oversight, partially limiting Mr Trump’s ability to wage and fund foreign wars, the president retains veto powers that can override Congress.
This means that those Democrats — and Republicans — opposed to American military action abroad must make a serious effort to halt strikes on Iran and prevent taxpayers’ dollars from funding Israel’s genocidal campaigns against the Palestinians.
While Mr Trump does not usually learn from his errors, perhaps seeing the response of the American voters he may attempt a wiser course. Candidate Trump had promised no more ‘forever wars’; President Trump must now extricate himself from a needless war he launched against Iran. It is time he heeded the call of the voters and worked on rebuilding and uniting his country, instead of destroying others.
Published in Dawn, November 5th, 2026

articles.title: Analysis: Midterms clip Trump’s wings at home, not abroad
articles.summary:

The verdict has been considerably harsher than many had anticipated, chiefly beca­use of...
articles.full_text:
THE world had good reason to watch the US midterm elections with bated breath, because their outcome would not only determine the balance of power in Washington, but also shape the course of major international conflicts — particularly in the Middle East — and establish how much political bandwidth Presi­dent Donald Trump would retain to pursue his foreign policy during the final two years of his presidency.
The verdict has been considerably harsher than many had anticipated, chiefly beca­use of the fallout of the Iran war. As the election outcome was influenced by an external issue, the implications will ac­c­ordingly be reflected more on the foreign policy front.
For foreign capitals, the significance of the result lies less in the change of congressional control itself but what it means for Trump’s ability, and willingness, to use American power abroad. A midterm defeat does not automatically diminish presidential authority over foreign affairs and military operations. Trump, therefore, retains considerable discretion over military operations and negotiations, as well as executive powers over sanctions and trade.
What he has actually lost is political room to manoeuvre as Democrats in the Congress can now investigate, obstruct funding and impose greater scrutiny on his decisions.
    
            
        
    
Compounding that would be the fact that some key Republicans, mindful of their own electoral prospects in 2028, may become less willing to defend his policies that come with a political cost.
The resulting situation could constrain the president over time, but it would not necessarily make him more cautious in the immediate term.
Iran
Iran will be the immediate test of how Trump responds to the Republican rout. The electoral setback has created a paradox for the president because while the war is the key reason for the debacle, many think he may still be tempted to intensify military pressure in the hope of securing a decisive outcome before the political space for doing so narrows further.
Christopher Clary, a non-resident fellow at Stimson Center, points out that “the Constitution grants the president enormous latitude on the use of force and the president can escalate despite the new Democratic Congress.”
But escalation carries the risk of aggravating the original problem. Iranian retaliation in that case could deepen the economic pressures and make the war an even greater political liability. The indications from Tehran further suggest that resumption of full-scale hostilities could also lead to widening of the conflict.
Importantly, Trump has a crucial window of two months before the new Congress takes office. But after the transition, political calculations will change with Democrats making the Iran war a major focus of oversight.
They could also pursue War Powers resolutions, requiring congressional authorisation for continued hostilities, in addition to attaching conditions or restrictions to defence appropriations.
Mr Clary warned that “the lame duck period before the new Congress is sworn in will be an especially dangerous time.”
He emphasised that while there are “no real binding constraints on Trump”, the Democrats can “use their budgetary authority to deny new funds to sustain the operation”.
The control of spending will give Democrats additional leverage, although it will not automatically enable them to terminate military operations because Trump retains veto power, which he has hinted that he will use, and Democrats don’t command the two-thirds majority needed to override it. Moreover, Democrats will not either want to be seen as curtailing support for American forces.
Quincy Institute Vice President Trita Parsi recalled that “the Vietnam war ended because Congress stopped funding it”, adding, “Democrats can do this to Trump’s illegal Iran war as well. If they don’t, they will become complicit”.
Sustaining an open ended campaign will, in any case, become politically more difficult and even Republicans, conscious of the electoral cost of the Iran war, may also become increasingly reluctant to support additional funding without a clearer strategy and exit plan.
If things do come to that point sometime next year, Trump can then become inclined towards a combination of military pressure and diplomacy by extracting concessions from Tehran through the threat of further strikes while pursuing an agreement, which he can present as an achievement and a resolution of the conflict.
Pakistan
For Pakistan, the Democrat victory presents a more gradual test. The turnaround in relations under Trump depended heavily on the president and his inner circle, rather than an actual shift in the relationship.
Islamabad had moved quickly to cultivate ties with the new administration after Trump returned to office — extraditing the accused in Abbey Gate Kabul bombing; praising the president’s intervention in the May 2025 conflict with India; nominating him for the Nobel Peace prize; and, joining his Board of Peace for Gaza.
The unprecedented White House working lunch with Chief of Army Staff and Chief of Defence Forces Field Marshal Asim Munir in June 2025 — sans PM Shehbaz Sharif — further underscored the importance of the military channel. Critical minerals and cryptocurrency also became prominent areas of engagement, alongside proposals involving Trump family-backed World Liberty Financial, the Roosevelt Hotel and drone manufacturing.
    
            
        
    
A Democratic Congress is unlikely to undo the relationship, but it could subject some of these dealings to greater scrutiny. Questions may be raised about foreign links of the Trump family’s commercial interests, the cooperation with Powerus and Pakistan’s governance and transparency.
Mentioning these aspects, Michael Kugelman of the Atlantic Council noted that “scrutiny of Trump and his family’s business dealings will increase… If so, that could spell bad news for Pakistan.”
    
        
    
        
    

        
    
Erik Sperling, executive director of Just Foreign Policy, recalled earlier congressional letters and legislation initiated by Democrats, raising concerns about the situation in Pakistan, and expected that with Democrats now controlling the House, these measures will have a clear path to floor votes.
    
            
        
    
Islamabad’s earlier effort to secure a $10bn US Treasury financial backstop has found little enthusiasm, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent emphasising self-reliance and IMF reforms. A Democratic controlled Congress would make congressional support for a large financial arrangement even more difficult.
There will, nevertheless, be areas of bipartisan convergence, particularly counterterrorism, regional stability, critical minerals and Pakistan’s diplomatic role in the Iran conflict. The challenge for Islamabad will be to translate the access secured under Trump into a relationship with a wider institutional base, including engagement with Democrats and a stronger case for durable economic cooperation.
Other arenas
A Democratic Congress could help preserve military and economic support for Ukraine and scrutinise arms transfers to Israel, without forcing Trump to abandon his preference for a negotiated settlement with Moscow or bringing about an abrupt change in US policy towards Israel.
Adam Weinstein, deputy Middle East director at the Quincy Institute, said: “Uncritical support for Israel, and more importantly, close ties to AIPAC, have become serious political liabilities in the US. These results reflect that shift.”
Noted commentator Max Blumenthal said that while “the ‘special relationship’ with Israel was once a matter of bipartisan unity among party elites, it’s become a polarising wedge issue and a poison pill for any president”.
He pointed out that Trump, while realising the gravity of the situation, had announced that he will cut $4 billion in annual aid to Israel, in a last-ditch bid to salvage the Republican situation ahead of the polls.
Saudi Arabia, too, may face closer scrutiny over nuclear cooperation and security commitments, while the UAE and Egypt could encounter greater congressional attention to human rights and military assistance.
On China, strategic competition is likely to remain bipartisan, although Democrats may place greater emphasis on alliances and supply chain resilience. They may also seek to reclaim some congressional oversight over tariffs and trade.
Washington-based analyst Shuja Nawaz thinks “Cuba may be the easiest target for President Trump. He might also try his hand at summitry with Putin and Xi but it is unlikely to gain much. They have consistently outplayed him”.
After facing increased opposition to his domestic agenda, Trump may now turn increasingly to foreign policy, trade and military decisions, where his executive authority is wider, but international partners will have to consider whether commitments made by this administration can survive a change of political direction in Washington, come 2028.
Published in Dawn, November 5th, 2026

articles.full_text:
ISLAMABAD: A parliamentary committee on Wednesday criticised the Ministry of Foreign Affairs for having no control over funds management and lax accounting procedures, instructing its new secretary Asim Iftikhar Ahmad to streamline and tighten accounting procedures and make rules and share them with the committee.

The directive came after the Public Accounts Committee, while discussing audit objections of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs 2024-25, observed that its staff posted in foreign missions was embezzling and mismanaging public funds without accountability.

One case in particular caused massive losses to the public exchequer, when an ex-accountant posted in the Pakistan embassy in Vienna, Austria, fraudulently drew 442,256 euros and $134,292 over a period of two years. 

Officials from the office of Auditor General of Pakistan suspected that the former accountant was not alone in tampering and transferring the public money into his personal and wife’s bank accounts and that senior officials in the Pakistani Mission were also involved in the scam.


  PAC told staff posted in foreign missions ‘embezzling funds’


The PAC expressed strong dissatisfaction with Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) for failing to recover the embezzled amount after a case was registered against the ex-accountant, Muhammad Sulaiman Qureshi, six years ago. 

Members of the panel were more surprised upon learning that Muhammad Sulaiman Qureshi was in Pakistan and he has been out on bail.

The chairman of the committee, MNA Naveed Qamar, directed officials concerned to summon the FIA director general for a better response.

Similarly, another accountant, during posting in Pakistan emb­assy in Sofia, Bulgaria, also frau­dulently withdrew 56,499 Lev and $74,415 between 2018-23. 

Audit officials expressed concern that the misappropriated public money had still not been recovered from the accountant. Furthermore, the accountant, after being dismissed from service, approached courts, which reinstated him in service.

In response to failure to recover the embezzled amount, the PAC chairman directed that officials investigating fraud should be exempted from travel bans introduced under austerity measures.

In another case pertaining to unjustified retention of heavy balance of Higher Education Commission (HEC) on account of overseas scholarship in the US, amounting to $4.5 million, the PAC expressed surprise why the funds had not been disbursed among needy students. 

“The Pakistani mission did not have clear instructions from HEC on the matter,” said Asim Iftikhar Ahmad.

In response, Mr Qamar argued that HEC should be held accountable over this. Similarly, in another matter pertaining to unauthorised borrowing of loan from HEC’s account of 360,000 euros, Mr Ahmad said that his office was in process of returning funds to the commission.

In the case of unjustified blockage of government funds in an unauthorised suspense account in Dhaka, Bangladesh, a sum of $1.143m was parked idle. Audit officials observed that holding a huge amount in suspense account without approval of the finance division was a clear violation of rules, which required settlement of inevitable payment at the earliest.

They also observed that the Pakistani mission maintaining the US dollar account in the name of suspense account for payment of rent of chancery whose ownership issue was disputed, had not been resolved yet. The PAC referred the matter to departmental accounts committee.

Published in Dawn, November 5th, 2026

articles.full_text:
US Vice President JD Vance said on Wednesday that the Iran war had doomed Republicans in the midterm elections, moving to distance himself from the unpopular conflict ahead of a possible 2028 White House run.
“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance said in a lengthy post on X — apparently referring to President Donald Trump’s remarks that the Iran war was “part of it” but that it was still justified.
“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest,” added Vance.
“But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”
    
        
    
        
    

        
    
The Democratic wave in Tuesday’s midterms has raised major questions over Vance’s previous status as the frontrunner for the Republican nomination in the 2028 presidential election. He has not yet formally declared that he will run.
Vance, a longtime vocal critic of US foreign interventionism, had reportedly been sceptical behind the scenes about the war on Iran that Trump and Israel launched in late February.
Vance also acknowledged that Republican voters who backed Trump and himself two years ago had switched sides due to the war and its effects on the US economy.
“The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026,” the vice president said.
    
            
        
    
He said a pollster that he respected showed that the Iran war and the economy were key factors in voters abandoning Republicans.
“In his polling, he saw that a lot of Trump 2024 voters were angry and planning to vote for Democrats,” Vance wrote. “He asked those voters who had abandoned us what would cause them to come back on our team. The top four answers, accounting for nearly all of the responses, were:

End the war
Focus on cost of living/inflation
Put America First
Change our relationship to Israel.”

Trump says war has been worth it despite election losses
Shortly after Vance made the post, Trump said it was “largely true” that the war caused his defeat.
    
        
    
        
    

        
    
“I think it’s largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term,” said Trump, when asked about Vance’s comment while speaking to reporters at his White House ballroom construction site.
“But at the same time, if I had it to do again, I’d have to do it again. Because long term, it’s the only answer. You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon,” he insisted.
However, the US president ruled out firing Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, a staunch proponent of the war, saying: “I think he’s doing a very good job.”
    
        
    
        
    

        
    
Meanwhile, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said that the Iran war “must end” and suggested his party’s incoming majority in Congress could use their control over government funding to press for that goal.
“The American people don’t know what the heck we’re fighting for in Iran,” Schumer tells journalists, adding that Trump has never made it clear and “changes his mind day to day, minute to minute”.
“This war must end. It must end,” Schumer added.
He later noted that the “power of the purse” is “one of the ways of deterring a president who does war without the consent of the American people”.
“Make no mistake: whenever Trump defies the will of the American people or the law, we will launch investigations, take him to court and entangle him in legislative razor wire,” Schumer warns. “The days of Trump’s supplicant Senate are over.”

articles.full_text:
Israel’s president on Wednesday opened talks on forming a new government with a call for compromise, saying neither side had won divisive elections, as he also condemned “racist” rhetoric against Arab parties that made sharp gains.
More than a week after Israel’s first election since the Oct 7, 2023 Hamas attacks, President Isaac Herzog began meeting party leaders to decide whether to give Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu or his rival Gadi Eisenkot the first chance to form a government in the deeply polarised country.
With neither bloc holding a majority in the 120-seat parliament after the Oct 27 vote, Herzog said both sides needed to accept that “not every commitment and promise can be fulfilled” and to avoid new elections.
“In the current reality, in which there is no clear winner after the elections, I ask for originality and creativity, courage and goodwill, so that the State of Israel emerges the winner,” Herzog said.
Eisenkot, who won the endorsement of a major Arab party, vowed to “deepen” the US-Israel partnership across bipartisan lines and to work with President Donald Trump to stabilise the region if selected as prime minister.
“I look forward to working closely and constructively with President Trump and his administration,” said Eisenkot, a former military chief who has vowed to turn the page on Netanyahu’s long, divisive reign.
“Together, we can advance our shared security interests, strengthen regional stability, and open new doors to prosperity for the peoples of the Middle East.”
    
        
    
        
    

        
    
His remarks follow criticism after Trump announced that he had agreed with Netanyahu to end nearly $4 billion in annual US military aid to Israel by the end of the year.
A leading Arab-Israeli party said it would recommend that Eisenkot form the next government.
“The parliamentary group of the United Arab List has decided to recommend Eisenkot to form the next government,” the party known by its Hebrew acronym Raam said in a press statement ahead of a meeting with Herzog, who is consulting with various political forces on the formation of a new government.
The election saw soaring support for lists from the Arab minority, descendants of Palestinians who stayed in Israel after its 1948 creation and who have often been outraged by the harsh rhetoric and actions of Netanyahu’s hard-right government.
Netanyahu has gone on the offensive against Arab-majority lists. He has pointed to the arrests of several people with envelopes of cash on election day in what authorities called localised incidents, and accused leaders of accepting money from Qatar, an allegation also levelled against the prime minister’s own aides.
Without naming any leader, Herzog, whose role is usually ceremonial, said he had “great respect” for the Arab minority, which makes up around 20 per cent of Israel’s population.
“I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently. There is no place for them (to be made) toward any community in Israel,” Herzog said.
No evidence found
The Central Elections Committee said it had conducted an audit of 9,069 polling stations following complaints and found no evidence that would question the results’ integrity.
The committee, which reflects the makeup of the outgoing parliament, approved the results with 15 members in favour and two against but 14 others abstaining.
Itamar Ben Gvir, the ultra-nationalist national security minister known for his provocative calls for Palestinian suffering, said his party did not accept the results and he urged the arrest of Arab-Israeli party leaders.
Several Israeli media outlets said authorities were investigating Arab lawmaker Ayman Odeh for allegedly taking foreign money. He is part of the largest Arab group, the Joint List, which in a statement denounced “political persecution”.
Eisenkot, a former military chief who has vowed to turn the page on Netanyahu’s long, divisive reign, accused the prime minister of trying to “undermine Israeli democracy” and inflame sentiment against elected officials.
“We will not allow the State of Israel to be dragged into a dark abyss, far beyond the bounds of democratic conduct,” Eisenkot said, as he marked the 1995 assassination of prime minister Yitzhak Rabin.
Buoyed by US elections
Eisenkot has warned Netanyahu against launching a new war with his ally Trump against Iran, which could help the Israeli prime minister push for a unity government or to run out the clock until new elections.
    
            
        
    
Opposition lawmakers said Tuesday’s midterm elections in the United States, in which Democrats trounced Trump’s Republicans, reinforced the need to remove Netanyahu.
Democrats have vowed a tougher line on Israel amid outrage over the devastation wrought by the assault on Gaza. Trump said as voting was underway that he had agreed with Netanyahu to end nearly $4 billion in annual US military aid to Israel by the end of the year.
“The continued tenure of Netanyahu and Ben Gvir could lead Israel down a path of international sanctions, international isolation and a clash with the US, our friend and most important ally,” said Yair Golan, who heads the most left-wing party within the opposition bloc.
Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister who has been in power on and off for nearly two decades, has called for a “broad national government” — with himself at the top. He faces corruption charges that could land him in jail if he leaves office.
Herzog’s statements have raised speculation that he could sound out leaders on a possible unity government, but Eisenkot and his allies have ruled that out.
Herzog will hold an initial two days of consultations and then give a contender 28 days to form a government, with a potential 14-day extension.
It took Netanyahu, who at the time had a better showing by Likud, 58 days to form a government after the last election in November 2022.
Israel held five elections between 2019 and 2022 after repeated deadlocks.

articles.full_text:
Opposition leaders on Wednesday gathered at the residence of Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman in Islamabad and agreed to strengthen their alliance and parliamentary coordination.
After a meeting during which they discussed several matters, including the emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, JUI-F and TTAP decided to form committees to resolve mutual differences and take forward consultations on a multi-party conference (MPC).
National Assembly (NA) and Senate opposition leaders, Mahmood Khan Achakzai and Allama Raja Nasir Abbas, respectively, attended the meeting. MNA Asad Qaiser, PTI Secretary General Salman Akram Raja, NA Chief Whip Amir Dogar and Senator Noorul Haq Qadri were present from PTI.
Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-i-Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP) — headed by Achakzai — termed it a meeting of a “united opposition”.
An earlier statement by JUI-F said the gathering was to discuss “the situation of emergency and governor’s rule” in KP, as well as plans for an MPC.
    
        
    
        
    

        
    
In its statement, TTAP said the meeting was also “discussing unity and solidarity among opposition parties, the supremacy of the Constitution and law, the protection of democratic rights, a joint strategy to address the current political situation, and a future course of action”.
On Aug 20, following a meeting between Fazl and Achakzai, the alliance and JUI-F had announced plans to form a “united opposition”.
    
        
    
        
    

        
    
Speaking to the media after the meeting, Achakzai said the delegation had called on Fazl with the objective of building an alliance to strengthen Parliament.
He condemned what he described as a character assassination campaign against the JUI-F chief and declared that the opposition stood firmly with him.
He added that the possibility of convening an MPC was also discussed during the meeting.
    
        
    
        
    

        
    
In his remarks, Fazl also said the opposition would work to strengthen its presence in Parliament and protect the interests of every part of the country.
Referring to the former Federally Administered Tribal Areas (Fata), he said his party had opposed the 2018 merger, adding that the issue was now being linked to a struggle over resources.
He also expressed concern over what he alleged were attempts to bring Gwadar, the coastal belt and Sindh’s islands under federal control.
The JUI-F chief said the opposition had already represented the people’s concerns regarding the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in KP, stressing that it was speaking about the public mandate and national interests.
The leaders agreed to continue consultations and establish a committee to address differences among opposition parties.
    
        
    
        
    

        
    
Senator Abbas alleged that the governor’s rule had been illegally imposed in KP and accused the authorities of targeting those who raised their voices for the country’s welfare.
On its part, the Centre maintains that the security situation in the province and the PTI-led provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the counterterrorism fight “compelled” it to take the measures on Oct 11.
Addressing reporters, the Senate opposition leader lamented that the sanctity of homes and the privacy of citizens were being violated as authorities detained people from their residences.
He warned of decreasing public confidence in the country’s institutions, claiming Pakistan had reached one of the worst periods in its history.
    
        
    
        
    

        
    
TTAP said its spokesperson Akhundzada Hussain Ahmad Yousafzai, PTI founder Imran Khan’s legal counsel Khalid Yousaf Chaudhry, and Agha Nasir Shirazi also attended the meeting.
The JUI-F team included its vice-president and KP chapter president Senator Maulana Attaur Rehman, senators Kamran Murtaza and Maulana Attaul Haq Darwish, alongside party members Akram Khan Durrani, Aslam Ghauri, Maulana Salahuddin Ayubi, Hafiz Hamdullah and Zahid Durrani.
    
        
    
        
    

        
    
PTI alarmed over Imran’s ‘high blood pressure’
Meanwhile, PTI’s Raja raised concerns about Imran’s health, saying his blood pressure was not under control. He thanked Fazl for supporting the PTI and alleged that the JUI-F chief was being “punished” for standing with the party.
Imran — in prison since Aug 5, 2023 in multiple cases — had complained of uncontrolled and fluctuating blood pressure along with palpitations, headache and restlessness in early August, according to annexures attached to a jail report submitted to the Supreme Court (SC).
    
        
    
        
    

        
    
In an official statement issued today, PTI expressed grave concern over its founder’s health, saying his blood pressure had surged to 192. It demanded his immediate transfer to Shifa International Hospital for independent medical treatment under the supervision of his personal physicians.
PTI Central Information Secretary Sheikh Waqas Akram said repeated fluctuations in the ex-cricketer’s blood pressure were a matter of extreme concern, stressing that protecting his health was the responsibility of the state.
He accused the government of denying Imran adequate medical facilities, family access and treatment of his choice.
He demanded immediate implementation of the SC’s Aug 18 order directing Imran’s transfer to Shifa International Hospital, with treatment supervised by his personal and family-appointed doctors.
Imran’s eye ailment — right central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) — came to light in late January. While he has undergone eye procedures and check-ups at the government-run Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims), his family demands that he be shifted to a hospital of his choice.
    
            
        
    
The government and the opposition have been engaged in a blame game, with the latter accusing the former of a lack of transparency on the matter, of not ensuring appropriate treatment for Imran, and of not allowing his personal physicians access to him.
The government denies these allegations, saying the required medical treatment is being ensured and ample facilities are being provided at the Adiala jail, including a healthy diet plan and exercise equipment.
Fazl’s PTI ties amid row with Centre
Wednesday’s gathering came a day after PTI said it would welcome support from Fazl in its struggle against the government, with Raja telling the media that the party would welcome anyone who stood by it and supported its struggle.
“It is possible that some may walk with us for one mile, some for 10 miles, and some may go with us till the end. But why should we reject them?” the PTI secretary general said.
Fazl has been critical of the federal government over the imposition of governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. He accused the Centre of reneging on its commitments amid his efforts to mediate between the federal and KP governments.
Since mid-October, the veteran politician and key federal ministers have also made harsh remarks against each other, after Fazl accused the Centre of depriving the provinces of their rights.
Last week, Fazl accused the government of misusing the Constitution and resorting to unconstitutional measures in imposing the emergency.
In September, TTAP and PTI leaders said they intended to hold consultations to call an MPC to discuss several issues, including the creation of new provinces, law and order, and the economy. This was prior to the government’s declaration of emergency and governor’s rule in KP on Oct 11.
In the days preceding the emergency, political tensions between the Centre and the opposition — including the PTI, which was in power in KP — had remained high since Imran’s party announced a protest march to Islamabad to demand his release.
